Pentagon awards RTX’s Raytheon $26.4 billion contract for AMRAAM missiles amid stockpile concerns
- The Pentagon awarded RTX’s Raytheon a $26.4 billion contract to speed up AMRAAM missile production amid concerns over depleted stockpiles from Middle East and Ukraine conflicts.
- AMRAAM missiles support air-to-air combat and air defence systems like NASAMS, used by the US and over a dozen allied countries, including Ukraine and Qatar.
- The deal aims to increase output as part of the "Arsenal of Freedom" initiative, with RTX planning to produce at least 1,900 missiles annually from 2026, pending Congressional funding.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - The Pentagon awarded RTX’s Raytheon business a provisional multiyear contract worth US$20.7 billion (S$26.44 billion) to accelerate production of AMRAAM missiles, as the military pushes to replenish stockpiles depleted by conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine.
The US has supplied large quantities of weapons to allies while also using munitions in its own military operations in Iran, raising concerns about inventories of key air defence and precision-guided weapons.
The AMRAAM is used in air-to-air jet fighter combat as well as in the National Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile System (NASAMS), which is used to defend the Washington area and is used by more than a dozen other countries, including Ukraine, Oman and Qatar.
The prospective AMRAAM deal is the latest in a series of large munitions contracts the Pentagon has pursued this year to pressure contractors into ramping output up faster.
The award follows a similar pattern to a US$58.6 billion Patriot interceptor deal awarded to Lockheed Martin in July, a seven-year procurement plan running through fiscal 2032.
As with that contract, industry executives have cautioned that Congress has not yet appropriated the funding needed to support the full multiyear commitment, meaning contractors may be unable to invest at scale in components and facilities until lawmakers act.
The production agreements are designed to entice contractors to move faster on increasing output, part of a broader push by the Trump administration to prioritise weapons production over shareholder returns.
The contract, if Congress ultimately appropriates the funds, would let RTX continue to invest in its workforce, supply chain and facilities as US demand surges.
The company said it nearly doubled AMRAAM production in 2025, compared with the prior year.
The deal would be part of the Pentagon’s “Arsenal of Freedom” initiative.
RTX said earlier in 2026 it would set an annual production goal of at least 1,900 AMRAAM missiles. REUTERS

In the US-China AI race, the real fight is keeping humans in control
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
21:30:12 UTC
06:30:12 KST

In the US-China AI race, the real fight is keeping humans in control
A crisis hotline is a start, but the deeper task is setting clear boundaries between human authority and machine autonomy – while we still hold the reins
The US-China AI competition faces a dilemma. Both countries see artificial intelligence as a source of economic, scientific and strategic power, so neither has much incentive to slow down. Yet the more capable and autonomous AI becomes, the more important the question of human control.
This is more than a disagreement over regulation. It reveals a deeper dilemma facing both powers. Competition rewards faster deployment and greater delegation to machines. Control requires limits, monitoring and the ability to intervene. The same systems that increase national power can therefore make human authority harder to preserve as AI becomes more autonomous.
Conventional geopolitics treats AI mainly as an instrument: the US builds better systems, China builds better systems and each side uses them to advance human-defined objectives. But what happens when the instrument can act for sustained periods without continuous human direction? AI could then become an independent agent in international politics, not merely a tool used by states.

Key Event
Another RBA rate rise could push home ownership further out of reach, according to one expert
An interest rate hike today could further reduce borrowing capacity, making home ownership harder to achieve for many Australians, according to Domain's Chief Residential Economist, Dr Nicola Powell.
"Every increase in interest rates reduces the amount buyers can borrow, limiting what they can afford to pay and pushing some aspiring homeowners out of the market altogether," she says.
"For many, that means delaying their plans while they save a larger deposit or work to meet stricter lending requirements."
Higher interest rates may also slow the delivery of new housing as building approvals remain subdued, and residential construction is increasingly competing with major infrastructure, renewable energy and data-centre projects for the same labour and materials.
All of this, according to Dr Powell, makes it harder and more costly to bring new homes to market.
"The bigger challenge is what higher rates could mean for future housing supply," she says.
"Australia's construction industry only has so much capacity. As labour and materials are drawn into other major projects, it becomes harder and more expensive to bring new housing developments to market.
"The risk is that today's fight against inflation becomes tomorrow's housing shortage. Higher rates may help cool demand in the short term, but they can also make it harder to increase housing supply and address Australia's long-term housing shortfall."
Key Event
A hike by the RBA is needed to 'maintain credibility', according to one analyst
In order to maintain credibility, the RBA will have to hike today, according to RBC BlueBay Asset Management's Malin Rosengren.
"They held rates unchanged in August on the concession that if any upside risks to inflation materialise verse their expectations, they will have to respond," she says.
July inflation data indicates both headline and trimmed-mean inflation remain elevated, and while the labour market loosened modestly, Rosengren says it doesn’t seem enough to soften demand.
"At this point it should appear evident to the RBA that policy is not yet restrictive enough. If they fail to hike at the September meeting, the market will turn to price in more inflation premia across the curve as the bank’s credibility will be tarnished," she says.
"A September hike will make another tightening step in November near unavoidable. The November meeting will include updated economic forecasts, where projections for inflation and growth are sure to be lifted over the horizon & suggest further tightening is required."
On the positive, Rosengren says two more hikes to a policy rate of 4.85% should be restrictive enough to "get the job done" for the RBA.
"Tightening will increasingly feed into the real economy, working with a significant lag, and eventually become more material in the data (though of course much depends on energy prices and the external environment)," she says.

Key Event
Rate hikes leave borrowers hundreds of dollars poorer
A 25-basis-point increase in the cash rate would add $91 a month on a typical $600,000 mortgage, said Sally Tindall, data insights director at financial comparison site Canstar.
"The true pain is in the cumulative impact,'' she said.
"Across what is likely to be at least four rate rises for the year, this borrower has to fork out an extra $364 a month compared to what they were paying at the start of the year."
The difference since October 2011 - the last time rates were that high - is that soaring house prices have resulted in home loan debt rising from $1.05 trillion to $2.51 trillion over the same period, Ms Tindall said.
Mortgage holders are set to shoulder hundreds of dollars more in monthly repayments compared to the start of the year, with interest rates expected to hit a 15-year high.
At 4.6%, the cash rate is set to be the highest experienced by a generation of borrowers.
That will lift the average owner-occupier variable rate to 6.49%, assuming the increase is fully passed on by lenders, which they usually are.
With the Middle East conflict and the artificial intelligence boom pushing up prices for commodities and technology components respectively, the Reserve Bank board has seemingly lost patience and is willing to inflict greater costs on the economy and unemployment to get inflation down.
Comments by RBA governor Michele Bullock that unemployment needed to be between 4.5 and 5.0% to help get inflation back under control were met with a furious response from union groups and the social service sector.
"Raising interest rates is creating unemployment by design, putting thousands of people out of work to slow the economy," Australian Council of Social Service chief executive Cassandra Goldie said.
"Since interest rates started to increase, an extra 200,000 people are out of paid work.
"Increasing unemployment towards five per cent would cause a human disaster, locking people out of paid work for years and forcing them to rely on grossly inadequate income support payments."
Treasurer Jim Chalmers also pushed back on Ms Bullock's comments.
"What we have seen is that it's possible in this country to have lower unemployment than (five per cent) at the same time as inflation comes off," he told reporters on Monday.
"We have an inflation challenge in our economy not because unemployment is too low but because the price of petrol is too high and we've got other inflationary pressures in our economy.
"I'm reluctant to blame the workers of this country for our inflation challenge."

Air Force, Industry Fears Continuing Resolution Could Hinder CCA Production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
21:22:36 UTC
06:22:36 KST

The Air Force’s emerging Collaborative Combat Aircraft program would suffer delays if Congress fails to pass a budget before the end of this calendar year, a top service official said Sept. 28.
Brig. Gen. Timothy Helfrich, the portfolio acquisition executive for fighters and advanced aircraft, said the program is ready for production, but advancing to that next stage requires a new budget. “You can’t go do production without production funding,” he said during a Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies appearance. “So that does provide limitations on what we can execute.”
CCAs are the semi-autonomous drone fighters the Air Force believes can bolster its manned fighter force. The first two models—General Atomics Aeronautical Systems’ FQ-42A Vengeance and Anduril Systems’ FQ-44A Fury—are designed for air-to-air strike missions. The objective is for the compact uncrewed CCAs to cost less than $20 million apiece for the airframe, and to rapidly grow the force to include at least 500 in 2032, on its way to at least 1,000 later on.
Fiscal 2027 starts Oct. 1, but Congress failed to pass a budget before taking its reccess, instead passing a funding measure that extends until Dec. 11 appropriations at 2026 levels. Under such a continuing resolution, new programs, such as CCA production, are not authorized. If Congress fails to pass a budget the government could be forced to shut down. Congress could also vote to extend the CR for a month or more at that time.
Helfrich’s comments echoed concerns raised by Anduril officials at the Air & Space Forces Association’s Air, Space and Cyber conference in National Harbor, Md., Sept. 14.
Erin Simpson, Anduril’s vice president of strategy execution for air dominance and strike, told reporters in a briefing that the company has worked to get a head start on procurement, including by building a new Arsenal-1 factory in Columbus, Ohio, buying parts in advance, and producing prototype Fury CCAs.
“We will not have a cold start to [launch] production in ’27,” Simpson said. “We will have assets rolling through. That said, even a company like ours can only do so much without procurement dollars.”
When asked about the CR’s potential effect on General Atomics’ production, a company spokesman pointed to a Sept. 21 release that said it is taking on risk by self-funding some of the first FQ-42s, to keep the program moving forward while the Pentagon’s funding is worked out.
“Production of FQ-42 Vengeance is underway on company investment as government funding plans mature, with GA-ASI continuing its longstanding tradition of working at-risk with its own funds to support U.S. procurement planning and prevent delays in delivery,” General Atomics’ statement said. GA-ASI plans to build multiple fighters for its own company aircraft fleet, to invest in inventing new technologies that reduce risk and increase capabilities for its global customers.”
Helfrich said the Air Force’s upcoming Emerald Flag exercise in December at Eglin Air Force Base, Fla., will be a significant demonstration of how far CCAs have come. And it will further the work done by the Air Force’s Experimental Operations Unit to figure out how best to use CCAs in operational environments, and how to operate it under the Agile Combat Employment construct of flying aircraft out of dispersed, small and rough airfields in a future conflict.
“Setting up for Emerald Flag, it’s all hands on deck, but the EOU is central to making that happen,” Helfrich said. “They’re at the heart of taking a capability and making it into something that we can actually integrate into the Air Force.”
Both initial CCA models will fly at Emerald Flag alongside different manned fighters, he said, possibly with multiple CCAs flying at once.
The Air Force announced in July that Anduril’s Fury CCA had fired its first live missile in a test. General Atomics’ Vengeance will soon follow, Helfrich said. Helfrich indicated that test fire would likely happen before Emerald Flag.
General Atomics spokesman C. Mark Brinkley declined to say exactly when the first FQ-42A live-fire test may take place, saying only that it would happen by the end of the year.
Helfrich said the FQ-42A’s live-fire test will focus on more than just launching the missile, and will be a test run of the entire process for firing weapons with an autonomous system, while still keeping a human “on the loop.”
“The human has to make the decision to use lethal force, and then go and engage on that target,” Helfrich said. “So we’re talking more like. Kill chain than we are about [a standard weapon firing] exercise.”

Ukraine trains military orphans to ‘replace fallen fathers’ – WaPo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
21:17:13 UTC
06:17:13 KST

Ukraine trains military orphans to ‘replace fallen fathers’ – WaPo
The Ukrainian government has set up five boarding schools for children whose parents were killed, went missing, or were left disabled in the conflict with Russia, preparing them for careers in the country’s military service, The Washington Post has reported.
The newspaper gained access to one of the institutions for a report published on Monday, describing the two-year boarding schools as “part grief counseling and part boot camp,” effectively sealing the fate of the vulnerable children.
“[The] school puts them into a funnel toward the Ukrainian security services that are desperate for recruits, along with hundreds of other cadets at new government academies devoted to the still-young children of fallen fighters,” the article reads.
The children are also being prepared for “university entrance exams in their second year” and are required to complete a degree even if they choose to enter service. School staff insisted that “no pressure” be put on the cadets to pursue such careers, the Post noted.
The Ukrainian military needs some 30,000 fresh recruits per month just to maintain its current force size, the Post noted, citing Ukrainian officials. “Officially, Ukraine reports that about 55,000 have been killed in the war and about 114,000 are missing. But aid providers say those figures don’t begin to reflect the number of children who have lost at least one parent,” the article reads.
Independent casualty estimates, however, differ drastically from the official Ukrainian figures, with the US-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating that Ukrainian forces have suffered between 525,000 and 625,000 casualties, including those killed, wounded, and missing.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk recently said that the Ukrainian military was suffering 27,000 casualties a month.
Kiev has long struggled to replenish its ranks through forced conscription, with its mobilization effort growing increasingly chaotic and violent over the course of the conflict.
The mobilization campaign, dubbed ‘busification,’ has often involved draft officers ambushing military-age men on the streets, at workplaces, and outside their homes, using violence against those resisting or attempting to flee. The draft has sparked several protests and riots across the country, which the authorities have dismissed as “helping the enemy.”
The involvement of children in paramilitary training has been on the rise in Ukraine since the 2014 Western-backed Euromaidan coup, with the process accelerating further in the wake of the full-blown conflict with Russia. The idea of lowering age thresholds for such training and, potentially, for active service has been repeatedly floated by various public figures. Moreover, boot camps for children have frequently been set up by openly neo-Nazi groups, with basic training going hand in hand with hateful indoctrination at such facilities.

Netanyahu asked UAE leader to deny he warned Israel before October 7 attack, report says
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29

06:13:33 KST

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu asked UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan to deny reports that he had warned Netanyahu of a Hamas attack shortly before October 7, 2023, during a meeting in Abu Dhabi on Sunday, according to the Associated Press.
The AP cited a person with first-hand knowledge of the meeting and a regional official briefed on the talks. Both spoke anonymously because the visit had not been announced in advance.
The UAE confirmed that the leaders met and said they discussed bilateral relations and ways to develop them. Emirati authorities did not confirm the reported request concerning the October 7 warning.
The meeting lasted about an hour, according to the AP. Israel's Channel 12 first reported Netanyahu's trip.
The visit followed a September investigation by Haaretz which reported that Mohamed bin Zayed called Netanyahu about 10 days before the Hamas-led attack and warned that then-Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was preparing a major operation.
Haaretz reported that the UAE president urged Netanyahu to take the threat seriously and raised measures aimed at reducing tensions in Gaza and the West Bank.
Netanyahu's office has rejected the account. It said Netanyahu did not speak with the UAE president during the period in question and received no such warning. Netanyahu has threatened legal action against Haaretz, while the newspaper has said it stands by its reporting.
The Associated Press reported on Monday that Netanyahu asked Mohamed bin Zayed during Sunday's meeting to deny the account
The UAE Foreign Ministry has declined to address reports about conversations between the leaders. In a statement earlier this month, it said the UAE and Israel maintain direct communication and share relevant intelligence through the appropriate agencies.
Recent reports have also focused on Israel receiving warnings from Egypt before the October 7 attack. The Wall Street Journal reported that former Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel contacted Netanyahu days before the attack about signs of an assault from Gaza. The Atlantic separately reported that Kamel travelled to Israel on September 26, 2023, and raised concerns that Hamas was preparing an attack.
Netanyahu has denied receiving such warnings from Kamel. In a statement on Monday, he said he neither met nor spoke with the Egyptian intelligence chief in the months before October 7 and said Israeli intelligence had not passed an Egyptian warning to him.
Reports of Egyptian warnings first emerged shortly after the attack. In October 2023, US Congressman Michael McCaul said after a congressional briefing that Egypt had warned Israel several days beforehand that an event of that nature was possible.
The latest reports have surfaced weeks before Israel's October parliamentary election, placing renewed attention on the government's handling of intelligence before the attack.
The UAE and Israel established diplomatic relations under the Abraham Accords in 2020 and have since developed ties in trade, security and other areas.

Airmen, Guardians Told to Select Religion Code from New Consolidated List
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
21:06:40 UTC
06:06:40 KST

Active-Duty Airmen and Guardians have until mid-October to update their personnel records with their religious preference using the Pentagon’s new consolidated list of Religious Affiliation Codes, according to a recent Department of the Air Force announcement.
The new list of codes—ordered by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth—slashed the number of religions specified in the Pentagon’s HR systems from more than 200 to roughly 30. Officials said in June that the consolidation was necessary to streamline the number of religious preferences for service members and shape the chaplain corps to support them.
The consolidation process collapsed roughly 170 denominations of Christianity down to 21 and includes widespread non-Christian religions such as Buddhism, Hindu, Islam, and Judaism, among other faiths. It removes Wicca, paganism, and other nontraditional faiths from the list, replacing them with an “Other Religious” category.
The department directs all Active-Duty members of the Air Force and Space Force to select their new Religious Affiliation Code in the Virtual Military Personnel Flight system and certify their record of emergency data is accurate by Oct. 16, the announcement states. Members of the Air Force Reserve and Air National Guard have until Nov. 9 to update their records.
“Transitioning to these standardized codes ensures our chaplain corps has the accurate demographic data they need to provide tailored resources and support to our service members, while continuing to respect their individual convictions,” Richard Anderson, assistant secretary of the Air Force for manpower and reserve affairs, said in the announcement.
Airmen and Guardians who fail to update their RAC before the deadline will have their records automatically updated to a selection that aligns with the new RAC list. For example, paganism would likely fall under the “Other Religions” category, according to an Air Force official.
Individual Airmen and Guardians, however, will not be limited by the new RAC list for the purposes of identifying their religious preference on the ID tags or “dog tags” they wear around their necks. The tags can be vital for helping chaplains determine the religious needs of service members wounded in battle.
Hegseth announced the effort to consolidate the list of religious preferences in a March 24 video on social media, calling the older list of Faith and Belief Codes “impractical and unusable.” Hegseth also directed chaplains to replace their rank insignia with their appropriate religious affiliation insignia in an effort to make them more approachable to younger service members. The announcement came six months after Hegseth singled out paganism in September 2025 because some troops have petitioned for religious exemptions so they could grow beards.
“If you want a beard, you can join Special Forces,” Heseth told hundreds of general officers at Quantico, Va., last Sept. 30. “If not, then shave. We don’t have a military full of Nordic pagans, but unfortunately, we have had leaders who either refuse to call BS and enforce standards, or leaders who felt like they were not allowed to enforce standards.”
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell has argued the new consolidated RAC list is not intended to provide a list of “officially approved” religions. Rather it is “designed to allow chaplains to quickly look at the religious composition of their units and determine how they structure resources to best provide for warfighters of all faith groups,” Parnell wrote in a June 5 social media post.
The Pentagon did not provide the older list of Faith and Belief codes for comparison, but Airmen and Guardians can compare the 2026 codes list to an older list taken from a March 2017 memo from the Armed Forces Chaplains Board:

06:04:22 KST

The Space Force is starting a new competition to bolster its network of antennas that track and manage Pentagon and other U.S. government satellites—and this time, acquisition officials are open to leasing commercial systems or even paying for commercial antennas as a service.
In a Sept. 24 notice, the Space Force and the Missile Defense Agency announced they are resetting the Satellite Communications Augmentation Resource program with a “Commercial Solutions Opening.” Instead of providing a list of detailed requirements, these openings define “areas of interest,” inviting vendors to pitch ideas based on commercially available technology.
The SCAR program is the Space Force’s effort to “revitalize” its Cold War-era Satellite Control Network, a collection of 19 antennas dispersed around the globe that track and maneuver satellites and collect data about their health and status. The service awarded and later canceled a $1.4 billion contract for Blue Halo, now part of AeroVironment, to build and deliver 12 multibeam, phased-array antennas for SCAR.
After cancelling that deal in March, officials explained they wanted to leverage commercial technology rather than acquire a bespoke, Space Force-centric design. This latest announcement offers more details on the approch, detailing three “areas of interest” for the SCAR program:
- A government-owned, contractor-operated model using commercial systems
- Long-term, exclusive government leases of commercially owned and operated systems
- “Antenna as a Service” giving the government access to commercial systems that could also be used by other customers
Each area of interest has benefits and drawbacks, the announcement states. Government-owned often means “bespoke technical solutions, Government-led maintenance,” and limited funding, officials wrote. Leasing or antenna-as-a-service carries security concerns, including “cyber risks that must be mitigated, such as multi-tenant data leakage, scheduling conflicts, and software interoperability bottlenecks.”
But the announcement lays out why Space Force leaders are eager to avoid rerunning the usual acquisition playbook.
“Space operations demand global, high-frequency satellite passes, yet owning and operating a globally distributed physical network is financially burdensome,” the announcement states. “Shifting to commercial ‘shared’ networks alleviates the need to establish dozens of Government-owned sites or dedicated leases.”
The current Satellite Control Network antennas can maintain contact with only one satellite at a time and not for very long. The network’s capacity is under strain as the Pentagon and other government agencies put up more and more spacecraft. According to a 2023 Government Accountability Office report, utilization rates have already been higher than the industry standard for the past decade, and Space Force leaders are expecting the number of satellites on orbit to greatly expand in the coming years.
Companies interested in SCAR have until Oct. 15 to submit white papers. The program office will then select one or more to move to a second phase of consideration.

RAF Fairford: AI-enhanced photos of suspects fuel false claims about their religion
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
Five men arrested over a suspected bomb plot at RAF Fairford have been released on bail as investigations continue. Meanwhile, AI-enhanced images purporting to show their faces have gone viral, with some users claiming it ‘proves’ the men are Muslim. SynthID confirms the sharpened images were created using OpenAI tools, meaning the AI has suggested different facial features. UK police have not disclosed any names or religion, only that the men are all British nationals. Vedika Bahl explains.
Five men arrested over a suspected bomb plot at RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire have been released on bail as the investigation continues.
The arrests sparked a wave of speculation online, fuelled by images purporting to show the suspects’ faces at the time of their arrest. But the images circulating on social media have been enhanced using artificial intelligence.
The men, who were arrested on suspicion of terror offences, were photographed being apprehended near the base. The original image is grainy and blurry, with the men shirtless and handcuffed though no faces are clearly disce. Several social media users have since shared sharpened versions of the photograph, claiming the images reveal the men’s faces.
However, the sharpened, refined photo contains a SynthID watermark, indicating that the image was modified using OpenAI tools.
A second AI-enhanced image showing the men being detained has also circulated online. The two versions show noticeably different facial features, and lighting highlighting the limitations of using AI to enhance blurry photographs.
Despite this, the altered images have been widely shared. Two posts on X containing one of the images have amassed almost two million views, with some users falsely presenting it as evidence that the five men are Muslim.
In reality, there is currently no publicly available information about the suspects’ religion. Authorities have identified the five men as British nationals from London, aged between 23 and 25.
AI image-enhancement tools can generate details that are not present in the original image. Whilst internet users may have tried to refine the grainy image to see the men's faces more clearly, AI does not know what the original face looks like, leaving it to effectively guess or invent facial characteristics that do not actually exist.

Six U.S. Air Force F-35A fighters and 200-plus Airmen deployed to India on Sept. 26 for their first appearance in a large-scale exercise on Indian soil.
Exercise Tarang Shakti will run from Sept. 26 to Oct. 12, according to the Indian Air Force, with eight countries contributing aircraft. First held in 2024, the exercise is India’s largest multinational aerial training event.
U.S. Ambassador to India Sergio Gor and Pacific Air Forces confirmed the arrival of the F-35s and released images of them at Jodhpur Air Force Station. The aircraft are from the 13th Fighter Squadron at Misawa Air Base, Japan.

In 2024, the Air Force sent A-10s to Tarang Shakti in 2024, and USAF has sent F-15s and F-16s to participate in previous editions of Cope India, a major joint air combat exercise.
The U.S. and Indian air forces have built up their interaction in recent years. A B-1 bomber landed in India for the first time for Aero India in 2021, then returned for its first exercise at Cope India 2023. Last year, President Donald Trump suggested the U.S. might eventually sell F-35s to India, but little has been said on that topic since.
On the flip side of U.S.-India relations, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has also worked to build ties with Russia and China. Modi met with Russia’s Vladimir Putin and Chinese Premier Xi Jinping earlier this month at the BRICS (Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa) summit, at which he stressed better relations with both Russia and China.
The Indian Air Force has an eclectic mix of aircraft, including indigenous HAL Tejas light combat aircraft, Russian Su-30s, French Rafales and Mirage 2000s, American C-17s, and more. Russia has also pitched its new Su-57 fighter to India—the Su-57 and F-35 were both at Aero India in 2025.

In France, the largest forest fire since 1949 was completely extinguished after two months

The fire in southwestern France destroyed 37,296 hectares and forced 224,000 people to evacuate. More than 3,300 firefighters fought it.
A massive forest fire in southwestern France, which broke out in July and became the largest in the country since 1949, has been fully extinguished. Yle reports this, citing AFP, writes UNN.
Details
The fire was brought under control as early as August 1, but it continued to smolder underground for several weeks. More than 3,300 firefighters were involved in fighting the blaze.
According to the French authorities, the firefighting operation was the largest in the modern history of the country's civil protection service. The fire destroyed 37,296 hectares of land, while the total area affected by the blaze reached approximately 42,000 hectares.
More than 200,000 people evacuated
The fire broke out near the village of Saumos in the Gironde department. The blaze threatened the Cap Ferret peninsula, popular with tourists, and the areas surrounding Bordeaux.
Because of the fire, approximately 224,000 people were forced to evacuate. Despite the scale of the disaster, there were no fatalities.
The last time France experienced a larger forest fire was in 1949, when approximately 50,000 hectares burned in the same region. According to preliminary data, fires have already destroyed approximately 98,000 hectares in France this year—the highest figure since 1976.

NASA announces plans to revive Boeing’s troubled Starliner spacecraft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
20:43:23 UTC
05:43:23 KST

After a failed maiden crewed voyage, Boeing’s Starliner is getting another shot at flying NASA’s astronauts to space.
At a press conference on Monday NASA administrator Jared Isaacman said the space capsule will head to the International Space Station (ISS) on an uncrewed test flight as soon as December—a technical step back for the multi-billion-dollar initiative.
The troubled Starliner hasn’t flown since its unsuccessful crewed mission in 2024. In that test, after several scrubbed launches, the vessel, named Calypso, carried astronauts Butch Wilmore and Suni Williams to the ISS for what was supposed to be an eight-day stay. But helium leaks and malfunctioning thrusters raised safety concerns, leading NASA to decide Williams and Wilmore could not return to Earth onboard Calypso.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The empty spacecraft did eventually make it back to Earth in one piece. Wilmore and Williams, however, ended up spending 286 days on the ISS before they returned in a SpaceX Dragon capsule.
In a report released in February, NASA said the botched mission resulted from several failures. There were issues with the ship’s design and engineering, particularly with the thrusters, but the report concluded that the biggest cause was lax NASA oversight of Boeing, a lack of data transparency with vital personnel and poor decision-making.
A number of changes have been made to Starliner’s design in the wake of Calypso, including alterations to seal designs, as well as the thruster system. Those changes will be put through their paces during the upcoming uncrewed mission, and data will be collected to “validate the recent remediation efforts,” Isaacman said on Monday. If that goes well, a Starliner vehicle could carry out a crewed mission sometime in 2028 under the command of NASA astronaut Woody Hoburg.
“He’s an absolutely brilliant guy who’s helping on a lot of our ignition priorities, and I am confident his experience will serve this mission incredibly well,” Isaacman said of Hoburg.
Another major change will be the rocket that will loft Starliner to space. Starliner originally flew onboard United Launch Alliance’s (ULA’s) Atlas V rocket, but the vehicle is no longer in production. Instead, Isaacman said, NASA plans to use ULA’s Vulcan Centaur heavy-lift rocket for future Starliner missions.
As things stand, NASA wants Starliner to work. Isaacman and other NASA officials at the press conference emphasized the fact that there is only one operational crew capsule, SpaceX’s Crew Dragon, that can ferry NASA astronauts to and from orbit. Elon Musk’s firm hasn’t been shy about wanting to sunset the Falcon 9 rocket that launches Crew Dragon, as well as the capsule, in favor of developing its Starship megarockets. At the same time, Isaacman said, having some redundancy and more options available for crewed missions is preferable when considering the needs of a thriving space economy.
Isaacman stressed that, at this point, there are no other contenders to supply capsules for missions to the ISS and that SpaceX and Boeing will be the only options for the foreseeable future.
“One of them is serving our needs very well,” Isaacman said. “The other one we’ve been committed to getting operational.”

peripheral vision and artwork that exceeds the eye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
20:35:43 UTC
05:35:43 KST

This article is part of designboom’s SPECTATOR AND SPECTACLE chapter, asking how wonder gets built, presented in partnership with SolidNature, and how it might return some mystery to a world that has measured most of it away. Discover more stories that turn onlookers into participants, alter perception and disrupt the everyday here.
peripheral vision and artwork that exceeds the eye
these artists make seeing everything at once impossible, and use that limit as material.
[ADVERTISEMENT]
when an artwork becomes too large for the eye
There is a familiar way of looking at art. Most of us tend to stand back, face the work, and take in the whole image. We can see it happen at any museum. There have been, however, some fascinating experiments across twentieth-century art and exhibition design which begin by making that position fail.
Mark Rothko enlarged fields of color until they could exceed the viewer’s central field of vision. Herbert Bayer mapped images above and around the eye. The Eameses arrayed thousands of photographs across seven screens at once, and Lina Bo Bardi pulled paintings away from the wall altogether. Across very different media, the same question still stands: what does art become when there is more to see than one viewpoint can contain?
Peripheral vision marks the edge of attention. We perceive color and movement beyond our line of sight, but detail begins to fall away. An artwork that extends into and beyond this territory behaves in a way that’s unique. Its edges become harder to hold at once, or other images enter behind it. Looking becomes physical, and involves distance, turning, and movement through space. The artwork can remain completely still while the viewer becomes active.
rothko makes scale intimate
Mark Rothko understood scale through proximity. His large canvases were never intended simply as monumental pictures to admire from across a gallery. Writing in 1949, he explained that he painted large because he wanted the experience to remain ‘very intimate and human.’ A small picture could be surveyed from outside, he argued, while a larger one places the viewer within the experience. ‘However you paint the larger picture, you are in it,‘ he wrote.
The idea becomes physical once we stand close to one of the large dark red canvases of the Seagram Murals, for instance. A wash of color extends far beyond our field of vision and we become immersed in a new, atmospheric world of total red. Rothko even specified that his largest pictures should be encountered at close range. The scale works through a strange inversion: the painting grows enormous so the distance between object and viewer can shrink.
barnett newman asks the viewer to come closer
Barnett Newman’s Vir Heroicus Sublimis, painted in 1950–51, stretches nearly eighteen feet across. Five narrow vertical bands, which Newman called ‘zips,’ interrupt an expanse of red. From across the room, the painting resolves fairly easily into a rectangle with a compositional structure. Newman wanted another encounter. He hoped viewers would approach the canvas closely enough for the red field to take over their vision.
At that distance, the painting becomes hard to see all at once. One zip appears clearly while another sits farther out toward the edge of vision. The perimeter of the canvas loses some of its authority. MoMA describes the effect as an ‘engulfing environment,’ though the canvas itself stays resolutely flat against the wall.
The spatial experience comes from the viewer standing too close for conventional looking to work. Newman compared the encounter to meeting another person, something understood physically before it can be surveyed from a safe distance.
herbert bayer draws the field of vision
Earlier in the 20th century, Herbert Bayer turned this problem into a diagram. His Diagram of the Field of Vision, first developed for the 1930 Deutscher Werkbund exhibition in Paris and reworked in 1935, places an eye at the center of an expanding field of images. Pictures occupy positions overhead and below the conventional eye line. The viewer faces several directions at once. Bayer described the arrangement as an ‘inclusive picture’ of possible viewpoints, with exhibition material extending beyond the frontal wall.
The drawing is almost funny in its bluntness. Exhibition design becomes a geometry problem built around a human head. Instead of assuming that vision travels straight ahead toward a wall, Bayer works with everything the eye can potentially register around it. The diagram also exposes something museums tend to conceal: every display already contains an idea of where the viewer should stand. Bayer just drew that relationship out in full.
the eameses give the eye too much
For Glimpses of the U.S.A., produced for the 1959 American National Exhibition in Moscow, Charles and Ray Eames projected 2,200 still and moving images across seven screens, each measuring twenty by thirty feet. Photographs of homes, highways, supermarkets, newspapers, and other fragments of postwar American culture appeared in rapid combinations across the enormous array.
Nobody in the audience could inspect all seven screens simultaneously. Looking meant choosing, even when the choice lasted only a second. One image sat at the center of attention while another registered somewhere beside it. Charles Eames later explained that the multiple projection system was meant to engage the viewer’s senses through reinforcement across images.
The installation turns visual excess into an organizational tool. Where Rothko stretches one image beyond comfortable viewing distance, the Eameses multiply images until attention itself becomes the scarce resource.
Charles and Ray Eames, Glimpses of the U.S.A., 1959 | video © Eames Office
lina bo bardi removes the wall
At the Museu de Arte de São Paulo, Lina Bo Bardi’s glass easels lift paintings onto transparent panes set into heavy concrete bases. The works stand throughout the open gallery instead of forming a procession along its perimeter. MASP describes the arrangement as a ‘forest’ of artworks, with visitors free to move among paintings that appear suspended in space.
The effect comes from overlap. Look at one painting and another may appear beyond its edge. Walk sideways and the composition of the room changes. Turn around and the back of a canvas enters view, complete with its label and support. A work that would usually claim an isolated patch of wall now shares the field of vision with other paintings and other people. Bo Bardi leaves each artwork intact while removing the architectural device that normally tells us how to approach it.
the viewer becomes part of the display system
Taken together, these works make the viewer unusually aware of the act of looking. Rothko uses distance. Newman uses scale. Bayer works through orientation, while the Eameses overload attention and Bo Bardi uses position. The work exceeds the easy frontal view in a different way each time. A visitor has to move, turn, choose a focus, or accept that part of the visual field will remain unresolved.
This is where the idea separates from the contemporary language of ‘immersive’ art. Filling every surface with imagery can create a powerful environment, although visual saturation alone says little about how a viewer is being asked to see.
The earlier experiments are compelling because their techniques remain exposed. Bayer literally diagrams the apparatus. The Eameses leave seven screens hanging above the audience. Bo Bardi forces you to view a massive collection of layered imagery at once. The experience comes from understanding that your own body occupies a specific position within a larger visual system.

Your exclusive invitation to steelman religion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

This post was originally published on this site.
Hello friends,
I want to share some backstage gossip with you that may or may not get me fired. But I do think it ultimately reflects well on the company.
Before we send any of our quarterly magazines to the printer, and then to members, the team will read every article a few times over, and then we’ll discuss them. Normally, it’s fairly easygoing. “Yeah, I loved all of these,” or “I think this one was my favorite.”
But recently, there was a furor. A good-spirited, intellectual roundtable.
About one article, the question was raised: “Is this narrative too simplistic?” Some said yes, some said no. The dialectic swayed for several hours, and Plato would have been happy.
You see, Big Think prides itself on bringing depth to the debate. And there are many ways to do this. We can line up and juxtapose a variety of sides. We can call upon oodles of empirical research and analyze the data. But first, and most importantly, we can try to “steelman” an argument wherever we can.
If you want to build a good argument, do not create a caricature or one-dimensional strawman to knock down. Lay out the best version you can of a position and then critique it if you will. Disagree, but disagree properly.
One area crammed with strawmen is debates about religion. It’s nearly impossible to have a debate about religion without it degrading into either a mudslinging battle of egos or embarrassing misrepresentations.
“Christians just worship a bearded man in the sky! It’s primitive!”
“Islam is a structurally violent religion. It’s incompatible with the West!”
“Wait, so if I’m rude to you, does that mean I’ll be reincarnated as a tapir?”
It’s often little more than a debate about faith conducted in bad faith. People are talking past each other, and there’s no hope of any progress or growth in the meeting. But we can do better. So, if you want to join me — and join Big Think’s mission to do better — you can hear me in a live conversation with the YouTuber and scholar of religion, Andrew Henry, about “What people get wrong about religion.”
Sign up on Big Think and get your questions ready.
Go well,
Jonny
Jonny is the creator of the Mini Philosophy social network. He’s an internationally bestselling author of three books and the resident philosopher at Big Think. He’s known all over the world for making philosophy accessible, relatable, and fun.

UK police release five men on bail after airbase incident

UK police release five men on bail after airbase incident
FAIRFORD, United Kingdom - British police said on Sept 28 five men arrested near an airbase used by the US were released on bail, as officers probed whether a “foreign state” could be involved in a suspected bomb plot.
US President Donald Trump, speaking in Washington, said he was “surprised that they released them”, adding that “I wouldn’t have done that”.
The release of the five – all London-based Britons in their mid-20s – came as British Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced an emergency meeting of top officials to ensure they have “the full picture”.
Earlier, Iran had denied involvement in any plot to target the Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford base in Gloucestershire, southwest England, following the security scare there early on Sept 27.
Counter-terror probe
UK counter-terror police are leading the investigation after authorities received reports on Sept 27 of three “suspicious” white vans near the airbase, which has been used by the US to bomb Iran.
Police said in their latest update on Sept 28 that the five men held, who all live in inner London boroughs, were being released on bail.
“This does not mean the investigation is over,” Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, the head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said, adding the five would be subject to “stringent” bail conditions.
He said officers were “considering this from every possible angle, including that this may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state”.
The men were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and “preparation of a terrorist act” under UK anti-terrorism laws, according to police.
They had been travelling in the three suspect vehicles, which have since been subject to “extensive examination, with the support of military assets and forensic experts”.
Bomb-disposal team
Amid huge questions about what happened, authorities have not confirmed any details of the threat, but bomb-disposal experts were seen at work at the scene.
The Daily Mail and Press Association both reported late on Sept 28 they understood from sources that tests on materials in the back of the vans established they were “not viable explosives”.
A farmer living in the village of Whelford near the airbase said she rang the police after seeing the vans blocking a road and a group of masked men.
The anonymous woman told media on Sept 28 that she believed the police had “dropped the ball” on the threat.
But UK defence minister Wes Streeting said she only had a “partial picture”.
Iran denies involvement
Trump on Sept 27 said the UK and US had the suspects “under investigation” for a while and alleged “they were looking to do big damage to our fort”.
On Sept 28, after hearing news of their bail, Trump said the case “might be” linked to Iran but declined to elaborate.
Pressed to give details, Trump said: “I’d rather not. I mean I know the answer, I could be very specific, but I’d rather not say. I would not have released them.”
Iran’s embassy in London said on X that it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns” speculation that Tehran was involved.
It criticised “the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran” to the incident.
US used base
In March, Britain gave the US permission to use Fairford for “specific defensive operations into Iran” to destroy Iranian missiles at source.
Since then, US bombers and other planes have been seen taking off and landing from the base – the only one on Britain’s mainland used for this purpose.
Residents in the rural Cotswolds area surrounding Fairford said the site, which hosts a range of US military equipment and personnel, had seen increased activity and security in recent months.
Around 85 households were evacuated from the village early on Sept 27, and had to stay elsewhere overnight, but were allowed back to their homes late on Sept 28.
Tehran has previously warned London against allowing its bases to be used by the US in operations against Iran.
In March, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi accused London of “putting British lives in danger” by allowing the bases to be used “for aggression against Iran”. AFP

New study links internet addiction to exhausted physiological stress systems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
20:00:55 UTC
05:00:55 KST

People who struggle with severe internet addiction might experience long-term changes in how their bodies process stress. A recent study analyzing human hair samples found that higher levels of internet addiction symptoms are linked to lower long-term accumulations of the stress hormone cortisol. The research was published in the journal Psychoneuroendocrinology.
Internet addiction is widely recognized as a behavioral disorder involving excessive and poorly controlled online activity. This can include anything from endless social media scrolling and online gaming to excessive internet shopping. The behavior becomes an addiction when it causes marked distress or impairs a person’s ability to function in their daily life, such as failing to fulfill obligations at school or work.
Psychologists have consistently linked internet addiction to high levels of psychological stress. Some theoretical models suggest that people who are highly vulnerable to stress may use the internet as a coping mechanism to escape negative emotions. However, studies looking at the physiological side of this stress response have yielded conflicting results.
The human body manages stress through a biological network known as the hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal axis, which ultimately produces cortisol. Cortisol is often called the primary stress hormone. In healthy amounts, it helps the body respond to immediate challenges, but chronic stress can alter how the system functions.
Previous research trying to measure cortisol in people with internet addiction has mostly relied on saliva or blood samples. These testing methods are highly sensitive to momentary fluctuations. A person’s cortisol levels can change based on the time of day, recent exercise, alcohol consumption, or a brief moment of anxiety just before the test.
To bypass these momentary spikes, scientists Hideki Tsumura of Tokushima University and Shuhei Izawa of the National Institute of Occupational Safety and Health in Japan turned to a different testing method. They chose to measure hormones trapped within human hair. Hair grows at an average rate of roughly one centimeter per month.
By analyzing a three-centimeter snippet of hair cut close to the scalp, researchers can measure the total amount of hormones secreted over the preceding three months. This provides a stable biological diary of long-term hormone production.
The researchers also decided to measure a second hormone called testosterone. Produced by a different biological network, testosterone is often associated with reward processing and risk-taking behaviors. Some neurobiological studies suggest that individuals who are prone to risk-taking might have heightened reward sensitivities driven by testosterone.
Because internet addiction often involves choosing immediate online rewards despite long-term negative consequences, the researchers suspected testosterone might play a role. The two biological systems that produce cortisol and testosterone also interact with one another. High levels of cortisol can suppress testosterone production, while testosterone can inhibit the release of cortisol.
Tsumura and Izawa wanted to examine both hormones simultaneously to see how each related to internet addiction symptoms. They recruited 155 Japanese university students for the study. The group included 94 women and 61 men, with an average age of roughly 21 years.
The researchers applied strict criteria to ensure the biological samples would be viable. They excluded individuals who had endocrine disorders, acute psychiatric conditions, or who were taking medications known to affect hormone levels, including hormonal contraceptives.
Participants completed a standardized survey known as the Internet Addiction Test. The questionnaire asks individuals to rate how often their internet use disrupts their sleep, academic performance, or social interactions. The students also completed a separate assessment to measure current depressive symptoms.
Following the surveys, the research team collected the hair samples from the back of each participant’s head. In the laboratory, they washed the hair samples in chemical solvents to remove external contaminants. The hair was then flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen and ground into a fine powder so the trapped hormones could be extracted and quantified.
To analyze the data, the researchers used statistical models that controlled for various outside factors. They adjusted the numbers to account for age, sex, body mass index, and depression scores. They also factored in hair care habits, such as bleaching, perming, and how many times a week the participants washed their hair.
The results showed that hair cortisol concentrations were negatively associated with internet addiction scores. Students who reported more severe symptoms of internet addiction had lower amounts of cortisol trapped in their hair. When the researchers divided the participants into two groups based on a standard cutoff score for internet addiction, the highly addicted group exhibited lower average cortisol levels than the low-risk group.
The initial hypothesis regarding testosterone was not supported by the data. The researchers found no association between internet addiction symptoms and long-term hair testosterone concentrations. The results remained consistent across both male and female participants.
Finding low levels of a stress hormone in people experiencing high psychological distress might seem counterintuitive. The researchers point out that chronic stress exposure can initially trigger high cortisol production, eventually leading to a state of biological exhaustion. Over time, the stress system may become blunted, resulting in lower baseline cortisol secretion.
Reduced hair cortisol levels have also been observed in people experiencing post-traumatic stress, severe depression, and prolonged adversity. The findings suggest that individuals with severe internet addiction might share a similar underlying biological profile characterized by an exhausted physiological stress response.
The authors noted a few limitations to their work. Because the study relied on a specific demographic of young university students, the findings may not represent the general population or older adults in clinical settings. The research was also cross-sectional, meaning it captured a single snapshot in time.
Without longitudinal data, researchers cannot determine the sequence of events. The data cannot show whether an altered stress system makes someone more vulnerable to internet addiction, or if the behavioral addiction eventually causes the stress system to burn out. Additionally, unmeasured conditions like past trauma could have influenced the biological markers.
The study, “Association of internet addiction symptoms with hair cortisol and hair testosterone concentrations,” was authored by Hideki Tsumura and Shuhei Izawa.

====================================================================================================

Trump Rolls Back Fuel Economy Standards. Will Cars Really Get Cheaper?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
20:00:39 UTC
05:00:39 KST

The Trump Administration released a rule on Monday to roll back Biden-era fuel economy standards, saying that the Biden Administration “previously broke the law by setting standards that went far beyond the requirements mandated by Congress” and arguing that they pushed for electric vehicles that Americans did not want.
The announcement, which came from Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, said that the previous regulations had been costly for automakers. The changes are meant to reduce their costs and encourage manufacturers to expand production in the U.S. Duffy claimed that, by extension, the rollbacks would make new cars more affordable for Americans.
When it was first proposed in December 2025, the rule was divisive, drawing ire from environmental advocates while garnering praise from auto-industry trade groups. The Administration finalized it last week with a signoff from President Donald Trump.
The President commented on the forthcoming rule Sept. 26, saying the new standards would “take the waste out of building cars in America.”
“That means LOWER PRICES, saving families thousands on a new, beautiful, and safe car,” he wrote on Truth Social.
The claim that the revisions will pass down cost savings to American buyers, however, relies on several factors, including automakers’ pricing decisions, fuel costs, and broader economic conditions.
What changes under Trump’s new fuel economy rule?
Former President Joe Biden’s regulations were put in place in 2024 to reduce car-based greenhouse gas emissions, decrease dependence on fossil fuels, and spur a transition to electric and hybrid vehicles. The Trump Administration has claimed that its revisions are more focused on bolstering the auto industry and making safer, newer cars more accessible.
The rollback reduces pressure on automakers to improve fuel efficiency or sell more hybrids and electric vehicles to meet fleetwide standards.
Two federal agencies have traditionally set rules that shape how much fuel vehicles use and how much pollution they produce. The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) regulates vehicle pollution and, until this year’s rollback, also limited vehicle greenhouse gas emissions. The Department of Transportation (DOT) sets fuel economy standards—how far vehicles must travel on a gallon of fuel.
The DOT’s Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards apply to the average fuel economy of an automaker’s new cars and light trucks. They ensure that if an automaker sold an inefficient vehicle, it would also need to sell efficient vehicles to reach the average standard.
It is these standards that sit at the center of the latest rollbacks: The Biden Administration projected its standards would bring average fleet fuel economy to approximately 50.4 mpg by model year 2031. The Trump Administration projects 34.9 mpg under its revised standards.
Environmental advocates have pointed out that the change reflects the Trump Administration’s wider deprioritization of environmental protection policies, since electric vehicles give off fewer greenhouse gas emissions than traditional gas-powered vehicles.
Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill” in July 2025 axed the $7,500 electric vehicle tax credit. That same month, the Administration eliminated fines for automakers that failed to meet federal fuel-efficiency requirements. And the EPA in February 2026 repealed vehicle greenhouse gas emissions standards.
TIME has reached out to the White House and the Department of Transportation for comment.
What does the rule mean for EV demand?
The Trump Administration believes that Biden-era CAFE standards overestimated consumer demand for electric vehicles. Sam Fiorani, the Vice President of Global Vehicle Forecasting at AutoForecast Solutions, says the story is more complicated.
“Americans have been less interested in the shift to electric vehicles than much of the rest of the world, but that's not to say nobody wants it,” he tells TIME. “The success of Tesla has been built on the back of millions of Americans looking for a practical EV.”
An August report from Kelley Blue Book (KBB) showed that new EV sales in the U.S. were down some 47% from 2025; however, the sales of used EVs were on the rise, with a nearly 15% increase.
The issue is that automakers “need to be incentivized” to produce electric vehicles, Fiorani adds—something that the second Trump Administration has deprioritized.
“Removing the federal incentives did not remove the demand, but it made the transition for the supply of EVs less profitable,” Fiorani says. “Demand for EVs will continue to grow, and manufacturers investing in the technology will ultimately take advantage of it.”
That reflects a trend that can already be seen playing out on the global scale: The International Energy Agency projects that electric vehicles will account for 29% of new-car sales worldwide in 2026.
Will it be more affordable to buy new cars with this rule in effect?
According to the DOT’s announcement, the Trump Administration’s reduced fuel economy standards will save Americans $138 billion over the next five years and reduce the average cost of a new car by $1,300. 
It’s “certainly true,” says Mark Jacobsen, a professor of economics at the University of California, San Diego, that making “a lower-technology car using ultra-gasoline engines” is cheaper for the manufacturer.
That is a key reason that trade groups representing automobile manufacturers support the change.
“NHTSA made the right call to better align fuel economy standards with the law and current market conditions,” John Bozzella, the President and CEO of the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, said in a statement. “The standards finalized under the previous administration effectively required a switchover to electric vehicles that was out of step with market realities and customer demand.”
But reducing the cost of production for automakers does not necessarily mean that cost-savings will be passed along to the customer, Jacobsen says, explaining that long-term savings for the average driver would need to take into account myriad additional economic factors.
One is the cost of gasoline. James Michael Sallee, an economist and professor at University of California, Berkeley, explains that customers may wind up paying less for a vehicle that is less fuel efficient—but ultimately spend more over the car’s lifetime.
“Fuel economy standards will tend to put upward prices—but a lot of that is offset, if not all of it, by future fuel cost savings that consumers enjoy over the course of the life of a vehicle,” Sallee says.
This question is especially pertinent as the world deals with a global oil shortage, with a barrel of Brent crude oil surpassing $108 on Monday. The U.S. has experienced a surge in gas prices in 2026, peaking around $4.56 per gallon after the start of the U.S.-Iran conflict in February. Even if negotiations proceeded and a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz were reached, economists predict that it would take months for gas prices to drop back to prewar baselines.
“If you look at the analysis the Administration has done, they're projecting very low gasoline prices in the future,” Jacobsen says. “That needs to be true in order to save the consumer money.”
New-car prices are also higher in 2026: Buyers paid an average of $50,089 in August, up 1.9% from a year earlier, according to KBB. Sallee says it is reasonable for the Trump Administration to try to address affordability. “The price of new vehicles is a real issue,” he says.
But there is reason to doubt that it will play out exactly as the Administration seems to suggest, according to Anna Stefanopoulou, a professor of mechanical engineering at the University of Michigan. She “highly doubts” that lower costs for auto manufacturers will trickle down into lower prices for consumers.
Many manufacturers will just be selling more “larger and more profitable trucks,” she says, once they no longer have to contend with “stringent” CAFE standards of average fuel economy.
The new rule will take effect 60 days after its publication in the Federal Register. Whether drivers ultimately save money will depend on how much automakers lower prices—and how much buyers spend on fuel. With standards extending through model year 2031, and the conflict in the Middle East adding uncertainty to future pump prices, the full impact on consumers’ wallets may take years to become clear.

Denmark buys Ukrainian-founded firm’s ground drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
19:50:28 UTC
04:50:28 KST

- Denmark bought nine Dropla 4x4 unmanned ground vehicles to train drone operators, including conscripts, at the Danish Defence Drone Center.
- The vehicles were delivered without weapon mounts, and Denmark is studying adding remote weapon stations and communications equipment.
Denmark’s armed forces have taken delivery of nine unmanned ground vehicles built by Dropla, a Danish company founded by Ukrainians, to train drone operators, including conscripts, at the country’s military drone center.
Denmark’s defense procurement agency, known by its Danish initials FMI, bought the Dropla 4×4 vehicles for the Danish Defence Drone Center, the agency said Sept. 28. An unmanned ground vehicle, or UGV, is a vehicle that drives itself or is steered remotely with no crew aboard. The agency did not disclose the price of the order or when the vehicles arrived.
The Danish version of the Dropla 4×4 was delivered without a weapon mount. FMI said it is already studying how to fit the vehicles with extra equipment such as a remotely operated weapon station, which lets a soldier aim and fire a machine gun from a safe distance, and new communications gear. The agency said those plans draw on lessons from the war in Ukraine and on its own trials of other UGVs in Denmark.
Colonel Thomas Øgendahl Knudsen, who heads FMI’s land division, said unmanned systems are developing quickly, so the Danish military needs to build experience with them and bring them into soldier training now. He said the new vehicles let the drone center work with ground drones while exploring how the technology could be used across the armed forces in the future.
The purchase is FMI’s second batch of UGVs this year. Earlier in 2026, the agency bought eight unmanned ground vehicles for the Danish Army, which FMI said have since been tested in a range of operational scenarios with strong results.
Dropla Tech was founded in 2023 by four Ukrainian entrepreneurs and is headquartered in Odense, Denmark, with its engineering and operations teams working in Ukraine. The company is best known for Blue Eyes, an artificial intelligence system that detects mines, improvised explosive devices and loitering drones without needing a cloud connection. Dropla says the system has confirmed more than 5,000 explosive threats in Ukraine.
The company builds two modular UGV platforms, the Dropla 4×4 and Dropla 6×6. Both can be configured for casualty evacuation, cargo delivery, reconnaissance, remote weapon stations and counter-drone missions. Dropla has also signed an agreement with Ukrainian company Frontline Robotics to integrate its Burya weapon turret onto the vehicles.
The Danish military has worked with Dropla before. During a six-month innovation project that ended this summer, the armed forces tested a Dropla prototype built for evacuation and logistics. That vehicle started out with four wheels but was fitted with two more on the military’s recommendation to make it more stable.
Dropla raised €2.4 million ($2.7 million) in 2025 from investors including Denmark’s state Export and Investment Fund, and in July 2026 it received an undisclosed investment from U.S.-Ukrainian group MITS Capital. The company says it wants to scale production to as many as 3,000 UGVs a year.

This TikTok home remedy could cause botulism—here’s what to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
19:47:33 UTC
04:47:33 KST

As flu season approaches, TikTokers are spreading a homemade elixir to supposedly boost the immune system that experts warn could in fact cause the fatal disease botulism.
In dozens of videos, some of which have hundreds of thousands of “likes” and “favorites,” wellness and herbalist influencers tout the benefits of garlic fermented in honey as an all-natural antibiotic and antimicrobial treatment and detoxifying potion. While both honey and garlic do have some antimicrobial benefits, the recipes used can promote the growth of Clostridium botulinum. This bacterium causes deadly botulism and is commonly found in both ingredients.
“Fermenting garlic in unpasteurized honey at room temperature can pose a risk of botulism,” says Karine LeBlanc, a spokesperson for Health Canada, the country’s national health policy organization. “Storing the mixture at room temperature may further increase the risk.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The number of foods that carry C. botulinum bacteria is small. The microorganisms grow best in low-oxygen conditions and require specific pH conditions. Both honey and garlic fall into the category of foods in which the bacteria can live, but under normal circumstances, the growth of spores would be inhibited, says Joy Gail Waite-Cusic, a professor of food safety at Oregon State University.
“There’s not enough available water in the honey for any bacteria to grow, and so it keeps, and it doesn’t mold either,” she says.
Combining the two ingredients is where trouble lies. Bacteria in the honey can pull water out of the garlic and then begin to multiply. If the fermentation process doesn’t decrease the mixture’s pH fast enough, this can also accelerate the bacteria’s growth further.
When ingested, the mixture could lead to infection with a bacterium that carries the nerve-attacking toxins that botulism is known for. Depending on how it enters the body, botulism can cause muscle weakness, slurred speech, difficulty breathing, stomach pain, diarrhea, nausea and vomiting. In extreme cases, the infection can cause death.
“If you consume that toxin, then it will exhibit its paralytic effects on you,” Waite-Cusic says. Among the most common targets, she says, are “your diaphragm, and so you stop breathing.”
The disease is rare, with only 243 confirmed cases and 30 additional probable cases recorded in 2021, the most recent year for which data is available, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Of the confirmed and probable cases, 181 were in infants, the highest incidence since 1976, when data started being collected.
The reason why the disease is so deadly for babies is that their gut microbiome is yet to develop the defense mechanisms needed to fight off the bacteria—by contrast, an adult’s gut biome and immune system is generally effective in fighting the bacteria when ingested.
“There are a few documented adult intestinal colonization botulism cases (mostly from Canada), where peanut butter was implicated and one infant in 2024” in the UK, says Haydee Dabritz, an epidemiologist with the California Department of Public Health’s Infant Botulism Treatment and Prevention Program.
Still, on rare occasions, it can continue to grow in an adult. While the disease is curable if the infected person seeks medical attention, it can be lethal if left untreated.
“The issue we're always facing with botulism discussions is it can kill you,” says Waite-Cusic. “It’s not ‘I’m gonna vomit for a few hours and get better.’ It’s ‘No, if you don’t get to a hospital and get the antidote, you’re dead.’”
While nobody wants to get sick during flu season, LeBlanc warns against relying on homemade remedies as a substitute for approved medications.
“If you think you may need an antibiotic or other antimicrobial medication, speak with a health care professional,” she says. “Antimicrobial medications, including antibiotics and antivirals, should only be used when prescribed.”
Waite-Cusic adds that you could see more benefit from garlic and honey by avoiding fermentation and eating them as they are. (Notably, raw honey cannot be given to babies under one year of age because of the potential for botulism.)
“You actually have the best antioxidant potential if they’re both raw," she says, referring to honey and garlic. “So you just want to eat the clove of garlic that’s now sweeter.”

CIA restores helicopter that took first Americans to Afghanistan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
19:40:40 UTC
04:40:40 KST

- The CIA restored the helicopter that flew its JAWBREAKER team into Afghanistan on Sept. 26, 2001, returning it to its 2001 paint scheme.
- Ronald Moeller, a self-described retired CIA paramilitary officer, noted on X that the aircraft is technically an Mi-8MTV, not an Mi-17.
The CIA has restored the helicopter that carried the first American team into Afghanistan after the Sept. 11 attacks, repainting it in the camouflage it wore in 2001 to mark the 25th anniversary of the mission.
The Russian-designed helicopter sits on the grounds of CIA headquarters in Langley, Virginia. It flew a seven-man CIA team, code-named JAWBREAKER, into Afghanistan’s Panjshir Valley on Sept. 26, 2001, just 15 days after the attacks. The agency calls the aircraft an Mi-17, but a retired CIA officer who says he was part of its history publicly corrected that.
“Actually an Mi-8 MTV. Nevertheless, she is a tremendous platform, performing flawlessly no matter the mission. Proud to have been part of her history,” wrote Ronald Moeller, who describes himself on X as a retired CIA paramilitary operations officer and former deputy assistant secretary of war for strategic readiness, in reply to the CIA’s anniversary post.
The two names describe closely related aircraft. The Mi-17 is the export designation for Russia’s Mi-8MTV family of medium transport helicopters, and the two are often used interchangeably. The CIA did not respond publicly to the correction.
The CIA bought the helicopter in the 1990s, reasoning that a Soviet-designed aircraft would draw little attention in Afghanistan, where both the Northern Alliance and the Taliban flew the same type. It could also handle the altitude. On the way to the Panjshir Valley, the crew had to cross the Anjuman Pass, which rises about 4,400 m (14,500 feet) above sea level.
The first flight carried the seven CIA officers, a three-member aircrew and two Afghan partners, according to the agency. Led by veteran officer Gary Schroen, the team brought millions of dollars in cash to recruit and equip Afghan fighters and prepared the ground for the U.S. military campaign against al-Qaeda and the Taliban. Their main partner was the Northern Alliance, whose leader, Ahmad Shah Massoud, had been assassinated by al-Qaeda operatives two days before the Sept. 11 attacks.
The helicopter went on to fly more than 300 missions in Afghanistan before its last operational flight in 2012. It was moved to CIA headquarters in 2018 and dedicated there on Sept. 26, 2019, exactly 18 years after the JAWBREAKER landing. Its fuel lines and other components were removed, and it was placed among rocks meant to resemble the Afghan landscape. It carries the tail number 91101, a reference to the date of the attacks.
Years outdoors took a toll. CIA Museum director Robert Byer told CBS News that the paint had badly faded in the sun and that animals had been getting inside. Over the past year, restorers sealed holes in the fuselage and repainted the aircraft to match its 2001 appearance. They also brought back “607,” the call sign of the Afghan pilot who flew the first mission.
