The workplace war over iced lattes is not about coffee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
16:40:16 UTC
01:40:16 KST

Is it acceptable to bring an iced coffee to a job interview?
This seemingly mundane question has somehow consumed various corners of the Internet, taking over social media feeds and group chats. Bloomberg Opinion is not immune. Not since the great shorts-in-the-office firestorm of 2024 has a workplace debate lit up our team’s Slack channel quite like this one.
What started the so-called iced-coffee discourse was a viral TikTok from corporate recruiter Caitlin Wehniainen, who also posts advice for job seekers on social media. In her video, Wehniainen said that younger candidates are showing up at job interviews with iced coffee, which to her reads as treating the interview like a “stop on your list of errands for the day.”
Her advice: “Don’t waltz into your interview all casual with an iced coffee,” adding: “It just looks like you didn’t have time to finish your coffee beforehand.”
I am not the first to say it, but the heated debate that has followed is not really about iced coffee. The very nature of work is in flux right now, with artificial intelligence (AI) accelerating the deepening structural shifts. Employers and their young employees are caught in a power struggle over who gets to decide the norms of this new workplace. Iced coffee is just the latest proxy for that tension — how each party feels both misunderstood and deep anxiety about their place in this evolving landscape.
To bosses from older generations, bringing an iced coffee to a job interview can signal either a complete lack of understanding of the workplace’s unwritten rules or, perhaps even worse, an unwillingness to play by them. Either interpretation reinforces the existing stereotypes that bosses have about Gen Z workers: They are unprofessional, unprepared, unmotivated and difficult to manage.
An iced coffee takes on outsized weight when many traditional cues of the hiring process have become obsolete. Applying for a job has turned into an AI doom loop: Candidates are using AI to write their resumes and cover letters, which are then assessed by AI to make sure they match the AI-written job description. That has raised the stakes of the in-person interview — the ultimate vibe check in the AI era. The logic is that if a prospective hire cannot get along and go along when it matters most, what other would they refuse to follow and conform to?
This comes at a moment when corporate America is highly attuned to signs of defiance, and management is working overtime to tamp down on any hints of rebellion in the workplace. As I have written before, bosses are in their command-and-control era. They are reclaiming their authority by quashing dissent, increasing surveillance and cutting benefits. They are controlling how workers express their personal views even when they are off the clock and demanding they return to the office five days a week.
Meanwhile, much of Gen Z is not having it. This is a generation that grew up with regular school shootings, came of age during a climate crisis and lived through a global pandemic — experiences that have eroded their trust in major institutions and what they view as arbitrary rules. Their desire to set boundaries and refusal to blindly accept marching orders can look to older managers like entitlement or insubordination. Gen Z’ers are launching careers at time when they are constantly being told AI might eliminate the jobs they desire. Against that backdrop, how could an iced coffee possibly matter? Instead, it just projects elitism and lazy gatekeeping.
It is worth remembering that not very long ago, job seekers were advised to cover up their tattoos in job interviews and scrub their resumes of clues as to their sexual orientation or gender identity. Obviously, an iced coffee is not nearly the same thing, but it is a reminder that norms around professionalism change and evolve. In the case of tattoos and identity, it was Gen X and millennials who helped rid the workplace of what they viewed as its outdated rules. Now that many of them are the ones doing the hiring, they might want to remember that and give a little grace the next time a Gen Z candidate waltzes in with an iced coffee.
Beth Kowitt is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering corporate America. She was previously a senior writer and editor at Fortune magazine. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

Dozens dead in several S Africa shootings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
16:40:16 UTC
01:40:16 KST

The death toll in a mass shooting in a South African tavern has risen to 18 after one person died in the hospital, police said yesterday, announcing at least two of the dead were Lesotho nationals. The shooting west of Johannesburg on Saturday was part of a bloody weekend in the crime-weary country, with 10 people killed in another mass shooting in Cape Town on Sunday.
Eight gunmen armed with assault rifles stormed the bar in the semi-rural township of Wedela, around 80km from Johannesburg, killing 13 men and four women, police said.
“One more victim has died in hospital, bringing the total number of deceased to 18,” they said yesterday. “Only four of the deceased have been identified, two South Africans and two Lesotho nationals.”
Photo: AP
The motive for the attack was not clear, but the area is reportedly gripped by rivalry between criminal organizations involved in illegal gold mining. Thousands of unregistered miners operate in abandoned mining shafts in South Africa, many coming from across southern Africa, including the kingdom of Lesotho, which is encysted within South Africa.
The illegal mining has been linked to organized crime, assassinations and other illegal activities.
In other parts of the country, including Cape Town, gangs involved in selling illegal drugs or extortion rackets have been responsible for mass shootings.
The acting provincial commissioner said police were investigating a possible lead that the shooting was a revenge attack as one of the victims was connected to another shooting.
DIFFERING MOTIVES
South Africa is awash with legal and illegal firearms, and shootings are common, often fueled by gang rivalry, extortion and competition between informal businesses.
The country of around 62 million people has one of the world’s highest murder rates, with about 60 people killed each day.
At least 38 people were killed and at least 30 were wounded in the separate late-night shootings in impoverished townships near South Africa’s three biggest cities. Two of the massacres happened in the space of a few hours late Saturday night and in the predawn hours of Sunday.
South Africa’s mass shootings often differ from lone gunman mass shootings seen in the US and other countries. The shootings in South Africa are mostly connected to criminality, rather than ideological motive or personal grievance.
There is no standard global definition of mass shootings. In South Africa, police define a mass shooting as when three or more people are shot in a single attack.
All three mass shootings this week involved multiple gunmen, according to police.
Multiple suspects carried out another mass shooting hours later that killed 10 at a store connected to a nighttime entertainment venue in Lwandle township near the city of Cape Town, although police did not say exactly how many shooters there were. Three gunmen — at least one of whom used an AK-47-style rifle — killed 11 people after forcing their way into a house party in a township near Durban on Tuesday night.
Authorities say many of the mass shootings are linked to criminal gangs fighting turf wars or using violence to establish control over communities and areas.
Illegal mining gangs are notorious for terrorizing communities in the gold-mining areas near Johannesburg, where they are involved in the lucrative illicit gold trade.
HOMICIDE RATES
South Africa has some of the highest gun homicide rates in the world, but they mostly affect impoverished communities where police have struggled to contain the violence. After a mass shooting killed 12 people in a poor Johannesburg neighborhood in June, residents said they had long complained about gangs and illegal guns in the area to police.
Factors such as distance from police stations or a lack of lighting make poor townships vulnerable to violent crime, according to experts. Bystanders, including children, are often killed in the mass shootings.
Crime in South Africa mirrors its larger economic inequality. Affluent suburbs — sometimes just a few miles from townships — are well lit, often patrolled by armed private security personnel and have much lower violent crime rates.
South Africa reached a turning point in March when President Cyril Ramaphosa deployed soldiers on the streets in a yearlong operation to support police in the fight against violent crime committed by organized gangs. Ramaphosa said that crime was the biggest threat to South Africa’s democracy and economic development.
One of the specific focuses of the operation was the illegal mining gangs operating in and around Johannesburg.
While some poor communities welcomed the soldiers as long-needed security for their neighborhoods, critics of the government said using the army to fight crime was effectively an admission that the police had failed.

Major canals in Bangkok filled with accumulated rainfall exceeding 20cm, officials said yesterday. Floodwaters spread across the city, particularly in the central and eastern parts, blocking roads and stopping traffic. The Thai Meteorological Department warned that the heavy rain would continue in most parts of the country through today, citing a strong low-pressure system over the central region and strengthening southwest monsoon conditions. Human trafficking tally reaches 3,401 in five years

A total of 3,401 people were investigated in human trafficking cases from 2021 to last year, 147 of whom were implicated in suspected organ harvesting, data released by the Ministry of Justice showed.
Forced labor accounted for the largest share of human trafficking investigations, involving 1,914 people, or about 56 percent, data on human trafficking cases handled by district prosecutors’ offices over the five-year period showed.
Sex trafficking investigations accounted for 1,281 people, or 38 percent, although the number rose from 168 in 2021 to 309 last year.
Photo: CNA
Those investigated for involvement in organ harvesting remained fewer than 70 people per year, with 34 investigated last year.
The number of people investigated in human trafficking cases rose from more than 600 in 2022 to 957 in 2023, the highest in the five-year period, although the figure declined to 802 last year.
Just 41 percent of the 3,401 people investigated were indicted, with 50.4 percent of those convicted aged 18 to 29 and 27.3 percent aged 30 to 39, an average age of 32, it showed.
The Taoyuan District Prosecutors’ Office has been investigating a human trafficking ring that attempted to send three people to China for organ harvesting, although the intended victims were found before they left Taiwan.
Seven suspects were indicted earlier this month in the case, with prosecutors seeking the maximum seven-year sentence for each defendant.
Under 2023 amendments to the Human Trafficking Prevention Act (人口販運防制法), the punishment for attempted human trafficking is five to seven years in prison.
The ministry said that the government is continuing to combat human trafficking by preventative measures, reviewing government anti-trafficking strategies and integrating resources from the public and private sectors.
The US Department of State’s 2025 Trafficking in Persons Report, released in September last year, placed Taiwan in the first tier for the 16th consecutive year, meaning the authorities fully meet the minimum standards for combating trafficking.

Dictators, and why we cannot help forgiving them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
16:40:14 UTC
01:40:14 KST

You might have missed it, but hostile regimes that were once shunned are now quietly being normalized. From Myanmar to Afghanistan, Belarus to Venezuela, military dictatorships, hardline Islamists and autocrats are edging their way back into the global order.
For some, that makes perfect sense. Governments naturally prioritize security and national interest, sanctions can be hit and miss, and businesses will pursue opportunities regardless of the optics. Yet there should be a cost for regaining a seat at the table.
Take the Taliban. Five years after it seized Kabul following the chaotic US military withdrawal, it has won a series of key diplomatic gains. Taliban-appointed diplomats now control missions across a growing number of countries, including China and the United Arab Emirates, and it has signed economic and security agreements with neighbors. Has this recognition come at a cost? Not at all. The regime’s repressive nature, its ties with al-Qaeda and transnational terrorism, and its crushing treatment of women and girls all continue unabated.
Illustration: YUsha
Aaron Zelin, a fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, calls it an “accreditation cascade” — through Gulf states, Turkey and central Asia — where governments have accepted Taliban outreach without formally recognizing its rule. He said in his analysis of five years of Taliban diplomacy that what began as meetings with a handful of nations has developed into joint commissions, trade councils and foreign missions. The regime is now making overtures to Washington on critical minerals.
On the sidelines of the UN General Assembly last week, High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk attended a meeting that implored the world to ensure that international engagement on Afghanistan was human-rights based and principled. The governments that are cutting deals with Taliban representatives are doing anything but.
This does not mean that isolating hostile regimes until they reform is the best way forward. The US has been negotiating with Belarus and easing sanctions in exchange for the release of political prisoners, while the UK is upgrading its diplomatic ties with Venezuela to support a democratic transition. Moreover, there are ways to engage without legitimizing states, or formally recognizing their governments. Representatives talk over technical and practical matters such as border movements and assistance during natural disasters. Germany, for example, explicitly says that while the Taliban hold de facto power it does not recognize them as the legitimate government.
Nations in Asia should follow suit, particularly when it comes to dealing with Myanmar. It is understandable that images of coup leader Min Aung Hlaing receiving an official welcome in regional capitals would cause despair among citizens, not to mention the National Unity Government that was formed by ousted lawmakers and other anti-junta figures.
Since the February 2021 coup, more than 100,000 people have been killed and 5.2 million displaced as fighting between the army and an array of ethnic militias and anti-junta groups tore the nation apart. Despite controlling as little as a quarter of the country, the military held widely condemned elections in December and January and started calling itself a government. Min Aung Hlaing was named president in April and soon embarked on a multination diplomatic mission to China, Russia, Belarus, Thailand, Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia in a quest for legitimacy.
India was his first port of call. The countries share a 1,643km border, and New Delhi has every reason to communicate on issues from illegal weapons trade, drug trafficking and refugee movement. Yet it has gone far beyond that. Unlike the US and Europe, it has maintained ongoing diplomatic, military and economic contacts with the junta. On his three-day visit, Min Aung Hlaing and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi discussed critical minerals, trade and healthcare. It is not clear whether Modi raised concerns about the discredited elections or the detention of Aung San Suu Kyi.
The ASEAN’s approach is no better. The group is pushing a five-point consensus that aims to end the political and humanitarian crisis, while some member states are pursuing bilateral relations. It is another clear lesson of what not to do. After denying the junta a seat at high-level meetings since 2021, ASEAN recently began testing that exclusion. To a chorus of criticism, foreign ministers held an informal meeting with their Burmese counterpart in Bangkok in July.
Still, perhaps the gathering managed to extract a small price. The regime has since released photographs of Aung San Suu Kyi meeting an International Committee of the Red Cross representative, although it continues to reject ASEAN’s calls for her unconditional release and has not allowed it access to her.
University of Stirling senior international politics lecturer Monalisa Adhikari has reviewed Myanmar’s outreach since the coup, tracking how the military-backed government projected normalcy through dealings with other states. She said that nations should be clear about whether diplomatic actions constitute formal recognition or are simply technical contacts on practical issues. That would prevent the regime from portraying such engagement as an acknowledgement of its legitimacy.
When hostile regimes are allowed to reintegrate into the global order without reducing any of their abuses, it can undercut the leverage used to resolve conflicts and strengthen their hold on power. Engagement is not the problem. Normalization without conditions is. If refusing every demand for change carries no lasting cost because relations are eventually restored anyway, why would anyone comply?
Ruth Pollard is a Bloomberg Opinion managing editor. Previously she was South and Southeast Asia government team leader at Bloomberg News and Middle East correspondent for the Sydney Morning Herald. New Zealand law enforcement personnel came to the rescue of a seal crossing a busy road, helping the perplexed pinniped pup back safely into the water, they said yesterday.

The creature then attempted to get back to the water, sparking swift action from police and Department of Conservation officials to make sure it did so unharmed.
Photo: AFP
“The pup appeared grateful for the assistance,” a police statement added.
“Our staff were able to uplift the seal and drive it to a safe place where it was released into the water,” Senior Sergeant Miriam Bentley from Wellington Police said. “This was collaborative problem-solving which prevented any further issues for the young seal and for road users.”
“When I joined the police 15 months ago they said to be ready for anything, so I guess this demonstrates that’s true,” said Constable Taylor, who assisted the pup. The seas around New Zealand are populated with multiple species of seals, who do occasionally wander ashore.
The Department of Conservation reported this weekend a 200 percent increase in sightings on land around Wellington, local media said, describing it as “seal silly season.”
Police urged the public to alert them to more runaway seals and not attempt to intervene themselves.

Taiwan bags 13 medals
Taiwanese competitors won three gold, three silver and seven bronze medals at the WorldSkills Shanghai in China last week, the Workforce Development Agency (WDA) said on Sunday. Taiwan also won 30 Medallions for Excellence, awarded to competitors who rack up a high number of points in an event, but fall short of winning a gold, silver or bronze medal, it said. In the Information and Communication Technology competition, Lu Zhi-kuan (呂治寬) took gold in the Software Applications Development category, while the team of Chiu Yu-hsiang (邱昱翔) and Yang Yong-xu (楊詠旭) won the gold medal for Cyber Security, the WDA said. EDUCATION
Lai supports educators
President William Lai (賴清德) yesterday marked Teachers’ Day by highlighting a government program to invest NT$11.755 billion (US$369.9 million) by 2029 to improve educators’ digital and artificial intelligence (AI) skills. In a Facebook post, Lai said teachers play an irreplaceable role in guiding students through learning and personal growth, while acknowledging the pressures they face from teacher shortages, parent-teacher communication, student counseling and administrative workloads. The Ministry of Education has launched the “AI Talent Ark Program” to build teaching capabilities and AI-enabled learning environments in elementary and secondary schools, he wrote. A ministry report released in May said the “AI Talent Ark Program” aims to enrich digital teaching materials, develop next-generation AI learning systems, provide hands-on AI training and support for teachers, and improve education data analytics to help educators deliver more personalized instruction. While technology can make teaching more efficient, teachers’ understanding of and guidance to students are irreplaceable, he said. The government will continue to listen to educators, improve teaching conditions and ensure teachers receive the respect and support they deserve so they can focus on teaching, he said.

The Taichung Fire Bureau received a report at about 2:02pm that the 52-year-old, who was visiting Lihpao Land in Houli (后里), appeared to have no vital signs when he was found unconscious, local media reported yesterday. Police yesterday said they would refer the case to prosecutors for an autopsy to determine the exact cause of death. Artificial intelligence (AI) requires safeguards that go beyond self-regulation, Microsoft Corp cofounder Bill Gates said in an interview that aired on Sunday, calling for legislation to be passed in US Congress.
“You need law enforcement and the politicians to get into the discussion about what safeguards and monitoring look like,” Gates said in a taped interview on NBC’s Meet the Press program. “And that has to be a required thing.”
A sudden groundswell has risen in favor of federal intervention after OpenAI in July said that an autonomous AI agent went rogue during a security test and hacked into another company, subverting human control. Gates joined that chorus, saying that government must be involved.
Photo: AP
“No one thinks self-regulation is enough,” he said.
In a rare show of unity, the CEOs of rivals Anthropic PBC, OpenAI, Google’s DeepMind, Microsoft and xAI have called for slowing the development of increasingly capable AI systems.
However, US President Donald Trump and other opponents of additional regulation for AI say new government restrictions would simply give China the upper hand in the AI revolution. Trump has publicly dismissed calls for new laws on AI as a “hoax.”
Gates said that safeguards would not dramatically hinder the industry, and that the risks of not implementing them are real.
“It’s not a hoax at all,” he told NBC.
Gates has said he wants to meet Trump to discuss AI.
“I hope that, given my life’s work in the field, my saying how unique and different this is and how concerned I am will add to what he’s hearing from other people,” Gates said.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei was expected to have dinner with Trump on Sunday, a source familiar with the matter said. Axios had reported the dinner earlier in the day.
Trump confirmed that he planned to have a dinner meeting with Amodei on Sunday night, but reaffirmed his stance against slowing the pace of AI development.
Although he acknowledged Amodei’s concern that going too fast on AI could expand risks, Trump said it was more important for the US to maintain a technological edge over China.
“We’re about maybe a year and a half up on China,” Trump told Fox News while attending the Presidents Cup golf tournament in Illinois. “We’re leading, and we’re building tremendous, trillions of dollars’ worth of places. And why should we give that up?”
Incidents of rogue AI agents are not a cause for alarm, Trump told Fox News.
“I don’t worry about it,” he said, adding that he remained confident in the technology and its potential.

MOTC meets holiday traffic goal: Chen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
16:40:06 UTC
01:40:06 KST

Minister of Transportation and Communications Chen Shih-kai (陳世凱) yesterday said that the ministry met its goal of preventing travelers from being stranded and ensuring they reached their destination during the holiday, adding that his trip to Germany did not interfere with his handling of holiday traffic.
Chen made the remarks on the sidelines of a groundbreaking ceremony for the first section of the Kaohsiung-Pingtung Second Expressway, when he was asked about the execution of the transportation plan for the four-day Mid-Autumn Festival and Teacher’s Day holiday, which ended yesterday.
The Ministry of Transportation and Communications (MOTC) drew criticism for its handling of holiday transportation, after chaos erupted at the high-speed rail (HSR) stations in Nangang, Taipei and Taoyuan on the day before the long weekend began. A large number of passengers of non-reserved seat cabins reportedly overflowed to reserved seat cabins, causing many with reserved seats unable to get on their train on time.
Photo: Lo Hsin-chen, Taipei Times
Chen and Taiwan High Speed Rail Corp (THSRC) chairman Shih Che (史哲) were in Berlin to showcase Taiwan’s railway systems at the international transportation technology fair InnoTrains before the long weekend began.
Chen said that he monitored the traffic online on the return flight to Taipei on Thursday last week, arrived at 5am on Friday and inspected the operations of all transportation hubs throughout the long weekend.
The number of HSR passengers on Thursday alone was a record-high 348,000, Chen said, adding that the high-speed rail operator reached the limit of the service capacity that day, running 200 train services.
Taiwan Railway Corp (TRC) also reported a record-high number of travelers, he said.
“The goal of the holiday transportation plan is not to leave any traveler behind at major transport hubs, and we achieved that goal on the first two days of the long weekend, whether they were at the airport, train station or bust station,” he said.
“I oversaw the holiday traffic the entire time, whether online or offline, and monitored trending holiday traffic posts on social media. I have also asked bus operators to increase Yilan-bound bus services to bring travelers home,” he said.
“Overseeing [the transportation system] does not have to be done in the office. The point is directing it and ensuring that all travelers reach their desired destinations,” he added.
Chen said that attending the InnoTrains was equally important, as this was the first time there was a Taiwan Pavilion in the world’s largest railway exhibition.
As Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co’s fab in Germany is slated to begin mass production next year and business travel between the two countries is expected to increase, Chen said he used the trip to meet with German civil aviation officials to discuss increasing flights between the two countries.
On Friday, the ministry issued a statement saying that the number of high-speed rail passengers on Thursday surpassed the 338,000 recorded during the Mid-Autumn Festival in 2023.
More than 846,000 passengers took TRC trains on the same day, about 1.3 times more than its daily average, the data showed.
While the number of freeway bus travelers was comparable with that of the same time last year, those traveling between Taipei and Yilan County topped 38,000 this year, 1.5 times more than the daily average, the ministry said.
For the last day of the holiday, THSRC set up an emergency command center at its Taichung Station at 11am yesterday to prepare for the post-holiday travel peak. Chen also visited the station to inspect preparations and hear a briefing from the operator.
The company said it had arranged for eight southbound trains running between Nangang and Taichung to park at the northbound platform upon arriving in Taichung, saving about one hour in preparation and turnaround time per train. The measure allowed the company to operate at least one extra northbound train per hour during the peak period, with nine-car trains providing unreserved seating to help clear crowds north of Taichung.
Starting at 1pm yesterday, the operator also added four northbound all-unreserved-seat trains, excluding business-class cars, stopping at all stations along the route. Two of the trains departed from Chiayi for the first time, reducing waiting time for unreserved-seat riders at stations in Chiayi, Yunlin and Changhua, helping ease congestion.
TRC also added a Chu-Kuang Express and increased stops by four Tzuchiang Express trains at the New Wuri Station, and added another Tzuchiang Express and a local express train between Changhua County and Cidu (七堵) yesterday afternoon.

DPP screens film honoring feminist Peng Wan-ru
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
16:40:05 UTC
01:40:05 KST

President William Lai (賴清德) yesterday attended the screening of a film marking the 30th anniversary of the murder of prominent feminist and women’s rights activist Peng Wan-ru (彭婉如).
Peng became the first director of the Democratic Progressive Party’s (DPP) Department of Women’s Affairs in 1996. On Nov. 30 that year, while in Kaohsiung for a party meeting, she disappeared after apparently taking a taxi. Her body was found several days later. Her murder remains unsolved.
The DPP’s Department of Gender Equality spent 18 months producing Dear Sisters (親愛的姊妹), a commemorative film about Peng and the history of women’s participation in politics.
Photo: Ge You-hao, Taipei Times
An 18-minute special edition was screened in Kaohsiung yesterday, with Lai, who is also DPP chairman, attending.
This year is also the 40th anniversary of the party’s founding and the 30th anniversary of the establishment of its women’s affairs department.
Lai said it was meaningful to gather to remember Peng, adding that the party has continued to pursue her vision of greater participation by women in politics.
“For me, Peng has never left us,” he said, adding that he keeps in mind Peng’s proposed “one-quarter quota” to guarantee women’s participation in politics.
The DPP and Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) later adopted the provision, and the government passed the Sexual Assault Crime Prevention Act (性侵害犯罪防治法) and Domestic Violence Prevention Act (家庭暴力防治法), he said.
“The ideals proposed by Peng are what we have continued to work on,” Lai said.
For the film, the Department of Gender Equality interviewed women from different generations about their experiences in politics and public life.
Department of Gender Equality Director Li Yen-jung (李晏榕) said the film is not only a documentary, but also a story about women’s participation in politics, democracy and the continuation of that legacy.

Protesters to call for lawmakers to get back to work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
16:40:05 UTC
01:40:05 KST

More than 40 civic groups are planning to protest outside the Legislative Yuan today, calling for opposition lawmakers to “stop slacking off,” as the new legislative session opens.
The campaign, called “No slacking off as the legislative session opens, citizens sound the alert after work,” is being organized by the Taiwan Citizen Front and Taiwan Economic Democracy Union, among others.
They are calling for legislators to not stall the review of the 2026 fiscal year supplementary budget, prioritize domestic drone development, stop “paralyzing state institutions” and end delays in funding social welfare programs.
Photo: George Tsorng, Taipei Times
Lawmakers from the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and the Taiwan People’s Party, who together hold a majority in the legislature, have repeatedly blocked the review of major livelihood bills, delayed reviewing the central government budget and boycotted the confirmation of personnel appointments, including Constitutional Court justices, and commissioners for the Central Election Commission and the National Communications Commission, Taiwan Economic Democracy Union convener Lai Chung-chiang (賴中強) said.
The campaign seeks to address concerns over national security, public welfare funding and the paralysis of constitutional bodies, he said.
The groups would also issue four “alerts” to convey the urgency of these demands, he added.
First, the Fifth Plenary Session of the 19th Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) in October 2020 set a goal to achieve a fully modern military by the centennial of the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) on Aug. 1 next year, Lai said.
The CCP is only about 10 months from its set goal to accelerate the PLA’s military modernization to target Taiwan and “safeguard its national sovereignty,” he said.
Second, the PLA is boosting its maritime combat capabilities, with its Type 076 landing helicopter dock the Sichuan (四川) already starting sea trials and three Type 071 amphibious transport dock vessels under construction, he said.
Both directly threaten security in the Taiwan Strait, he added.
Third, Taiwan should learn lessons from Ukraine and develop drones to engage in asymmetric warfare, constructing a “hellscape” in the Taiwan Strait, Lai said, citing a report by Washington-based think tank Center for a New American Security.
However, the legislature cut the budget for those efforts from the special defense budget in May, he said, adding that the Executive Yuan has proposed restoring it in a supplementary budget for this year.
With only 93 days remaining in the year, if the legislature fails to complete the review, the supplementary budget would lose its legal effect, he said.
Last, the Legislative Yuan should pass the supplementary budgets by the end of next month, Lai said.
Even after the supplementary budget passes the legislature’s third reading, the defense budget still needs to go through bidding, contracting and processing, he said.
Therefore, the legislature must pass it within one month in the new legislative session, leaving at least two months for the military to execute the budget, he added.

Military seeks to quadruple ammo stockpile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
16:40:04 UTC
01:40:04 KST

The military aims to quadruple its stockpile of combat ammunition from 30 days to 120 days under a six-year, NT$27.59 billion (US$868.16 million) procurement program to bolster its ability to sustain operations in a blockade, according to the Ministry of National Defense’s budget proposal for next year.
The ministry allocated NT$7.3 billion for the ammunition replenishment program after the Executive Yuan approved it on Sept. 3.
The ministry is expected to allocate the same amount to the program next year.
Department of Strategic Planning Director Lieutenant General Huang Wen-chi (黃文?) earlier this month said the program must be accelerated to replenish ammunition depleted during military exercises and drills, which have become more frequent in the past few years.
The defense budget documents for next year that the ministry submitted to the legislature showed that it is not a single-year procurement, but a six-year program.
In a special briefing at the legislature in March, the ministry said that before newly built and expanded domestic defense production lines are fully operational, the military plans to prioritize one-off purchases of 120mm and 105mm tank rounds, 30mm cannon rounds, 155mm howitzer propellant charges and high-energy explosives to replenish wartime stockpiles and meet the heavy ammunition consumption expected during high-intensity combat.
The ministry previously included ammunition procurement, as well as the construction and expansion of domestic defense production lines, in the Executive Yuan’s Special Act for Strengthening Defense Resilience and Asymmetric Capabilities (強化防衛韌性及不對稱戰力計畫採購特別條例), which provides for an eight-year special defense budget of NT$1.25 trillion.
The purpose was to replenish the ammunition stockpile and increase the domestic production capacity for ammunition.
However, the legislature capped the special defense budget at NT$780 billion, prioritizing the procurement of US military weapons while excluding funding for general-purpose ammunition purchases and the construction or expansion of arms production lines.

Taiwanese students rank among the world’s top five in major international assessments 台灣學子國際評比表現亮眼　數學、科學、閱讀等多項進入全球前五
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
16:40:03 UTC
01:40:03 KST

Taiwanese students have achieved impressive results in four major international assessments in recent years. Across mathematics, science, reading, civic knowledge, computer and information literacy, computational thinking and problem-solving, Taiwanese students ranked among the world’s top five. They ranked first in the world in civic knowledge and computational thinking, reflecting concrete results from the 12-year Basic Education Curriculum’s emphasis on competency-based learning.
Concrete Results from the 12-year Basic Education Curriculum
The Trends in International Mathematics and Science Study (TIMSS) assesses fourth- and eighth-grade students in mathematics and science, with 70 countries and education systems participating. In 2023, Taiwan’s fourth-graders ranked second in the world in mathematics and third in science, while eighth-graders ranked second in both mathematics and science.
The International Civic and Citizenship Education Study (ICCS) assesses civic knowledge among eighth-graders, with about 24 countries and education systems participating. In 2022, Taiwan ranked first in the world in civic knowledge.
The International Computer and Information Literacy Study (ICILS) assesses eighth-graders’ computer and information literacy as well as computational thinking. A total of 35 countries and regions participated. In 2023, Taiwan ranked first in the world in computational thinking and fourth in computer and information literacy.
The Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) assesses the mathematics, science and reading literacy of 15-year-old students, with about 91 countries and education systems participating. In 2025, Taiwan ranked fourth in science, third in reading and fourth in mathematics, while ranking fifth in computational problem-solving.
Education Minister Thanks Teachers for Their Dedication
Education Minister Cheng Ying-yao said the results Taiwanese students have achieved in the international assessments are a source of pride. In addition to the government’s forward-looking education policies and investment in education, he expressed his gratitude to teachers for upholding their professional commitment and devoting themselves to educating students, as well as to parents for their support.
“Teachers are the unsung heroes supporting the talent and development of Taiwan’s technology industry,” Cheng said. Ahead of Teachers’ Day, he paid tribute to teachers and called on society to have greater confidence in Taiwan’s education system.
Strong Performance in Academic, Digital and Civic Literacy
Tseng Fen-lan, deputy director of the National Taiwan Normal University Center for Educational and Psychological Research and Testing, said Taiwan ranks among the world’s leading group in three major areas: academic, digital and civic literacy.
Taiwan’s strength is no longer limited to outstanding performance in a single subject, she said. Instead, it has developed a comprehensive advantage in talent development. The results stem from stable basic education, a strong tradition in mathematics and science education, competency-based curriculum reforms and the long-term accumulation of efforts in reading, information technology and civic education.
Students Receive Balanced, High-Quality Education
Tseng said the 12-year Basic Education system has enabled most students to receive relatively balanced educational opportunities and quality.
Taiwan’s mathematics and science education emphasizes logical reasoning, problem analysis and mastery of knowledge and skills. The 2019 curriculum guidelines, commonly known as the 108 Curriculum, further strengthened inquiry-based learning, hands-on exploration, interdisciplinary learning and problem-solving.
International assessments increasingly emphasize the application of knowledge to real-world situations, civic judgment and digital problem-solving. Taiwan’s students consistently rank near the top in these areas, indicating that the competency-based curriculum reforms are increasingly reflected in student performance.
International Assessments Provide Important Reference for Curriculum Review
Deputy Education Minister Chang Liao Wan-chien said the strong results reflect the achievements of the 12-year Basic Education Curriculum in strengthening competency-based learning, inquiry-based practice and interdisciplinary learning.
International assessments can also help identify students’ learning outcomes and areas that need improvement, providing an important reference for reviewing curricula and education policies, he said.
(Translated by Lin Lee-kai, Taipei Times)

Asian Games put regional sports in limelight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
16:40:01 UTC
01:40:01 KST

One of the joys of the Asian Games is stumbling onto sports that do not get wide attention beyond the continent. There are many regional sports being played — sepak takraw or wushu or kurash, for instance — but the curiosity champion is probably kabaddi.
The Games offer all the Olympic regulars, but they share the stage with the regional offerings that are not dominated by powerhouse countries such as China and Japan.
Kabaddi origins are believed to be on the Indian subcontinent, and it is so popular that professional leagues there draw millions of viewers. It is a contact team sport, and early history says it was played to enhance strength, agility, breath control and self-defense skills.
Photo: AP
India won both finals in these Asian Games, defeating Iran on the women’s side 37-34. The Indian men defeated Iran 40-34.
Pawan Kumar, a top Indian player, talked after the victory the same way any winning team player would, explaining strategy, in-game adjustments and delving into the nuances of the game.
“Once we had the lead, we wanted to protect it,” Kumar said. “So we played [it] safe ... and used the time available to us. That helped us maintain our advantage until the end.”
Photo: EPA
The sport involves no ball, no bat, no goals, no rackets. It showcases tags, tackles and wrestling moves, and was played in the 1936 Berlin Olympics as a demonstration sport, but did not gain a global following,
The sport bears a rough resemblance to the schoolyard game known in the US as “red rover,” or a game known in England as “British bulldog.”
In the format used at the Asian Games, two teams with seven players each compete on a small court. The court is rectangular, but another version is played on a circular surface.
A single player on the offense — called a “raider” — crosses the centerline and tries in 30 seconds to touch as many players as possible on the other side and return across the centerline without being tackled.
It is played in a pair of 20-minute halves. Points are earned by tagging opponents, or by stopping the raider.
Meanwhile, sepak takraw is essentially volleyball, with a few big differences: Players cannot use their hands — they can use anything else — and the ball is primarily kicked over a 1.55m high net. There are two, three or four players on each side. In the US, the sport is often known as “kick volleyball.”
Like volleyball, the goal is to get the ball to hit the ground on the opponent’s side of the net. The ball is smaller than a volleyball or soccer ball — about the size of a cantaloupe or a large grapefruit . The game has its roots in Southeast Asia.
Wushu, also known as kung fu, is the Chinese term for “martial arts.” It has had a presence in the Asian Games since 1990 when it was introduced at the games in Beijing. It has also been proposed as an Olympic sport, but has never been voted in.
Competition in taolu involves performing sets and choreographed routines that show off principles of attack and defense. Sanda is the full-contact version of the sport and is often known as Chinese kickboxing.
Kurash involves a range of folk wrestling styles that are popular in Central Asia. It was first introduced into the Asian Games in 2018 in Indonesia when Uzbekistan topped the medal table in the sport. Historians say the sport dates back thousands of years. Taiwan, Iran, Mongolia and India also won multiple medals in 2018.
Japan has been starved of swimming success in recent times but with the Olympics two years away junk food-loving teenager Shin Ohashi has emerged as their next big hope. The 17-year-old, who stands just 169cm, has posted the two fastest 200m breaststroke times in the world this year and is aiming for the world record at this year’s Asian Games. Earlier this year he came within almost a second of the 2:05.48 record held by China’s Qin Haiyang. Ohashi has already won gold at the Asian Games in the 100m breaststroke after a dead heat with China’s Dong Zhihao, beating Qin into third

After hours of fraught meetings among the players and occasionally involving coaches and officials, FAI chief executive officer David Courell said at a news conference that had been delayed by several hours that a “significant majority” of the squad had agreed to play the game in Hungary, but it was far from a unanimous decision. Cambodia says it is fighting scammers, but skeptics persist

Cambodia is gathering evidence against “masterminds” of massive cyberfraud operations, the country’s anti-scam minister said, amid criticism that the government’s crackdown has failed to get to those ultimately responsible.
Legal action, “whether it involves the mastermind, the co-conspirator, owner, enabler or protector, it requires time and also it requires evidence,” said Senior Minister Chhay Sinarith, who heads a government commission on combating fraud, said on the sidelines of a global anti-scam conference in Phnom Penh on Thursday.
He said that information given by international partners had enabled action against some suspects and that premature disclosure of investigations could allow suspects to flee.
Photo: AP
Cambodia this week hosted representatives of more than a dozen countries for discussions about tackling scam groups.
Cambodia and other Southeast Asian nations emerged after the pandemic as hubs for industrial-sized scam centers where workers are trafficked, detained in grim conditions and forced to defraud strangers online. The US said scam compounds in the region stole US$10 billion from Americans alone in 2024.
Chhay said last month that Cambodia had dismantled large-scale scam compounds since it began a year-long crackdown, although it did not provide a full list of the sites it has raided. Analysts are skeptical, saying that the operation left high-level figures and guardians of the industry unscathed.
“It’s clear that many large compounds remain active despite other operators clearing out and dispersing into smaller, decentralized sites,” said John Wojcik, a senior analyst at blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs. “The technology, payment rails, money-laundering networks and facilitators underpinning the industry also continue to operate at scale.”
Chhay said authorities are expanding their investigation into the financial network of Prince Group, a Cambodia-based conglomerate the US said was a front for multibillion-dollar online fraud and money laundering operations.
Its Chinese-born founder, Chen Zhi, was arrested and deported to China from Cambodia earlier this year.
Reporters toured two facilities outside of Phnom Penh that Cambodian authorities said were scam centers belonging to Prince Group — complexes that officials said housed thousands of workers. One had a fake Singaporean police station allegedly used for impersonation fraud.
A Prince Group spokesperson said the facilities “have not been and never were associated with,” the company.

Taiwanese recruiters host event in US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
16:39:58 UTC
01:39:58 KST

Fourteen Taiwanese tech companies and the National Development Council (NDC) on Saturday held a talent recruitment campaign at the annual Taiwan Tech Summit in Silicon Valley, which offered more than 1,000 job openings in Taiwan.
The campaign, called Taiwan Career Day, has been a staple in one form or another at the summit since the summit’s inception in 2022, and this year’s version attracted 3,000 visitors, the NDC said.
NDC Minister Yeh Chun-hsien (葉俊顯) said that locating the overseas talent recruitment platform in Silicon Valley was critical given that Taiwan continues to develop key tech sectors such as artificial intelligence (AI) and semiconductors, and faces global competition for talent.
Photo courtesy of the National Development Council
The initiative is aimed at bringing talent services directly to where talent is, and promoting job and career development opportunities in Taiwan, Yeh said.
It gives skilled international tech workers an opportunity to learn more about Taiwan and explore career opportunities through direct contact with Taiwanese companies, he said.
Among the Taiwanese companies participating in Taiwan Career Day were Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (台積電), Delta Electronics Inc (台達電), Taiwan Mobile Co (台灣大哥大), Micron Taiwan, Wistron Corp (緯創), MediaTek Inc (聯發科) and Applied Materials Taiwan, the NDC said.
At the fair, 14 companies were seeking skilled tech workers in such fields as semiconductors, information and communications technology, software and AI development, it said.
Several Taiwanese research institutions, including Academia Sinica and the Industrial Technology Research Institute, and universities also took part in the job fair and arranged one-on-one interviews for teaching and research positions.
In addition to the NDC, the Ministry of Digital Affairs, the National Immigration Agency, the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Taiwan’s overseas offices set up booths at the job fair to promote the nation’s efforts to recruit foreign talent.
At the recruitment event, Michael Foley, a senior software engineer at US software developer Salesforce Inc, received his Employment Gold Card from Yeh.
Launched by the NDC in 2018, the Employment Gold Card program aims to attract skilled professionals in 12 fields, including digital technology, finance, arts and culture, law, and science and technology.
The card combines a work permit, resident visa, Alien Resident Certificate and re-entry permit, allowing holders to seek employment freely in Taiwan. It also grants work rights to spouses, access to the national health insurance system for dependents and tax incentives.

Italy's Meloni passes by-election test against new far-right rival
ROME, Sept 28 - Italy's ruling coalition won a closely watched by-election in the southern region of Calabria on Monday, the first major test for Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni against a new far-right foe ahead of a general election due next year.
National Future, led by former army general Roberto Vannacci, has surged to around 9% in opinion polls since its launch in February, overtaking Meloni's junior coalition partners and challenging the right in the conservative constituency of Reggio Calabria.
However, the party's bid fell short, with the government candidate taking about 53% of the vote, while Vannacci's nominee secured roughly 10%, according to a partial count.
Analysts had predicted a stronger showing for Vannacci in a traditionally rightist stronghold, saying he might have split the right-wing vote and handed victory to the centre-left.
"We won by a landslide," Roberto Occhiuto, governor of Calabria and deputy leader of the coalition party Forza Italia, said in a video posted on X.
AI-MANIPULATED IMAGE
Support for Vannacci has grown nationwide on the back of his anti-migrant rhetoric and calls for what he describes as traditional Italian values.
His rise has unsettled Meloni and could complicate her re-election prospects, drawing away voters who backed her coalition at the last national ballot in 2022.
Pollsters have said she could keep hold of power if she forged an alliance with Vannacci. But any such tie-up would cause tension within government ranks.
Parliament undersecretary Matilde Siracusano, a Forza Italia lawmaker and Occhiuto's partner, warned that any electoral pact with National Future would pose "a serious problem". She has said she will sue Vannacci after he posted an AI-generated image on social media showing her wearing a revealing, low-cut top.
The centre-left candidate in the by-election won about 35% of the vote, improving on the bloc's performance in 2022, although turnout was just 22% against 49.4% four years ago.
"With turnout extremely low, strong media attention and a candidate with significant personal backing, I believe Vannacci expected a far better showing," said Lorenzo Pregliasco, the head of polling firm YouTrend.
Vannacci himself did not immediately comment on the result. REUTERS

Psychedelics reduce bottom-up brain activity in the default mode network
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
16:00:53 UTC
01:00:53 KST

Psychedelic drugs like LSD and psilocybin reduce the amount of bottom-up brain activity flowing into a network associated with self-reflection. These altered trajectories of brain signals occur consistently across humans and mice, offering a biological explanation for how these drugs reshape the mind. The findings were published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
Psychedelics are gaining attention as potential psychiatric treatments for conditions like depression and trauma. To understand their therapeutic benefits and risks, researchers need to know exactly how these substances alter brain function. Prior research has identified that psychedelics affect the default mode network, a collection of brain regions responsible for introspection, daydreaming, and mental rigidity. Many psychiatric conditions involve abnormal activity in this specific network, making it a primary target for new treatments.
The default mode network sits at the top of a processing hierarchy in the brain. Brain activity constantly moves across the surface of the cortex, which is the brain’s outer layer. Information travels from lower-order sensory areas up into higher-order areas like the default mode network, a process known as bottom-up processing. The reverse movement, from higher cognitive regions down to sensory regions, is called top-down processing.
In a healthy brain, bottom-up processing updates our internal models with new information from the outside world. Top-down processing uses our past experiences and expectations to make sense of that incoming sensory data. An imbalance between these two directions of information flow can lead to psychological distress or perceptual errors.
Past imaging studies typically measured brain activity in static regions, treating the brain as a set of fixed locations. This approach ignores the continuous, wave-like movement of signals across the brain’s surface. Analyzing static brain regions is similar to measuring the total rainfall in a single county without tracking the movement of the storm system on a weather radar. By treating the brain as a collection of isolated points, traditional research methods might obscure the true dynamics of how different brain areas communicate over time.
Adam R. Pines, Leanne M. Williams, and their colleagues at Stanford University wanted to observe these moving signals directly. They adapted an analytical technique called optical flow, which tracks the frame-by-frame movement of pixels in a video. The team used this mathematical approach to track the direction and size of brain activity waves moving across the cortex.
The researchers first analyzed a small study of 14 human volunteers who received MDMA. They compared functional magnetic resonance imaging scans taken after the participants took MDMA to scans taken after a placebo pill or no drug at all. The optical flow analysis revealed a consistent pattern across the subjects.
The team found that MDMA reduced the overall magnitude of brain waves moving through the default mode network. The drug also reduced the proportion of signals traveling in a bottom-up direction into the network.
Next, the team examined a second small study involving six human participants who ingested psilocybin. The researchers compared brain scans from the psilocybin sessions to baseline scans and to an active placebo condition. For the active placebo, participants received a dose of the stimulant methylphenidate. This stimulant mimics the physical arousal of psilocybin without the psychedelic effects.
As with MDMA, psilocybin reduced the overall magnitude of propagating brain waves in the default mode network. The reduction in bottom-up directionality was also present but was not statistically significant. The researchers suspect this weaker result occurred because the effects of psilocybin lingered for days. This persistence may have artificially altered the baseline scans taken shortly after the drug sessions.
In a third small study, 18 human volunteers received an intravenous infusion of LSD. The researchers compared their brain activity to scans taken after a saline placebo infusion. Consistent with the other substances, LSD reduced both the magnitude of the moving brain waves and the proportion of bottom-up signals entering the default mode network.
To ensure these effects were not unique to humans or specific to magnetic resonance imaging, the team looked at a small study of 14 mice. They used widefield calcium imaging, a technique that directly records the physical activity of brain cells with high resolution. The mice received LSD, a sedative called diazepam, or a different sedative called dexmedetomidine.
Like the human participants, mice given LSD showed reduced magnitude and bottom-up flow of brain activity in the default mode network. Diazepam, an anti-anxiety medication, also reduced bottom-up signals, though to a lesser extent than LSD. Dexmedetomidine produced the exact opposite effect, increasing the proportion of bottom-up signals entering the network. These animal results confirmed that the optical flow technique measures actual changes in nerve cell activity rather than artifacts of blood flow.
The researchers also investigated whether these changes in moving brain activity related to the subjective experiences reported by the human volunteers. In the MDMA study, participants who experienced the greatest reduction in bottom-up processing also reported the most intense feelings of impaired control. They also reported a greater dread of ego dissolution, which is a fearful reaction to losing one’s sense of self.
This psychological correlation suggests that suppressing bottom-up information flow too much could trigger the negative experiences sometimes associated with psychedelics. Bottom-up processing normally grounds individuals in their immediate sensory environment. A severe drop in this grounding input might leave individuals feeling detached or at the mercy of their unanchored internal thoughts.
Some psychiatric conditions, such as ruminative depression, are characterized by excessive automatic thoughts and abnormal bottom-up signaling. Reducing bottom-up flow might explain why psychedelics offer relief for some patients with depression. The drugs could temporarily quiet the intrusive signals feeding into the default mode network.
Individuals at risk for psychosis already suffer from impaired bottom-up processing. Giving psychedelics to these vulnerable patients could exacerbate their symptoms. The drugs might overpower their ability to update internal beliefs with external reality.
The sample sizes across all four datasets are small, which limits the ability to account for individual differences in how people react to these drugs. Larger datasets will be necessary to map out how different psychedelics affect people with varied biological backgrounds. Expanding the number of participants could reveal more subtle alterations to brain activity flow that this initial analysis missed.
The optical flow analysis focused exclusively on the outer surface of the brain. Psychedelics also heavily influence deep brain structures, but tracking moving signals between these buried regions and the surface remains computationally out of reach for this specific technique. The imaging technologies used in human participants also have limits in their spatial and temporal resolution. These equipment limitations mean researchers might miss faster changes in brain signaling.
Finally, the studies relied entirely on healthy volunteers and laboratory mice. Future research will need to test these observations in clinical populations to determine how these changes in brain activity relate to therapeutic outcomes. Understanding the exact mechanisms of psychedelic action could help doctors identify which patients are most likely to benefit from these treatments and which patients might be harmed by them.
The study, “Psychedelics disrupt hierarchical cortical propagations in the default mode network of humans and mice,” was authored by Adam R. Pines, Xue Zhang, John Kochalka, Sam S. Vesuna, Isaac V. Kauvar, Divya Rajasekharan, T. Rick Reneau, Teddy J. Akiki, Laura M. Hack, Joshua S. Siegel, and Leanne M. Williams.

French far-right leader Bardella says he has filed lawsuit over antisemitic remarks claim
PARIS, Sept 28 - French far-right leader Jordan Bardella said on Monday he had filed a defamation lawsuit against investigative website Mediapart over a report alleging he made antisemitic remarks in private messages over a decade ago, saying the story was an effort to "destabilise" campaigning ahead of next year's election.
The 31-year-old leads the far-right National Rally (RN) party which is seeking to clear its racist image and build close ties with Israel. The party's candidate, Marine Le Pen, is leading polls for the April presidential election.
Mediapart, in a report published on Monday, said it had reviewed dozens of private messages from 2013 to 2015 — the early years of Bardella's career in the National Front, the forerunner of the RN — that it said showed a pattern of antisemitic and conspiratorial rhetoric.
Mediapart cited one message in which it said Bardella claimed "all the banks are owned by Jews".
The left-leaning outlet, which has a long history of unearthing political scandals in France, said it had independently authenticated the private messages. Reuters did not independently authenticate them.
Mediapart said it also drew on first-hand accounts of former party colleagues, whom it identified by first name and last initial.
Speaking on broadcaster CNews, Bardella said: "These statements are completely delusional. They are not mine."
He added, "There is clearly an attempt to destabilise the campaign, coincidentally, just months before an election where we are leading in the polls. Again, I believe the French people are not fooled. They see that everything is being done to undermine us."
Bardella has become the face of the RN's decade-long effort to "de-demonise", or normalise, its image. He was the party's de facto presidential candidate until July, when an appeals court cleared Le Pen to hold elected office after a conviction over misuse of funds. Bardella will be France's prime minister if she wins next year's vote.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot wrote in a post on social media platform X: "To all those with short memories: antisemitism is not a mere blip for the RN; it is the very history of this party. This is the true face of the far right."
Le Pen, speaking with reporters on Monday, said she believed the report could "only be a fake, a manipulation, a dirty trick".
A Monday poll showed her coming first in next April's first-round vote and beating both leftist and centrist candidates in a May runoff.
A slew of antisemitic, Islamophobic and racist comments by some RN candidates derailed the party's hopes of winning a parliamentary majority in France's legislative vote in 2024. Bardella at the time pledged to avoid such "casting errors" in the future by systematically kicking out any candidates with a history of toxic statements. REUTERS

Renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia as MSF teams scale up medical response to increase in war-wounded
Share
Project Update28 September 2026
The current situation in northern Ethiopia is very worrying, as conflict between the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and their allies, and the Ethiopian National Defence Forces has resumed. The conflict resumes following a period of increased tensions, large-scale fighting, and drone strikes, which has shattered a fragile 2022 peace agreement. Since 22 September, teams from Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) have increased activities to respond to the increase in the number of patients as a result of the current hostilities.
The number of war-wounded patients received in Korem and Alamata hospitals rose over a 48-hour period from around 180 to more than 420 between 22 and 25 September. In northwestern Tigray, MSF teams supported the influx of patients at Suhul hospital in Shire, as more than 300 war-wounded patients arrived up to 25 September.
Our teams continue to support healthcare activities in hospitals in Shire, Sheraro, and Korem, including providing maternal and child health care. Due to the current situation, activities at Alamata hospital have now been suspended. Outreach activities have also been suspended due to the security situation, and staff were redirected to provide additional support to hospitals, where we are seeing a sharp increase in war-wounded patients.
We are monitoring community displacement as people flee the conflict, and are preparing to respond to the needs of displaced people in Tigray, Amhara, and Afar regions.
MSF remains concerned for the safety and access to health care for civilians during this period of increased fighting.
Across Ethiopia, MSF supports health facilities in Oromia, Somali, Amhara, Tigray, Afar, Gambella and Southwest Ethiopia regions, providing basic, advanced, and emergency medical care.

ADDIS ABABA, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- The United Nations World Food Program (WFP) on Monday warned of deepening natural and man-made humanitarian challenges in Ethiopia as a "severe" funding shortfall hampers its relief operations.
In its latest Ethiopia country brief, the UN agency noted that Ethiopia, with a population of approximately 140 million, continues to advance a far-reaching economic reform agenda aimed at unlocking long-term growth and strengthening its development trajectory.
It, however, stressed that despite these ambitious reforms, persistent inflation, combined with insecurity, displacement and climate shocks, "continue to erode household resilience and heighten food security concerns."
The agency noted that El Nino-driven rainfall disruptions are further exacerbating the situation by threatening the October-to-January harvest, worsening drought conditions, and heightening food security risks across the Afar, Amhara, Tigray, and Oromia regions, with humanitarian needs expected to rise further through 2027.
To mitigate anticipated impacts, the WFP has advanced preparedness for El Nino-related shocks, including plans for a phased emergency response in the Afar, Amhara, and Tigray regions starting in September, targeting a total of 1.43 million people. The WFP's operational update also noted that some 1.9 million people were assisted in August.
Meanwhile, the UN agency warned that "a severe funding shortfall" is hampering its life-saving operations, with its country portfolio just 46 percent funded for October 2026 to March 2027, leaving a net funding requirement of 251 million U.S. dollars.
It noted that although government emergency response capacity continues to strengthen, funding shortfalls "pose a growing risk to humanitarian operations amid rising food insecurity, displacement, and climate-related needs."
The WFP further voiced concern that increasing insecurity in multiple regions continues to constrain supply routes and delay the timely delivery of assistance. The agency highlighted that its emergency relief operations in Ethiopia prioritize the most food-insecure and vulnerable populations.
Ethiopia also remains one of Africa's top refugee-hosting countries, currently accommodating more than 1.13 million refugees and asylum-seekers, driven by ongoing inflows from Sudan and South Sudan. ■

China Focus: China marks 2,577th anniversary of Confucius' birth
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
23:47:14 CST
00:47:14 KST

JINAN/TAIPEI, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- From Confucius' hometown Qufu in east China's Shandong Province to Taipei on the other side of the Taiwan Strait, various ceremonies were held on Monday to commemorate the 2,577th anniversary of the ancient philosopher's birth.
The celebrations, reflecting the enduring influence of Confucian culture across the Strait, stood as a symbol of China's longstanding efforts to draw strength from its ancient traditions.
Wearing yellow ribbons, participants entered the venue in Qufu at around 10 a.m. and laid flower baskets in front of a statue of Confucius. Zhou Naixiang, governor of Shandong Province, read the eulogy and led the guests in bowing as a sign of respect. The grand ceremony concluded at around 11 a.m.
The tradition of commemorating Confucius dates back to 478 B.C., the year following his death. Today, the ceremonies, featuring traditional music, dance, and other ceremonial forms, embody the essence of propriety in Confucian culture.
"Performing the ancient dance has deepened my understanding of the order and respect embedded in Chinese ritual and music culture," said Liu Junbing, a student at Qufu Normal University who participated in the dance at the commemoration.
"It was my first time witnessing the authentic performance, and I was truly captivated by the unique charm of China's ritual and music culture," said Korepanova Svetlana, a student from Russia.
The commemoration included a live online broadcast, featuring ceremonies from more than 60 Confucius temples and cultural institutions around the world. This allowed people everywhere to connect with and experience Confucian culture.
This year's online platform added interactive features, such as AI-driven dialogues with Confucius, certificate generation and interesting trivia games.
"I learned about Confucius while studying Chinese in Tajikistan, and I've always admired his philosophy," said Khusenov Farzinshoh, a student from Tajikistan.
Scholars at the event also emphasized the global significance of Confucian thought.
Bali Ram Deepak, a professor at the Centre for Chinese Studies, Jawaharlal Nehru University, who has translated the Confucianism classic Four Books into Hindi, told Xinhua that mutual learning between cultures helps enhance understanding and promote harmony.
Meanwhile, in the southeastern corner of the country, on the other side of the Taiwan Strait, another solemn ceremony was held in Taipei Confucius Temple to commemorate the sage's 2,577th birthday, drawing hundreds of people from across the city.
The 90-minute ceremony began at 6 a.m. on Monday and followed a traditional ritual of 37 ceremonial procedures accompanied by traditional music and dance, regarded as the most completely preserved in Taiwan.
Among them was Chang Tsung-i, a student at Taiwan Normal University who served as a ceremonial attendant. He has participated in the annual ceremony for several years, taking on roles such as dancer, musician and ceremonial attendant, and also helps train musicians for the ceremony.
"This is also a form of inheritance," Chang said. "Through the ceremony, people can gradually understand the meaning of 'Li,' or ritual, and, in turn, gain a better understanding of how to live."
The Taipei Confucius Temple was originally built during the late Qing Dynasty (1644-1911). It was demolished during Japanese colonial rule to make way for a Japanese-language school and was later relocated and rebuilt.
Lin Yi-hua, Taipei deputy mayor who served as the principal presentation officer, said in a speech that the temple is an important cultural landmark in Taipei and a historic site where the Confucian tradition has been preserved and continued.
The annual ceremony not only commemorates and carries forward the spirit of Confucius, Lin said, but also helps ensure that traditional ritual and music culture remains visible and appreciated in contemporary society.
There are more than 40 Confucian temples of various sizes across the island. Similar ceremonies were also held on Monday in cities including Taoyuan, Tainan and Taichung.
"Commemorating Confucius today is not only about honoring the sage, but also about revisiting and passing on the values of Chinese civilization," said Kong Deli, president of the China Confucius Research Institute.
Confucius (551-479 B.C.) founded a school of thought that profoundly influenced later generations, which became known as Confucianism. He was also the first to establish private schools in China, admitting students from all social classes.
Kong noted that Confucius' advocacy of "harmony without uniformity" and "people-centeredness" provides an important value foundation for managing relations among individuals, nations and civilizations. ■

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Lin Shidong walked out of the players' tunnel Monday night with a calm look in his eyes, his first Asian Games campaign finally over.
The 21-year-old Chinese competed in four table tennis events at the 2026 Asian Games and left with three gold medals and a silver, winning the men's singles, mixed doubles and men's doubles titles.
"I had asked some of my seniors what to expect, but you only really understand it once you're here," Lin said. "You may not get many chances like this in a lifetime, so I really treasured it."
Facing world No. 1 and compatriot Wang Chuqin in the men's singles final Monday night, Lin produced one of his most convincing performances of the tournament, winning 4-0 to claim his first Asian Games singles title.
"I didn't expect to win 4-0. I was able to attack well and connect my shots effectively," Lin said.
Wang said Lin was a deserving champion after emerging from a difficult period.
"I think he fully deserved the title," Wang said. "He may have gone through a difficult period, but he has bounced back. Athletes all go through ups and downs. As long as you have what it takes, there will always be another chance."
Lin's path to the title had been anything but straightforward.
In Monday's semifinal, he trailed Chinese Taipei's Lin Yun-ju 2-0 before fighting back to win 4-3.
"He played particularly well in the first two games, but I didn't give up," Lin said. "Even when I was trailing by a lot, I kept thinking about chasing one point at a time."
He had faced another stern test in the quarterfinals, beating Japan's world No. 3 Sora Matsushima 4-2.
"I think I ultimately lost to him in terms of concentration and the will to win," Matsushima said.
Those victories formed part of a demanding campaign in which Lin repeatedly switched between events.
In mixed doubles, Lin partnered Kuai Man to a 4-0 victory over defending champions Wang and Sun Yingsha in the final.
"I had just finished the singles and didn't have much time before going into the mixed doubles final," Lin said with a smile. "I was still in the state of the match, so I could just go straight in and play."
Lin also claimed the men's doubles title alongside Huang Youzheng. The Chinese pair trailed Japan's Tomokazu Harimoto and Hiroto Shinozuka 2-1 in the final before recovering to win 4-2.
By the end of his first Asian Games, Lin had played 20 matches across four events, collecting three gold medals and a silver.
More important for the 21-year-old was the experience of navigating the pressure and intensity of a multi-sport Games for the first time.
"The intensity was very high, the pressure was huge, and every opponent was strong," Lin said. "All I could do was focus on myself and take it one point at a time."
That approach had carried him through his toughest matches and, eventually, to the top of the men's singles podium.
"Getting through such difficult matches means a lot to me," Lin said. "I hope I can build on this and take another step forward after the Asiad." ■

BEIJING, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- China plans to complete a new-generation geologic map of Mars by the end of 2028, aiming to reconstruct the red planet's watery past and introduce a Chinese system for dividing Martian geologic time.
Hou Zengqian, an academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and chief scientist of the Tianwen-3 Mars sample-return mission, revealed the plan at a symposium held Monday at the Institute of Geology under the Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences.
Zhurong, the rover China landed on Mars in 2021 as part of its Tianwen-1 mission, has offered new clues to the planet's water history: a vast ancient ocean still existed some 3.5 billion years ago, and short-lived floods possibly occurred 1.6 billion years ago. These findings, which help fill gaps in the evidence chain of how Mars' ancient climate evolved, will be incorporated into the new map.
On that basis, the new map will lay out a Chinese scheme for dividing Martian geologic time. The current timeline splits Mars into the Noachian, Hesperian and Amazonian periods, defined by densities of visible craters rather than absolute dates. China aims to make its new scheme an international consensus, Hou said.
The project will primarily utilize the data from Tianwen-1, supplemented by U.S. and ESA (European Space Agency) Mars probe data, enabling the integration of orbital and ground-based data. By fusing imagery, spectra, radar, gravity and magnetic readings, a global database will be built that couples the planet's multiple physical fields.
Artificial intelligence will sit at the heart of interpreting those data: geologists' expertise will be embedded in large models through rule engines to keep the results explainable, while multi-scale attention techniques will help form progressive feature extraction from local mineral identification all the way to global tectonic units division.
The deliverables, due by the end of 2028, include a 1:5 million-scale Martian geologic map, a 1:50,000-scale map of the landing area and a series of thematic atlases. The project will also release the world's first intelligent geologic map of Mars and provide a template for future mapping of the moon, Venus and asteroids.
Geologic mapping has been a core task of the institute for 70 years, said its director Yang Zhiming, with its maps extending from regional and national charts to the moon and now Mars. That work, he explained, has given China's planetary program the scientific grounding to decide where to go, what to explore and why. ■
