Surprising result seen in primordial matter inside atom smasher
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
14:50:26 UTC
23:50:26 KST

When the universe was born, space was too hot and dense for atoms to exist. Even the constituents of atoms—the protons and neutrons that make up atomic nuclei—couldn’t immediately coalesce. Instead the newborn cosmos was filled with even smaller and more fundamental building blocks, quarks and gluons, which formed a smoothly flowing soup called quark-gluon plasma.
Soon, though, the universe expanded, cooling down the soup. Gluons glued quarks together to make protons and neutrons, which floated around as a gas rather than a plasma. The change marked a phase transition, just as water can switch from vapor to liquid to solid ice. But key details of this profound primordial transition, such as its threshold energy and density, have remained deeply mysterious.
That began to change around the turn of the millennium, when physicists started smashing gold ions together at nearly the speed of light inside the giant particle accelerator at Brookhaven National Laboratory on Long Island in New York State. Those smashups were so powerful that they briefly re-created the quark-gluon plasma from the big bang. Now researchers analyzing data from those collisions have seen an unexpected signal that offers new clues about how the cosmic transition happened eons ago.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The signal comes from an experiment called the Solenoid Tracker at RHIC (Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider), or STAR. After the gold ions annihilated in collisions and produced new bits of matter, STAR tracked the paths of that debris. One measurement it made compared the particles’ momentum changes with a baseline—in particular, the so-called transverse momentum, the momentum perpendicular to the direction in which the gold ions had been traveling. The STAR data showed a surprising dip in fluctuations of this value—that is, a potential phase transition—at an energy that represents some of the densest states physicists have ever achieved in their studies of nuclear matter. The findings were reported in a paper published recently in Physical Review Letters.
“This measurement is a possible signature that, yes, a phase transition does exist here,” says Rutik Manikandhan of the University of Houston, a member of the STAR team and a co-author of the new analysis. “It hints at the existence of a critical point.”
If scientists discover a critical point—a change in how the phase transition happens at different temperatures and densities—they will better understand how the universe evolved just after it was born. They could also learn what happens to matter at its highest densities, such as within neutron stars, where the mass of an entire star is squeezed into a space about the width of a city.
“We are trying to probe the different phases of matter,” Manikandhan says. “We don’t fully understand what phase of matter is inside neutron stars. We can learn things like ‘What would be the speed of sound inside the core of neutron stars?’” Answering that question would allow astrophysicists to address other mysteries, such as the precise threshold where a neutron star will collapse to form a black hole.
But figuring out what the signal seen by STAR means isn’t easy. “The current data represent an intriguing hint, but they are insufficient to identify the origin of the phenomenon,” says Berndt Mueller, a physicist at Duke University, who wasn’t involved in the experiment. “The problem is that this is only one observable, and it is insufficient to isolate an explanation.”
For instance, instead of a critical point, the dip in momentum fluctuations glimpsed in STAR’s data could simply reflect the fact that as the energy of gold-ion collisions changes, the types of particles being created change, too. At higher energies, more mesons (pairs of quarks and their antimatter counterparts, antiquarks) are present. But at lower energies, more protons and neutrons form. “To make a substantiated claim about the QCD critical endpoint, it is important to rule out such 'trivial' effects, or at least estimate their magnitude with respect to any signals from a critical point,” says Jan Steinheimer, a physicist at the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research in Darmstadt, Germany, who studied this alternative explanation.
Researchers plan to analyze more STAR data to further unravel the mystery. RHIC operated for 25 years and shut down earlier in 2026. Yet the machine gathered reams of data that scientists haven’t been able to study yet. “We still have a lot of STAR data left to analyze,” Manikandhan says.

Beyond melodrama: Khajepasha on war, childhood and duty of Iranian cinema
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
14:47:38 UTC
23:47:38 KST

Beyond melodrama: Khajepasha on war, childhood and duty of Iranian cinema
TEHRAN- Iranian filmmaker Babak Khajepasha believes cinema should do more than portray suffering. For him, a film dealing with war, the death of children, or a social tragedy should leave audiences with questions rather than simply tears.
Khajepasha, whose “In the Arms of the Tree” was selected as Iran’s submission for the 2025 Academy Awards, has repeatedly turned to children and family in his films. His latest feature, “The Land of Angels”, deals with children in Gaza. The film has also taken part in international events, including the Altyn Minbar Kazan International Film Festival, where it received the Grand Prix for Best Feature Film. Khajepasha is also among the jury members of the 2026 BRICS+ International Film Festival in St. Petersburg.
In an interview with the Tehran Times, he spoke about the possibility of making a film on the recent tragedy in Minab, the difficulty of depicting the death of children without reducing cinema to melodrama, his decision to make films during the 40-day war, and what he saw during a recent visit to Hiroshima. He also discussed the international position of Iranian cinema, his earlier criticism of the Oscars and some major festivals, and why family remains one of the subjects he wants to pursue in his future work.
Looking beyond the tragedy
Speaking about the possibility of making a film about the tragedy in Minab, Khajepasha said he would be more interested in exploring the reasons behind such events than simply depicting their devastating consequences.
“The aspect that I, as a filmmaker, can enter and that deserves to be explored is the reason behind this tragedy,” he said, stressing that society should ask why it has been forced to experience such pain.
The filmmaker pointed to the loss of children in different parts of Iran, including Minab, Lamerd, Tabriz and Kermanshah during the recent war, saying that while addressing the suffering of children is important, cinema should also investigate why children repeatedly become victims of conflict and violence.
This concern, he explained, was also central to his research for “The Land of Angels”. During his research and conversations with Palestinians, he encountered stories that demonstrated the profound psychological impact of losing a child.
Khajepasha recalled speaking with a Palestinian father who had been holding his child when the child was killed. According to the filmmaker, the man later repeatedly returned to the same place, hoping that he too would be killed so that he could join his child. The father said he could not understand why he had been left alive.
For Khajepasha, such stories demonstrate that the killing of a child affects much more than the immediate victim. It leaves a psychological wound on the family and, ultimately, the wider community.
Yet he believes that cinema must be careful not to turn such suffering into an exercise in emotional manipulation.
From tears to questions
That is also why Khajepasha is wary of making films about war and children that rely entirely on emotion.
If simply seeing the suffering of children were enough to change the world's response to violence, he said, the many films and documentaries made about Gaza and other conflicts would already have brought about such a change.
“Just talking about how much pain we are in does not necessarily take us a step forward,” he said. “We have to look at this from an intellectual perspective. We have to search for its causes and ask where this pain is supposed to take us.”
For “The Land of Angels”, he wanted the audience to leave with a question.
A viewer may accept that there are fighters, a military conflict and casualties in a war, he explained. But the death of thousands of children should lead to another question: why are these children being killed?
That question, in his view, can open the door to wider discussions about the position of children in contemporary society, the pressures placed on them and even the declining importance attached to having children in some parts of the world.
Khajepasha prefers this kind of cinema to a film that simply asks its audience to cry.
“I don't want to make a film merely so that audiences cry,” he said. “We have to value the film itself. There have to be other reasons for making it.”
He pointed to techniques used in dramatic literature and epic theater, including distancing, which encourage audiences to think about a work instead of simply surrendering to its emotional effect. A film, he said, should stay with the viewer as a question after the screening.
When filmmaking becomes a duty
The same idea of responsibility was behind Khajepasha's decision to work during the 40-day War.
At the time, Tehran and other parts of the country were facing an extraordinary situation as they came under US and Zionist regime airstrikes. Khajepasha said he saw people from different professions doing more than their normal duties: bakers working additional shifts, doctors and nurses continuing their work in hospitals and other citizens finding ways to contribute.
For him and some of his colleagues, filmmaking became another form of service.
“Sometimes we make films because we are filmmakers. Sometimes, as Iranians, we have another national duty,” he said. “At that point, it is no longer simply about filmmaking. It is a form of service.”
Under ordinary circumstances, he acknowledged, starting a production so quickly and without the usual preparation would not have been logical. But he felt that the circumstances demanded a response.
“As someone working in the arts, I felt I had a responsibility,” he said. “My instrument is cinema and television.”
He began work only a few days after the war started and now looks back on the experience with particular satisfaction.
The reason, he explained, was not necessarily that the films were more successful than his other work. It was the feeling that he was doing something directly for his own people.
“I am happy that, during that period, instead of standing on the sidelines, I was able to take a step,” he said.
Hiroshima: between memory and spectacle
A recent trip to Hiroshima gave Khajepasha another opportunity to think about the way major human tragedies are remembered.
He attended the annual ceremony commemorating the victims of the atomic bombing of Hiroshima and found the gathering visually striking and, from a filmmaker's perspective, fascinating. Yet he said the event left him with mixed feelings.
The scale of the tragedy, he argued, seemed much greater than what was being conveyed by the ceremony.
“I felt that, instead of the truth being fully expressed, I was watching more of a show,” he said.
Khajepasha extended that observation to the way peace is sometimes represented internationally. He questioned the gap that can exist between institutions and governments that publicly promote peace and countries whose policies have contributed to conflicts elsewhere.
But his experience in Japan did not leave him simply pessimistic. He said he encountered ordinary people who appeared genuinely concerned about events beyond their own borders.
When some Japanese people learned that he was Iranian, he recalled, they immediately brought up the victims of the recent tragedy in Minab and other Iranian victims.
He said he had encountered similar reactions in other countries and believes that ordinary people may ultimately understand such tragedies more deeply than political rhetoric suggests.
Iranian cinema and the international festival circuit
Khajepasha also returned to comments he made while “In the Arms of the Tree” was Iran's Oscar submission. At the time, he had questioned whether artistic quality alone determines a film's international success.
His criticism, he explained, was not simply about whether his own film would advance in the Oscar race. He was talking about the broader position of art and cinema.
In his view, political considerations, lobbying and relationships can influence some major international cultural institutions. He also believes that the influence of politics has become particularly visible in some film festivals.
That does not mean he considers the entire international festival circuit politicized.
He mentioned festivals held in South Korea, Morocco, Egypt, Armenia, Russia and Turkey among festivals that continue to offer valuable platforms for filmmakers. Iranian cinema, he stressed, has also received genuine international recognition through films by directors such as Asghar Farhadi and Majid Majidi.
The quality of an individual film, he argued, should not be reduced to the festival at which it appears or the prize it receives.
“A festival award alone cannot determine the value of a film,” he said.
He also believes filmmakers themselves have a responsibility not to allow the desire for international recognition to dictate their artistic choices.
Family at the center
Children feature prominently in both “In the Arms of the Tree” and “The Land of Angels”, but Khajepasha does not see himself primarily as a filmmaker of children's stories.
His deeper interest, he said, is the family.
He usually tries to include children in his films because their presence gives the story another dimension, but he would like to explore the family itself more extensively in future work.
“I would like to make more films about the family itself,” he said, describing it as one of the most important and vulnerable foundations of human societies.
He believes the issue has particular importance in Iran because family relationships are deeply connected to the country's cultural identity.
Iran cannot simply reproduce changes that have taken place in other societies, he argued. Relationships among parents, children and extended family members have a particular cultural meaning in Iranian society.
For that reason, he believes Iranian cinema should address the pressures facing families instead of treating changes in family structures as inevitable.
‘First make a good film’
Khajepasha will soon have an opportunity to examine films from the other side of the filmmaking process, as a jury member of the BRICS+ International Film Festival in St. Petersburg.
At the time of the interview, the festival's films had not yet been sent to the jury, so he had not begun watching them. But he already knew what his first criterion would be.
The film itself comes first.
For Khajepasha, a film needs to have a sound story and plot as well as convincing cinematic elements such as mise-en-scène and visual language. A political or social message cannot make up for weaknesses in the filmmaking.
He is particularly critical of films that appear to have been made primarily to deliver a message.
“If we want to criticize a society, we first have to make a good film,” he said. “If we simply shout our message at the audience, the audience will realize immediately that the filmmaker has an agenda.”
The same principle applies to films carrying messages that he himself agrees with, he added.
“A good film that disagrees with our beliefs can sometimes be less damaging than a bad film that is trying to promote our beliefs,” he said.
As a juror, Khajepasha said his first priority would therefore be cinematic quality.
“Before a film can make an audience believe in its message, it has to make the audience believe in the film itself,” he concluded.
SAB/

Options for the Royal Brunei Air Force’s Fast-jet Decision
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
14:45:00 UTC
23:45:00 KST

The Royal Brunei Air Force (RBAirF), which turned 60 in June, finds itself in a rapidly changing geostrategic environment, characterized by conflict and instability. Brunei is unlikely to suffer outright military aggression but could face spillover effects of increased super power confrontation in the region.
Brunei’s recent defense white paper identified major power rivalry, regional and global conflicts, radicalization, and rapidly advancing disruptive technologies as sources of concern. It also laid out a path to secure national sovereignty and territorial integrity. The RBAirF is actively looking to expand its means to do so, including with plans to acquire medium-range ground-based air defense systems and fast-jet combat aircraft.
Currently, the RBAirF operates a small fleet of modern turboprop-powered fixed-wing aircraft and helicopters. In May, Brunei took delivery of the last two CASA (Airbus) C295W medium-airlift aircraft, first ordered in 2022. The aircraft replaced older C235 aircraft in the No. 15 Squadron in territorial and maritime surveillance, airlift, and humanitarian assistance and disaster relief missions.
For rotary-wing tactical airlift, search and rescue, and combat air support (CAS), the RBAirF operates a fleet of 12 S-70i Black Hawk helicopters and a handful of ageing BO105 helicopters. The latter is slated to be replaced by six Airbus H145M multirole helicopters.
Finally, for basic flight training, the RBAirF flies four Pilatus PC-7 Mk.II turboprop aircraft. The aircraft were put into service in 1997, which makes them among the oldest aircraft in Bruneian service and in dire need for replacement.
To meet the air force’s mission – “to deliver responsive air power in securing Brunei Darussalam’s territorial integrity and national interests” – amid a changing security environment, more capable combat aircraft are also needed urgently.
As the RBAirF considers the acquisition of a squadron of fast-jet combat aircraft, original equipment manufacturers (OEM) are lining up to offer their fighters to Brunei Darussalam.
Options like the Lockheed Martin’s F-16 Viper offer a leap in capability for the RBAirF and come with closer ties with the U.S. defense industry and Washington D.C. However, the F-16 or an equivalent is not the best solution for the RBAirF as it seeks to enter fast-jet operations. Any decision regarding the RBAirF’s future combat aircraft should go beyond simple fighter comparisons and consider the air force’s broader requirements across its stated roles.
Entering fast-jet operations also poses new training demands for the air force. Brunei will need a revised flight training syllabus and modern training aircraft to ready its future generation of pilots.
Training Jets
Brunei could consider adopting the Singapore model by dispatching pilots to another country for advanced jet training (Phase 3-4), or join international advanced military flight training courses in Italy or Canada, while maintaining the elementary and basic training (Phase 1-2) at home.
Alternatively, the RBAirF could acquire the Embraer A-29 or Textron Aviation T-6 Texan II turboprop trainers to replace the aging PC-7 Mk. II fleet to meet its own advanced training (Phase 3) demands.
Some air forces like Switzerland, for example, employ modern turboprop aircraft to fulfill their pilot training needs entirely (Phase 2-4), enabling pilots to transition from turboprop aircraft directly to jet combat aircraft.
Moreover, both Embraer and Textron offer missionized and armed variants of their aircraft, which would offer Brunei an affordable light combat aircraft capability. The A-29 and AT-6 can be equipped with advanced electro-optical and infrared search and track, and laser track sensors, gun and rocket pods, and a variety of precision-guided munitions.
Critically, this would allow the RBAirF to meet many of its CAS, counterinsurgency (COIN), combat search and rescue, airborne forward air controller, armed reconnaissance, helicopter escort, and border and maritime surveillance patrol missions assigned to it with greater efficiency and capability than is possible today.
Therefore, the two types offer substantial value at low cost. They would help support the Bruneian ground forces and navy, and other government agencies, and offer major savings that come from maintenance, operational, and training synergies of operating a common platform that meets the RBAirF’s basic military flight training requirements while fulfilling many of its lower end combat needs.
To effectively protect Brunei’s airspace against intruders and assist in land and maritime border surveillance, rapid response (i.e., Quick Reaction Alert or QRA) is of essence.
Neither the current turboprop aircraft or helicopters, nor turboprop light combat aircraft, can effectively intercept fast-moving and high-flying intruders near Bruneian sovereign airspace or above the exclusive economic zone. Therefore, the RBAirF requirement for fast jet combat aircraft is understandable.
Multirole Light Combat Aircraft
To meet the requirement, Brunei should consider acquiring modern multirole jet-trainer aircraft and their light combat aircraft variants, which could also fulfill the majority of the air force’s border protection and combat requirements.
Good candidates to fill this role include, for example, the Leonardo M346F Block 20 and the Korean Aerospace Industries (KAI) TA/FA-50 Block 70 advanced jet trainer and light combat aircraft from Italy and South Korea respectively. Like the previously discussed turboprop options, Leonardo and KAI aircraft offer many synergies like in maintenance, training, and operations.
The M346F Block 20 is a missionized advanced jet trainer, which is equipped with a modern active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar, advanced cockpit with large-area display, and a helmet-mounted sight, datalink, targeting pod, short- and medium-range air-to-air missiles and a range of precision-guided air-to-ground and antiship weapons.
Similarly, the latest FA-50 versions, such as the FA-50M and FA-50 Block 70 destined for Malaysia and the Philippines respectively, are fitted with an AESA radar, a targeting pod, a datalink, and a range of air-to-air and air-to-ground weapons.
Critically, the AESA radar, targeting pod, datalink, and the ability to carry both within-visual-range and beyond-visual-range missiles, enable the aircraft to take up the essential QRA and combat air patrol duties and respond to any airspace violations with force, if needed.
The FA-50 holds an important advantage over the M346 in this regard. It can use its afterburning F404 powerplant to accelerate to a supersonic speed and reach the farthest reaches of Brunei’s EEZ faster than what is possible with the subsonic Italian aircraft.
Besides their light combat aircraft attributes, both types were originally designed as advanced jet trainers to meet the common Phase 3 training requirements. The addition of a radar, fire-control computer and associated data bus, hardpoints, and weapons have enabled the use of the aircraft in lead-in fighter training (Phase 4) as well.
In addition, both aircraft are equipped with large-area displays, helmet-mounted sights, and Virtual, Live, and Constructive (VLC) training aids, which promise to transform jet training in the coming years. The use of VLC allows air forces to achieve many previously difficult to resource training, such as large-force operations or weapons deployment at a significantly lower cost.
For example, VLC can emulate a fire-control radar and simulate a beyond-visual-range missile engagement with all associated target and missile-launch symbology and cues projected on the displays and the helmet. Air forces can dispatch a pair of aircraft into air (“live”) while other trainees may join the same mission in simulators (“virtual”), while facing virtual enemy aircraft (“constructive”) – all linked to the same VLC environment.
Moreover, due to the rapid technological change and observations drawn from conflicts around the world, one-way attack drones (OWAD) have become a prominent aerial threat that requires solutions from air forces and the industry.
Understanding this demand, OEMs like Embraer, Textron, and Leonardo market their aircraft as cost-effective counter-OWAD platforms, equipped with AESA radar and/or targeting pods, datalink, gun pods, short-range air-to-air missiles, and semi-active laser-guided rockets to address the threat.
Therefore, light combat aircraft offer the RBAirF a cost-effective solution to stand up fast-jet operations from zero.
Lessons From Brunei’s Neighbors
A good point of reference is the Philippine Air Force (PAF), which made a return to fast jets with the FA-50PH between 2015 and 2017, after a ten-year pause in operating fighter aircraft. The PAF took delivery of 12 aircraft and signed a follow-on order in 2025 consisting of 12 FA-50 Block 70 aircraft.
During the last decade, the PAF has made great strides in training and reacquiring the skills needed to operate fast jets. Today, Manila is not just looking to expand the well-liked FA-50 fleet but also to acquire a higher-end multirole combat aircraft.
The Philippine example shows that it can take a decade or more to develop required operational proficiency and human resources, and capacity to operate fast jets.
The KAI aircraft has become a popular type in Southeast Asia and is operated by four air forces, including the Philippines, Indonesia, Thailand, and Malaysia.
In comparison, the M346 remains a less well-known type in the region, although it is used by Singapore for basic jet training, with its entire fleet based in France due to training area constraints in the island state.
In addition, Indonesia recently placed an order for a total of 48 M346F Block 20 aircraft, which will transform the Indonesian Air Force’s flight training and help replace ageing BAE Hawk aircraft in both jet training and light combat duties.
Modern trainer aircraft, which also come in light combat aircraft versions and are equipped with modern sensors, datalinks, air-to-air missiles, and precision-guided munitions offer significant cost benefits and training, operational, and maintenance synergies for small air forces.
For the RBAirF, these aircraft offer the most cost-effective pathway to fast-jet air power. One must not run before learning to walk.

Centre discusses drought measures to protect Rabi crops in the country
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
14:43:16 UTC
23:43:16 KST

Centre discusses drought measures to protect Rabi crops in the country
NEW DELHI: Apprehending a threat of deficient monsoon rainfall to the upcoming sowing season, Centre on Monday discussed contingency measures to minimise its impact on Rabi (winter-sown) crops, with Union agriculture minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan calling for data-driven planning, stronger centre-state coordination, weekly crop monitoring, balanced fertiliser use and water budgeting.Amid indications that the kharif (summer-sown) crops’ output may not match last year’s level despite progress in acreage, the minister, while addressing farm scientists and policymakers during a national conference, also emphasised the need to drive the Rabi strategy through less water-consuming pulses and oilseeds. The latest acreage data shows the total sown area at 1,107 lakh hectares (ha) as of Friday was about three lakh ha more than the ‘normal’ (average of last five years) acreage (1,104 lakh ha) despite a cumulative deficit of 12% in monsoon rainfall in the country. It was, however, 14 lakh ha less than the same period of 2025, a year which recorded 8% more than normal rainfall.
The conference was convened to discuss the farm strategy, keeping in view the current drought situation in many states, so that the impact of low moisture content in the soil and shortage of water for irrigation due to deficient rainfall may not impact farming operations much. Sowing of rabi crops such as wheat and mustard begins in October.
The Centre will, meanwhile, send teams to Karnataka and Maharashtra to assess the drought situation. Nearly two-thirds of Maharashtra has been affected and the state has already declared a drought, while Karnataka is also facing drought-like conditions due to the monsoon rainfall deficit of 30%.
The monsoon season will end on Wednesday with a strong possibility of an overall rainfall deficit of more than 10% in the country as a whole — a deficient condition which is considered a drought. As of Monday, India recorded a deficit of 12% in cumulative (June 1–Sept 28) monsoon rainfall, with 12 states reporting a deficit of 20% or more.
Underlining the current situation, Chouhan asked every district to assess the water available for irrigation before finalising crop plans. “Areas with limited water availability should prioritise less water-intensive crops such as pulses and oilseeds, while areas with assured irrigation can plan other crops accordingly,” he said while noting that the rainfed areas, in particular, require careful planning as the availability of soil moisture largely determines the crop choice and outcome.Rabi crops are normally sown in a total area of about 638 lakh hectares, out of which wheat generally covers nearly 50% of it, with the remaining around 50% being covered by pulses, oilseeds and coarse cereals.

These Extremists Are Running for Election in November
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
14:41:08 UTC
23:41:08 KST

There are five weeks left until the midterm elections, and extremism is on the ballot in much of the US. A WIRED review of candidates running for statewide and federal positions in November, along with exclusive data on candidates running for state-level positions, reveals hundreds of Republican candidates who openly express virulently hateful ideologies, share racist content online, have close ties to white supremacist and antisemitic figures, and are members of far-right groups online. President Donald Trump and his administration have openly embraced, endorsed and defended many of these candidates.
At a local level, over 500 candidates running for state legislator positions in November are members of far-right groups on Facebook that promote militias, gun rights, and Christian nationalism, according to data collected by the Institute for Research and Education on Human Rights and shared with WIRED.
While many extremist candidates—such as groyper James Fishback and antisemitic influencer Dan Bilzerian— didn’t make it through GOP primaries, many made it to the general election, and a number of them are expected to win.
“The candidates are taking a page out of the Trump administration’s playbook,” Luke Baumgartner, a former research fellow at George Washington University’s Program on Extremism, tells WIRED. Baumgartner claims that many of the candidates running in November have been inspired by those in the White House. “In essence, the executive branch has handed them a permission slip to say and do what would have been unthinkable during the George W. Bush, McCain, or [Mitt] Romney eras of the GOP,” he says.
Extremist rhetoric has led to real world political threats. In 2025, terrorism and targeted violence incidents rose 19 percent compared to 2024, according to researchers at the University of Maryland; the US Capitol Police reported an increase in “threat assessment cases” against members of Congress for the third year in a row, with a 58 percent increase from 2024; and the US Marshals Service documented threats against almost 400 judges, a roughly 5 percent increase from the previous year.
Here are five races involving candidates who have shared extremist ideologies or have close ties to extremist figures, that WIRED is watching ahead of the November midterms.
The Texas Railroad Commissioner Race
Bo French, the GOP candidate for Texas Railroad Commissioner, is so extreme that Republican strategist Karl Rove has said he would vote for a Democrat rather than supporting a “bigot.”
Earlier this month, French posted racist comments about students celebrating at a University of Texas at Austin football game. “Like bodycam footage exposed criminals, social media is exposing how many Americans have been displaced by foreigners,” French wrote alongside a picture of students of South Asian descent celebrating a victory over Ohio State. “It’s everywhere and far worse than any of us could imagine.” (Former Border Patrol leader Greg Bovino wrote in reply, “Mass deportations will solve it in very short order.”)
While many Republicans, including senator John Cornyn from Texas, criticized French for his post and called on him to take it down, French instead doubled down, telling a conservative radio host that while he didn’t “have anything against the people specifically in that picture,” he wanted to “prioritize Americans.”
This wasn’t the first controversy for the candidate: French has previously called for the removal of 100 million people from America, including US citizens, and repeatedly used homophobic slurs.
The Texas Railroad Commissioner is an incredibly powerful position that has no role in regulating railroads, but instead oversees the state’s oil and gas industries, which in Texas drill more oil and other hydrocarbons than the rest of the US combined. The role will also be critical to deciding how the burgeoning data center industry in Texas will be powered.
New polling this week suggests French, who has not been publicly endorsed by Trump, is a slim favorite to win the seat.
Arizona’s 5th Congressional District Race
Mark Lamb, the GOP nominee for Arizona’s 5th district congressional race, is a former sheriff and reality TV star. He has deep ties to paramilitary groups, anti-immigration organizations, and the far-right constitutional sheriffs movement.
Lamb has protested Covid lockdowns and vaccine mandates, expressed support for the “stop the steal” movement,” and sympathized with the rioters who stormed the Capitol on January 6. He is in favor of private militias and even authorized the formation of a civilian posse while serving as sheriff of Pinal County in response to Black Lives Matter protests in 2020. He is a regular on right wing podcasts, including those hosted by white nationalists and conspiracy theorists.
Lamb, who is supported by Trump and conservative student organization Turning Point USA, won his primary despite accusations of multiple sex scandals. When one woman threatened to expose him, a Facebook account featuring an avatar of Lamb’s face threatened to use Arizona’s revenge porn law against her.
Lamb is almost certain to be elected in the deeply red district that includes Phoenix.
Texas’ 23rd Congressional District Race
Brandon Herrera, who rose to fame as a so-called “guntuber,” is running for Congress in Texas in the district that represents Uvalde. Incumbent GOP congressman Tony Gonzales resigned after admitting to an affair, making Herrera the GOP candidate.
Herrera has a very long history of sharing sexist, racist, and antisemitic opinions. He has said that a Nazi-era submachine gun was “the original ghetto blaster” and “Hitler’s street sweeper.” He has compared feminists’ weight to whales, elephants, and nuclear bombs and described liberal women discussing guns as “both fat and wrong.” While talking about Shannon Watts, the gun control activist who set up Moms Demand Action following the Sandy Hook school shooting, Herrera said: “The fact that you kept your cum trophy doesn’t make you any less wrong about the dumb shit that you say.”
“HE WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN,” Trump wrote about Herrera in a Truth Social post in March.
When questioned about Herrera’s opinions of women, Speaker of the House Mike Johnson dismissed them as part of his online “persona.” Johnson also called Herrera a “very serious candidate” and a “very thoughtful guy.”
Herrera is in a tight race with Democrat nominee Katy Padilla Stout.
Georgia’s Senate Race
Mike Collins, the Trump-backed GOP senate candidate in Georgia, is running against Democratic incumbent Jon Ossoff.
Collins has spent a large part of his campaign battling accusations that he supports or is indifferent to white supremacy and antisemitism—not because of anything he has said, but because of who he has surrounded himself with. In May, NOTUS reported that former Collins staffer William Paul (son of Kentucky senator Rand Paul) hurled antisemitic insults at representative Mike Lawler from New York while both were at a bar.
Later the same month, Slate revealed that Collins’ then chief-of-staff, Kip Talley, was in a group chat with known white supremacists like Nick Fuentes and Richard Spencer. In the texts, Talley said he was working to help Charles “Chuck” Johnson, a Holocaust denier who has been accused of (and denied) being a white nationalist, who was in jail at the time as he was in contempt of court as part of a racketeering lawsuit. Talley told Slate that he was concerned about an “acquaintance I have known for years was being mistreated in custody and denied basic medical care.”
In July, CNN revealed that Collins’ son-in-law, David Alan Scheer II, is a social media influencer who has shared antisemitic content and Nazi imagery. And finally, last month, the Washington Post revealed that a former intern and contractor for his PAC had shared images on X of a swastika and an image of himself in what appear to be KKK robes.
Collins has repeatedly said that he condemns antisemitism and hate speech of any kind. He also secured Trump’s endorsement earlier this month.
Polling shows Ossoff comfortably leading Collins in the general election.
Florida’s State House’s 10th District Race
Marshall Rawson, a 34-year old citrus farmer and GOP activist, was the surprise winner of the Republican primary in August for the Florida legislature’s 10th District House race.
Talking Points Memo revealed this month that Rawson marched at the Unite the Right rally in Charlottesville and was pictured close to the neo-Nazi who later would drive his car into a crowd of protesters, killing Heather Heyer.
On social media, Rawson has repeatedly posted racist remarks. He has also suggested that gay people should be criminally charged and possibly executed. He has been associated with the racist and antisemitic League of the South movement, which seeks secession for southern states from the US.
Talking Points Memo revealed that his campaign is getting donations from the daughter of former KKK leader David Duke, along with another individual who marched in Charlottesville and admitted to organizing a birthday party for Duke.
There is no public polling available for the race, but the district leans heavily red, with Republicans winning the seat by a 48-point margin in 2024.

Liminal’s mass-producible UGV heads to Pentagon trial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
14:40:17 UTC
23:40:17 KST

- Liminal Industries advanced to Phase II of GroundBreaker 1 and will demonstrate its DUEL-V unmanned ground vehicle at Camp Grafton, North Dakota, in mid-October.
- Companies that perform well may be invited to propose for a prototype Other Transaction Agreement award.
Liminal Industries, a U.S. startup building unmanned ground vehicles meant to be produced and fielded in large numbers, has advanced to the second phase of the GroundBreaker 1 competition and will demonstrate its DUEL-V vehicle to U.S. military evaluators in North Dakota next month.
The company announced Sept. 28 that its Phase I submission passed technical evaluation and that it will bring multiple DUEL-V vehicles to Camp Grafton in mid-October. An unmanned ground vehicle, or UGV, is a vehicle that operates on land with no crew aboard, driven by a remote operator or by its own software.
DUEL-V, short for Dynamic Unmanned Expendable Light Vehicle, is a compact, remotely operated platform that Liminal designed around three priorities: low cost, adaptability and the ability to build it at scale. It uses a modular layout that accepts different mission payloads, runs on four-wheel drive and can operate in either orientation. The company has not released its size, weight, speed, range, payload capacity or price.
“Scale has been a design requirement from the beginning,” said Bradley Balzer, founder and CEO of Liminal Industries. “Cost, manufacturing, and operator usability determine whether a ground system can become a widely deployed capability. GroundBreaker gives us an opportunity to demonstrate that approach and put DUEL-V in front of the people who will shape its deployment at scale.”
Liminal says its development relies on field testing, feedback from operators and rapid hardware changes between versions. It first unveiled DUEL-V on Oct. 14, 2025, when Balzer pitched it as the ground equivalent of an FPV drone, the cheap first-person-view quadcopters that armies in Ukraine now use by the hundreds of thousands. At the time, the company did not disclose payload options, how much the vehicle can drive itself or whether it can keep working under electronic jamming, and it has not released those details since.
GroundBreaker 1 is a joint Department of War demonstration meant to speed up the military’s adoption of unmanned ground vehicles. U.S. Army Contracting Command issued the call for white papers on Aug. 21 through the Department of War Drone OTA Consortium, which limited the competition to companies already enrolled in that consortium. Government teams from the Office of the Secretary of War and the military services are supporting the event.
The U.S. Army is looking for complete systems that troops can use in both combat and non-combat settings. The solicitation lists missions including reconnaissance and surveillance, tactical logistics, explosive ordnance disposal and route clearance, search and rescue, and force protection. White papers were scored out of 100 points: 40% for technical merit and design, 35% for readiness to deliver and demonstrate, 15% for cost and affordability, and 10% for past performance. The recommended threshold to reach Phase II was 75 points.
At Camp Grafton, service members will operate the vehicles in realistic field conditions and give feedback on how easy they are to use and how well they perform their missions. Companies will also make live pitches to government evaluators. Vendors whose vehicles show “high tactical value and technical maturity” may then be invited to submit a full technical and cost proposal for a prototype Other Transaction Agreement, a contract type the Pentagon uses to buy and test new technology faster than through traditional procurement.
GroundBreaker follows the demonstration-first model of the Department of War’s Drone Dominance Program, which runs aerial drones through competitive “Gauntlet” trials before placing large orders. The department has not said how many UGVs it plans to buy after GroundBreaker 1 or how many companies will take part in the October event.

Kerala HC calls for Centre's intervention on exorbitantly priced patented medicines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
14:31:55 UTC
23:31:55 KST

The Kerala high court has determined that the Centre is authorized to invoke the Patents Act to produce medicines.
NEW DELHI: The Kerala high court has said the Centre can invoke provisions of the Patents Act to manufacture and distribute a patented medicine to patients in need when the drug is being sold at an exorbitant price.The court made the observation while dealing with a 2022 petition filed by a woman suffering from breast cancer, who had sought affordable access to the drug Ribociclib, news agency PTI reported. She died while the case was pending.Justice Harisankar V Menon, in a 65-page judgment, said the Centre can use a patent or invention to manufacture a patented medicine and sell it on a non-commercial basis to a person in need under Section 100 of the Patents Act, which deals with the government's power to use inventions for government purposes.The court held that Section 100 "is required to be invoked in circumstances, where the government is required to intervene", including cases where a patented medicine is being sold at an exorbitant price, PTI reported.The court, however, said the government would first have to collect the relevant information and assess whether the price of a particular medicine is affordable before taking action under the provision.
The petition was filed by a former bank employee who had been diagnosed with HR+/HER2-metastatic breast cancer and was undergoing treatment with a CDK 4/6 inhibitor, Ribociclib.According to the petition, the medicine cost around Rs 58,140 for a 21-day course. She had approached the court seeking a reduction in its price or access to the drug at an affordable cost.After her death, the high court took suo motu cognisance of the larger issue of the high prices of patented life-saving medicines, PTI reported.During the proceedings, the Centre and pharmaceutical industry representatives argued that Section 100 could be invoked only for government purposes and could not be used in the circumstances before the court.The high court rejected that interpretation.The court said the expression "for the purposes of government" must be understood to include the government's power to sell or supply products manufactured using a patent or invention to a buyer on a non-commercial basis."In that event," the court said, Section 100 would include the government's entitlement to manufacture the patented medicine and sell it on a non-commercial basis to a person who could be "none other than the needy patient".The court also said the government has an obligation to ensure access to healthcare, including life-saving treatment.In reaching its conclusions, the high court referred to the 139th Report of the Department-Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health and Family Welfare on cancer treatment. The report had emphasised the need for government and private-sector participation to make cancer care more affordable.The court also referred to the Malayalam film 'Sukrutham', starring Mammootty, which depicts the difficulties faced by cancer patients and their families.
The court observed that it was "highly distressing" that despite nearly three decades having passed since the film's release, the situation had not changed substantially.The judgment stressed the need for a balance between ensuring affordable access to medical treatment and maintaining adequate incentives for innovation."It is imperative that, we, as a community and as a system that caters to billions, strike the balance between affordable access to medical treatment and maintaining adequate incentives," the court said.

KYIV, Sept 28 - Ukraine's military has used drones to deliver food and medicine to the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, the governor of Ukraine's Kherson region said, as officials warn about a worsening humanitarian crisis.
Governor Oleksandr Prokudin said on Sunday that, in the latest operation, heavy-lift drones delivered about four tons of food and medical supplies to 100 locations across the town simultaneously.
Oleshky, a frontline town on the Dnipro River, which separates Russian and Ukrainian forces, has been under Russian occupation since 2022.
Prokudin said that close to 2,000 people, including about 50 children, were being held "hostage", without food, electricity and water, and accused Moscow's forces of preventing them from escaping the town.
Ukrainian officials have warned of the situation in Oleshky becoming more dire.
The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine has said that residents have endured months of food shortages and "extremely limited" access to basic necessities.
Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets told Ukrainian media this month that Russia had not agreed to Ukrainian proposals to allow civilians to evacuate from Oleshky.
"People in the temporarily occupied Oleshky are being deprived of the basic means of survival. Russia bears full responsibility for this humanitarian catastrophe and its consequences," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on Sunday.
The Kremlin said last week that Oleshky had critical problems with food and medicine supplies, but that Russia's military was working to resolve them. REUTERS

Europe’s Read of the Trump-Xi Summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
14:09:00 UTC
23:09:00 KST

The summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping achieved one central objective: stabilization. It did not resolve the China-U.S. rivalry but helped contain it, by restoring a more predictable framework for managing tensions over trade, technology, and geopolitics.
Its main concrete outcome was modest: a two-month extension, until January 2027, of the trade truce first agreed after the Trump-Xi meeting in Busan a year ago, when Washington lowered tariffs and Beijing suspended export controls on rare earths and other critical minerals.
The two sides also activated the China-U.S. Boards of Trade and Investment and mutual support for each other’s G20 and APEC presidencies. The message is clear: not genuine rapprochement, but more disciplined management of strategic competition.
Yet the summit’s most consequential exchanges may have taken place behind closed doors over Iran. The public readout was brief, but Trump pressed Xi over Chinese support for Tehran, while both leaders publicly agreed that Iran must not acquire a nuclear weapon.
For the world’s two largest economies, which together account for nearly half of global economic output, de-escalation makes strategic sense, though for different reasons. Both sides would like to use a period of relative stability to buy time to reduce vulnerabilities, strengthen resilience, and recalibrate economic dependencies.
Diplomatically, both leaders are also playing to domestic audiences. Trump is seeking tangible economic gains, from agricultural purchases to aircraft orders, consistent with his long-standing focus on reducing the U.S. trade deficit and addressing structural imbalances that have weakened American manufacturing. Xi, meanwhile, wants to show that Washington is treating China as an equal, while easing the economic pressure Washington has steadily increased toward Chinese companies. For Beijing, stability is economic as well as diplomatic: détente buys time to support a weak domestic economy increasingly reliant on external demand as consumption at home remains subdued.
The European Union was another important audience for the summit. Decisions taken in Washington and Beijing increasingly shape European trade, technology, energy, and security.
First, Brussels and major European capitals have a strong interest in stable China-U.S. relations, particularly at a time when instability in the Middle East is generating mounting economic pressures on Europe through higher energy costs, disrupted trade routes, inflationary pressures, and weaker industrial competitiveness.
Second, Europe fears becoming an adjustment variable in the China-U.S. strategic competition. Washington holds technological leverage; Beijing controls minerals and key manufacturing supply chains. Europe remains exposed to both. The question is whether the EU can turn its own economic weight into strategic agency rather than simply absorb the consequences of decisions taken elsewhere.
Consider trade relations. When China-U.S. trade tensions intensify, Chinese goods shut out of the American market are increasingly redirected toward Europe, raising fears of a deeper China shock. The automotive sector is already reshaping European perceptions of China, but the pressure extend well beyond card. The question is how many other industries will follow.
In 2025, the EU increasingly became China’s primary export destination and trade deficit with China reached nearly 360 billion euro, with Chinese exports to Europe almost double the value of EU exports to China. Additional U.S. restrictions on Chinese imports could deepen this imbalance further.
At the same time, any China-U.S. managed trade arrangement that redirects Chinese purchases toward American goods could come at the expense of European exporters. Europe therefore faces pressure in both directions, from trade diversion when tensions rise and from preferential bilateral deals when they ease. On the other side, if China-U.S. relations stabilize, Beijing has less incentive to make concessions to Brussels. Either way, Europe risks becoming the adjustment variable in China-U.S. competition: absorbing displaced Chinese production while bilateral deals between Washington and Beijing are struck largely over its head.
Third, like the United States, the EU remains heavily dependent on China for rare earths, permanent magnets, and critical minerals, essential for Europe’s green, digital, and defense industries. 98 percent of EU demand for rare earth magnets is met by Chinese imports. The Trump-Xi Busan agreement in October 2025 brought relief also to Europe by easing immediate supply pressures. The recent China-U.S. summit produced no major new breakthrough, only an agreement to keep working on shortages and shipment levels.
For Europe, this may preserve some near-term stability, but it does little to reduce the underlying vulnerability. There is still a risk that a bilateral China-U.S. accommodation could improve supply security for American companies without resolving Europe’s exposure. In response, Brussels is increasingly aligning with U.S.-led initiatives, such as Pax Silica, and its own Critical Raw Materials Act to diversify supply chains, though reducing dependence on China will require years of investment, industrial capacity building, and transatlantic coordination.
Fourth, artificial intelligence. The Trump-Xi meeting produced no binding agreement, although the two sides launched an AI dialogue and a channel to manage serious incidents. Disputes over advanced chip exports remain unresolved. Beijing has an interest in buying time to reduce its dependence on U.S. technology, without the added burden of new tariffs and restrictions on Chinese companies.
For the EU, the risk is that the rules of AI race are increasingly shaped in a China-U.S. channel where Brussels has little influence. In the meantime, Europe remains heavily reliant on American processors and cloud providers and Chinese supply chains. The EU produces less than 10 percent of global semiconductors. Brussels is responding with its Technology Sovereignty Package paired with the Chips Act 2.0 and the Cloud and AI Development Act that aim to triple European data center capacity within five to seven years. Both acts are still proposals, however, with binding law months or possibly years away.
Attention will now turn to the next EU-China Summit, which is slated to take place in Beijing on December 7, as Brussels is seeking tangible results from the EU-China Trade and Investment Council. The European Union has considerable leverage of its own, through its market, regulatory power, trade instruments, and industrial base. The question is whether is prepared and unified to use that leverage with China.
That is also why transatlantic coordination matters. Beijing benefits when U.S. and European positions diverge, while Washington has a clear interest in closer European alignment with its economic security approach. Europe’s strategic challenge is to avoid becoming merely the arena in which China-U.S. competition plays out and instead use its own agency to shape the terms of that competition.

BANGKOK, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Thailand's auto production increased in August, mainly due to higher output of electric vehicles (EVs) and export-oriented pickup trucks, data from the Federation of Thai Industries (FTI) showed on Monday.
Automakers produced 124,646 vehicles in Thailand last month, up 10.93 percent from a year earlier, accelerating from a 6.12 percent gain in July, according to the FTI.
The surge was attributed to notable growth in battery EV passenger car output and export-oriented pickup trucks, while combustion-engine passenger car output fell 20.51 percent, the FTI said in a statement.
For the first eight months of 2026, auto production rose 1.27 percent over the same period last year to 959,711 units, even as fuel-powered passenger cars sank 32.62 percent on lower export-oriented output, said FTI Automotive Industry Club spokesperson Surapong Paisitpattanapong.
Domestic auto sales jumped 25.59 percent year-on-year to 59,809 units in August, driven by higher deliveries of passenger battery EVs, which rose 113.29 percent and accounted for 32.97 percent of total sales, Surapong told a news conference.
Meanwhile, passenger cars with internal combustion engines dropped 17.04 percent, making up 13.33 percent of total sales, he said.
The Southeast Asian nation's finished car exports fell 2.04 percent from the year before to 69,724 units in August, as shipments to the Middle East fell 40.24 percent owing to the ongoing geopolitical conflict, he noted. ■

====================================================================================================

China Focus: China opens four high-speed rail lines, expanding national network
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
22:02:23 CST
23:02:23 KST

The first train of Yichang-Xingshan high-speed railway, G6888, departs from Xingshan Railway Station in Xingshan County, central China's Hubei Province, Sept. 28, 2026. The 101-kilometer Yichang-Xingshan high-speed railway officially entered service on Monday. The railway, with a designed speed of 350 kilometers per hour, is an important part of the country's high-speed rail network. (Photo by Zou Yuanjing/Xinhua)
BEIJING, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- China, home to the world's largest high-speed rail network, opened four major high-speed railway sections to traffic on Monday, improving transport links across several regions.
The new sections connect Xiong'an in Hebei Province with Shangqiu in Henan Province, Xi'an with Ankang in Shaanxi Province, Yichang with Xingshan in Hubei Province, and Harbin with Yichun in Heilongjiang Province.
Spanning northern, northwestern, central and northeastern China, the new lines will facilitate travel for residents, improve regional connectivity and support economic development.
In north China, the Xiong'an-Shangqiu section runs through Xiong'an New Area, Cangzhou, Hengshui and Xingtai in Hebei Province, Liaocheng in Shandong Province, Puyang in Henan Province, and Jining and Heze in Shandong Province before reaching Shangqiu in Henan Province, with the main line measuring 552 kilometers long.
"Once the section begins operations, the fastest journey from Xiong'an to Shangqiu will take just 2 hours and 27 minutes," said Han Yong, deputy director of the passenger transport center of China Railway Beijing Group Co., Ltd., adding that the route will further strengthen communications between Xiong'an New Area and China's vast northern and central markets.
In northwest China, the 171-km Xi'an-Ankang section crosses the Qinling Mountains, overcoming complex geological challenges while also prioritizing ecological protection. With a design speed of 350 km per hour, the train can travel between its two terminal stations in just 45 minutes.
Construction of the Yichang-Xingshan section in central China faced similar challenges, with the railway traversing the Daba Mountains through a 16.9-km-long deep-buried tunnel and a high-rise mega bridge.
The Yichang-Xingshan line connects China's two major high-speed railway arteries, namely the Shanghai-Chongqing-Chengdu high-speed railway along the Yangtze River and the Zhengzhou-Chongqing high-speed railway, and will unleash fresh development momentum along the Yangtze River Economic Belt, according to China Railway Wuhan Bureau Group Co., Ltd., its operator.
In northeast China, the 318-km Harbin-Yichun section is China's northernmost high-speed railway ever constructed. Its terminal, Yichun West Station, is located at 47 degrees north latitude, making it China's first high-speed railway station building constructed in a permafrost region, said Shi Qinwei, head of the Yichun West Station project at China Railway Construction Group Co., Ltd.
Linking Harbin, China's renowned winter destination in Heilongjiang Province with Yichun, the province's forest-enclosed haven for summer retreat, the route will cut the railway travel time between the two cities from about seven hours to roughly two hours, while extending China's modern high-speed rails to the lesser-tapped northern regions.
Opened shortly before the National Day holiday, the new railways are also expected to boost tourist flows between China's major cities along the route, as well as iconic attractions such as Yichang's Three Gorges Dam and Yichun's emerald forests.
China State Railway Group Co., Ltd., the country's railroad operator, is expecting some 284 million passenger trips during the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holiday period, which extends from Sept. 23 to October 8.
China is expanding and optimizing its high-speed rail network to better serve its booming domestic markets and industries.
By the end of 2025, the country's total operating railway mileage had reached 165,000 km, including more than 50,000 km of high-speed rail.
Fixed-asset investment in the railway sector totaled 511.8 billion yuan (about 75.9 billion U.S. dollars) in the first eight months of the year, up 1.5 percent year on year, according to China State Railway Group Co., Ltd.
Under national plans, China's high-speed rail network is projected to hit 70,000 km by 2035, with eight north-south vertical lines and eight east-west horizontal lines. Once complete, the network will connect major cities, city clusters and key economic zones throughout the country. ■

"This is my first Asian Games, so there was a lot of uncertainty," Lin said. "The intensity was very high, the pressure was huge, and the opponents were all very strong. All I could do was focus on myself and take it one point at a time."
Chinese Taipei's Lin Yun-ju and Iran's Noshad Alamiyan took bronze.
In the women's doubles final, Kuai and Wang made a blistering start by winning the opening game 11-0 before edging a tighter second 12-10.
The Chinese pair took the next two games 11-4, 11-9 to complete the victory in 36 minutes.
Doo Hoi Kem and Ng Wing Lam from Hong Kong, China and Thailand's Suthasini Sawettabut and Orawan Paranang took bronze.

"I think both of us were in good form this time, and we were able to make a good run through the team, singles and women's doubles events," Wang said. "I gained different experiences and learned different things from each event."
China finished the table tennis competition with six of the seven gold medals available, missing out only the men's team title. China also collected four silvers and one bronze, while Japan finished with one gold, three silvers and three bronzes. ■

Bach says Confucian thought and Olympism share common ground
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
22:02:13 CST
23:02:13 KST

JINAN, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- International Olympic Committee honorary president Thomas Bach called for greater dialogue between civilizations and cultures on Monday, highlighting the common ground between Confucian thought and the Olympic movement.
"You are deepening the dialogue between Confucian wisdom and the Olympic spirit," Bach said in a video address to the Nishan Forum on World Civilizations in Qufu, the birthplace of Confucius.
Bach recalled his visit to Qufu in 2023, saying the trip had allowed him to see firsthand the similarities between Confucian thought and Olympism.
"I have indeed very fond memories of my visit to the birthplace of Confucius a few years ago," Bach said. "It gave me the opportunity to discover firsthand how much Confucian thought and Olympism have in common."
Bach said Confucius' emphasis on developing both body and mind reflected an idea also found in the ancient Roman saying "Mens sana in corpore sano," meaning "a sound mind in a sound body."
"This same understanding is at the heart of Olympism," he said.
Bach said Pierre de Coubertin, founder of the IOC and reviver of the modern Olympic Games, viewed sport as being about more than physical competition, emphasizing education and values as well as building bridges and fostering understanding among nations and peoples.
"In our divided world, we need such dialogue between civilizations, people and cultures more than ever," Bach said.
He welcomed the return of the Nishan Forum's Sports and Culture Forum, first held in 2024, saying it continued to provide a platform to explore connections between Confucian thought and the Olympic spirit. ■

Economic Watch: Inbound travelers revel in Chinese goods, culture during Mid-Autumn holiday
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
22:02:10 CST
23:02:10 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- At Yuetan Park (Temple of the Moon) in Beijing, six-year-old Serena from Ireland pointed at a glowing panda lantern and tugged her father's sleeve. For her family, this Mid-Autumn Festival fair was not just a stop in their China trip, but a holiday event they could touch, taste and carry home.
"We came to admire the moon and lanterns, but the girls ended up with their pockets full of handmade crafts and local snacks," her father Marcus Rood said. Around this traditional Chinese festival of family reunion, more international visitors are coming to China and diving into experiences that go beyond just sightseeing.
The Mid-Autumn Festival falls on the 15th day of the eighth lunar month. During this year's Mid-Autumn Festival holiday, from Sept. 25 to 27, foreign nationals made 728,000 border crossings, up 37.7 percent year on year.
Among inbound foreign visitors, a total of 247,000 entered under visa-free policies, an increase of 32.7 percent from a year earlier, data from the National Immigration Administration showed.
In the bustling Dashilar area, a renowned tourist destination in downtown Beijing, time-honored shops and restaurants rolled out various Mid-Autumn cultural experiences. Overseas visitors flocked there to enjoy China's traditional song-and-dance performances and local delicacies.
For Celia Praetzas from Germany, an evening stroll turned into a shopping spree. Along a street decorated with giant installations blending Chinese pavilion architecture and heritage craft, she picked up low-sugar mooncakes, herbal tea and traditional Chinese health products.
Seeing so many families laughing together reminded Praetzas of hers. "I bought these for my parents, hoping they stay healthy and share in the joy of my trip here."
The Mid-Autumn Festival tells the story of home yet stirs a universal human yearning for belonging. "That's why the celebrations can touch foreign visitors," said Wang Yi, an associate professor at Tianjin University in north China.
Behind these scenes featuring overseas visitors soaking up China's festive atmosphere, is a sustained push to make the country more welcoming and easier to travel in.
In March, Chinese authorities released a package of measures to improve tourism services, including optimizing departure tax refund services, encouraging everyday service apps to offer multilingual versions, and further improving visa procedures.
These efforts are already paying off. Official data revealed that foreign nationals made nearly 61.29 million border crossings in the first eight months of 2026, up 19.5 percent year on year, while one of the leading mobile payment platform Weixin Pay reported that both the value and number of e-wallet transactions made by overseas users rose by more than 80 percent during the same period.
On Sept. 24, China's Ministry of Culture and Tourism announced plans to develop more travel experiences that combine traditional culture with modern life during 2026-2030, aimed at helping foreign visitors travel more conveniently, enjoy more comfortable stays, and gain a closer view of contemporary China.
Clutching a villager's ID card and breathing in the sweet aroma of local tea, Thai tourist Pam wandered through earthen courtyards and cave-like alleys in "See Minning," an immersive drama village in northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, where every few minutes she could run into another live scene.
Pam, who was visiting with her family during the Mid-Autumn Festival holiday, most enjoyed "Loess Cave," a story about villagers who once struggled with water shortages but now cherish a better life. "I was thrilled. It's hard to describe how amazing it is," she said.
The village has received almost 1,000 inbound visitors like Pam since it opened on July 1, and "Loess Cave," her favorite, now has an English version. Feng Xinxin, brand director of the village, said more plays will be translated into English as part of a regular international performance and exchange program.
"Inbound consumption by foreign visitors is shifting from products to immersive experiences, and thanks to the expanding visa-free policy, overseas tourists visit more often and tend to explore in greater depth, with varied and increasingly satisfying experiences," said Sun Jiashan, a researcher with the Central Institute of Socialism.
In July, China announced ambitious inbound tourism goals. The country's 2026-2030 tourism development plan proposes attracting 190 million inbound tourist visits a year by 2030, with annual inbound tourism spending exceeding 150 billion U.S. dollars.
As Dai Bin, president of China Tourism Academy, observed, tourism offers an immersive showcase of China's progress in manufacturing and services.
"Easier access to China for foreign visitors is not enough. We should provide better services to help them travel to more places, stay longer and have a good experience," Dai said. ■

"I think I performed at the level I should have. My condition was even a little better than in regular training," he said.

He joined China's senior national team in February and has since had to adapt to the demands of competing alongside more experienced teammates.
"My mindset has matured a lot, and my technique and ability have improved. But there is still a gap between me and the team's standards," Guo said. "I need to keep honing my skills and try to catch up with my older teammates."

As the youngest member of the team, Guo has also found support from his older teammates, who help him refine movements and adjust to new routines.
"After more than half a year of training together, he has become an inseparable part of the team," Zhang said. "Though he is the youngest, he has also become someone his older teammates can rely on."
With new routines and more difficult elements already on the training agenda, Guo is looking toward next year's World Championships, which will also serve as an Olympic qualifier.
Asked about his longer-term ambition, the teenager smiled shyly before giving a two-word answer.

BEIJING, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- China is accelerating the integration of its BeiDou Navigation Satellite System (BDS) with frontier technologies, expanding its application from consumer devices to industrial operations and powering growth across sectors.
Integration with frontier technologies, such as 5G and 6G, artificial intelligence, remote sensing and low-Earth-orbit satellites, is unlocking new capabilities for BeiDou-enabled devices.
"BeiDou has established real-time centimeter-level positioning coverage across China and global high-precision positioning services with fast convergence," said Gou Ping, chairman of China Satellite Network Group Co., Ltd. "The system can support stable connectivity for billions of terminals, hundreds of millions of consumer users and millions of industrial users."
On the consumer end, more than 98 percent of smartphones sold in China now support BeiDou positioning, and over 100 million passenger vehicles are equipped with BeiDou onboard systems, according to an industry report released by the GNSS and LBS Association of China (GLAC).
Liu Zhenfei, chairman of Amap, Alibaba's mapping platform, said the company's AI-native agent -- described as the world's first built on map-based spatial intelligence -- relies on BeiDou's precise location and timing services.
The platform, now one of the world's largest civilian BeiDou service providers, makes approximately 1 trillion positioning requests per day, supporting a daily navigation distance of roughly 9 billion kilometers.
Beyond consumer applications, BeiDou is reshaping traditional industries. In Shanghai's suburban farmlands, more than 10,000 mu (about 667 hectares) of high-standard farmland have become a showcase for smart agriculture, with BeiDou-enabled machinery handling every step of rice cultivation -- from plowing to harvesting.
"The automatic navigation system for agricultural machinery, integrated with next-generation BeiDou positioning terminals, delivers more precise positioning and more stable signals," said Liu Bolin, an executive at a Shanghai-based tech firm.
According to data from the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, by the end of 2025, cumulative shipments of domestically produced BeiDou-compatible chips and modules had neared 2.6 billion units, while the total installed base of BeiDou-enabled terminals had exceeded 2.2 billion.
By the end of 2025, BeiDou had penetrated key sectors such as transportation, energy, urban development and emergency relief, while expanding into emerging areas such as the low-altitude economy, marine economy, and cultural and sports events.
Buoyed by its domestic reach, BeiDou is accelerating its global footprint. As one of four global navigation satellite systems recognized by the United Nations, BeiDou-related products have been exported to more than 140 countries and regions.
Chinese companies have formed an overseas alliance of 40 enterprises, running short-message application tests in Indonesia and Malaysia and establishing cooperation hubs in Brazil and Kazakhstan.
The efforts underpin a broader industry shift from simple product exports to localized, integrated solutions, with Chinese BeiDou companies increasingly delivering turnkey packages to overseas markets.
"With more sectors adopting BeiDou and more companies joining the industry, we are confident the sector will break through the 1 trillion yuan mark," said Li Zhisong, vice president of the GLAC. Sustained technological advancement and mature business models would be essential to better serve socio-economic development, Li added. ■

FAO report urges large-scale forest, landscape restoration to boost food security

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
22:01:37 CST
23:01:37 KST

ROME, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Large-scale restoration of forests and landscapes is a cost-effective way to address food security, biodiversity and climate challenges, according to a report released Monday by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO).
The 2026 edition of the FAO's flagship State of the World's Forests report, released during the 28th Session of the Committee on Forestry, calls for greater investment, inclusive governance and sustained political commitment to scale up restoration efforts.
Forests cover about 4.14 billion hectares, or 32 percent of the world's land area, and store an estimated 714 gigatons of carbon. They also support food security and livelihoods for nearly one-third of the global population, according to the report.
However, about 489 million hectares of forest were lost to deforestation between 1990 and 2025, while more than 460 million hectares of forests are degraded worldwide. An estimated 1.56 billion hectares of land are degraded, driven by population growth, land-use change and growing demand for natural resources.
The report estimated that failing to restore degraded ecosystems costs the global economy between 878 billion U.S. dollars and 6.3 trillion dollars annually. By contrast, restoring more than 1 billion hectares of degraded land could generate 1.8 trillion dollars in annual benefits through improved biodiversity, water regulation and soil health.
FAO Director-General QU Dongyu said forest and landscape restoration is "more than an environmental priority," describing it as a strategic investment in resilient agrifood systems and rural development.
The report identified four priorities for expanding restoration: strengthening people's rights and participation, adopting landscape-scale approaches, mobilizing long-term financing, and improving policies, laws and institutions.
Governments in 91 countries and areas have pledged more than 190 million hectares for forest restoration, the report said. It cited China's Three-North Shelterbelt Program, the Great Green Wall initiative in Africa's Sahara and Sahel region, and the Trinational Atlantic Forest Pact in South America as examples of large-scale restoration efforts. ■

It designates the academy's important priority fields, strategic high-technology fields, sustainable development fields, as well as basic frontier and interdisciplinary fields in its sci-tech innovation layout, targeting to cultivate a batch of key development directions and make the layout more strategic, forward-looking and systematic.

In this system, Beijing (the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region), Shanghai (the Yangtze River Delta) and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area are considered as the strategic highlands, and Hefei, Chengdu-Chongqing, Wuhan and Xi'an as strategic pivots, with a number of key regions as strategic nodes.

This includes the ScienceOne Omni foundation model, intelligent scientist systems, a sci-tech corpus, and a scientific data center. The goal is to accelerate efficient, collaborative support for research.
The plan will actively promote the digital, networked and intelligent iterative upgrading of facilities and platforms such as major national sci-tech infrastructure as well as national field scientific observation and research stations.
It will also step up efforts to collect and integrate data, unify standards and specifications, and strengthen data security. At the same time, it aims to improve data fusion, interoperability, and application, providing strong support for scientific research in key areas and the implementation of major sci-tech projects.
Guided by the needs of building a modern industrial system, the plan will focus on important fields, key regions and major projects, and adopt a two-pronged approach that combines supply-side advances in sci-tech innovation with demand-side pull from industry, so as to accelerate the transformation of sci-tech achievements into real productivity.
Aiming to build a world-class research institution, the plan also outlines reform and development tasks in areas including integrated development of education, science and technology and talent, construction of a national science and technology think tank, reform and management innovation of research organizations, transfer and application of sci-tech achievements, and international sci-tech exchanges and cooperation. ■
