How adults feel about their ADHD depends heavily on their specific symptoms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:00:42 UTC
22:00:42 KST

A new study published in the Journal of Attention Disorders suggests that how adults feel about their attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder depends on their specific symptoms. Researchers found that individuals with higher levels of hyperactive and impulsive symptoms tend to view their condition more positively, while those with primarily inattentive symptoms are less likely to see their diagnosis as an advantage. These findings highlight the diverse ways people experience and interpret their neurodevelopmental differences.
Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, commonly known as ADHD, is a condition that begins in childhood and often continues into adulthood. The diagnosis is based on two main categories of symptoms. The first is inattention, which involves difficulty focusing, sustaining attention, or staying organized. The second category is hyperactivity and impulsivity, characterized by excessive physical movement, restlessness, or acting without thinking. For many years, medical and psychological research focused heavily on the negative impacts of these symptoms, such as difficulties in school, struggles with emotional regulation, and challenges in relationships.
Recently, the rise of the neurodiversity movement has encouraged scientists to look at the other side of the coin. Earlier qualitative studies gathered personal stories showing that people with ADHD often identify real strengths and silver linings in their condition. For example, a study covered by PsyPost in 2025 found that adults diagnosed with ADHD reported experiencing notable personal strengths, identifying positive themes like high energy, unconventional thinking, and a drive for novelty. Similarly, a 2018 interview-based study revealed that many adults with ADHD identify distinct personal strengths and resilience linked directly to their diagnosis.
This qualitative foundation sparked recent efforts to study these positives numerically. A 2024 study took early steps to measure these strengths, finding that people with more ADHD traits in the general population also scored higher on traits like cognitive flexibility and sensory processing sensitivity. The new research, led by Gili Katabi of Tel-Aviv University, builds on this momentum by creating a formal scale to measure positive attitudes toward ADHD. The authors wanted to test whether these positive feelings depend on whether someone’s symptoms are mostly hyperactive or mostly inattentive.
To explore this, the researchers developed the Positive Attitudes Toward ADHD Scale. This questionnaire was designed to capture how individuals perceive the positive aspects of their own condition, based on themes from previous interviews like creativity, dynamic energy, and resilience. Participants rated their agreement with various statements on a five-point scale. The team then recruited three distinct groups of adults with ADHD to test the scale and see how scores related to symptom types.
The first sample included 84 young adults in Israel with formal ADHD diagnoses who completed the questionnaires in a laboratory setting. This initial group helped the researchers confirm that the new scale was reliable and captured a wide range of attitudes. The second sample involved 125 adults in Israel who also participated in the lab. For this group, the researchers conducted structured clinical interviews by phone to verify that the participants still met the criteria for ADHD at the time of testing, while excluding those with heavy alcohol or cannabis use.
The third sample was an online group of 126 English-speaking adults residing in 24 different countries. These participants provided detailed written information about their diagnosis and treatment history to confirm their status. Across all three groups, participants filled out the new attitude scale alongside a widely used checklist that measures the frequency of their inattentive and hyperactive/impulsive symptoms over the past six months.
When analyzing the results, the researchers found that more frequent ADHD symptoms overall were associated with more favorable attitudes toward the condition. However, breaking the symptoms down into the two main categories painted a more detailed picture. Across all three samples, a higher frequency of hyperactive and impulsive symptoms strongly predicted more positive attitudes toward having ADHD.
In contrast, inattention symptoms showed a very different pattern. Higher levels of inattention tended to associate with less positive attitudes toward the condition, though this negative association was not statistically significant across every sample. The researchers also ran a follow-up test with 35 participants from the second sample to measure their general life satisfaction. They found that the link between hyperactive symptoms and positive attitudes remained distinct, indicating that the new scale was capturing specific feelings about ADHD rather than just a generally happy outlook on life.
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2024, which found that young adult hyperactivity and impulsivity predicted higher relationship and job satisfaction later in life. Together, this body of research suggests that the physical and mental energy associated with hyperactivity might foster traits like curiosity and enthusiasm that people learn to appreciate over time.
There are a few things to keep in mind about these findings. The new scale relies entirely on self-reporting, meaning it captures how people feel about their own condition, not objective measurements of their abilities. Endorsing statements about creativity or flexibility does not necessarily mean a person would score higher on a behavioral test of divergent thinking. The study focuses on subjective opinions, which are important for understanding self-esteem and coping, but are separate from observable advantages.
Another detail to consider is the potential for reporting biases based on how society views different symptoms. Hyperactive and impulsive traits might be easier to reframe in a positive light, such as viewing restlessness as boundless energy. Inattentive traits, like spacing out or forgetting things, might feel less socially acceptable and harder to spin positively. Additionally, the researchers noted that their scale did not include questions about hyperfocus, a common experience where people with ADHD become intensely absorbed in tasks they find interesting, which might have skewed the results away from the inattentive dimension.
Future studies could incorporate reports from friends or family members to provide a more rounded view of how these traits manifest in daily life. Scientists might also test whether these contrasting attitudes exist in children and adolescents, or if they are unique to adults who have had more time to adapt to their neurodevelopmental differences.
The study, “ADHD Individuals’ Positivity About Their Condition Varies by Their Levels of Hyperactivity/Impulsivity Versus Inattention Symptoms,” was authored by Gili Katabi, Merav Huss, Steve Lukito, Tycho J. Dekkers, Edmund Sonuga-Barke, and Nitzan Shahar.

Peru’s penguins are on the brink. A super El Niño could make it worse.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Peru’s penguins are on the brink. A super El Niño could make it worse.
Scientists running a ‘living laboratory’ are preparing for the birds’ eventual return
The first time I was in Punta San Juan, the desert was flooded with birds. It was 2012, and I was making a short documentary film about the cormorants, pelicans and penguins that made this arid peninsula in southern Peru one of the largest gatherings of seabirds on Earth.
At the time, this 133-acre reserve — a patch of rock and sand jutting into the frigid waters of the Pacific Ocean — was home to more than a quarter million seabirds, including 300,000 Guanay cormorants (Leucocarbo bougainvilliorum) and some 3,000 Humboldt penguins (Spheniscus humboldti).
One of the few species of desert penguin, the Humboldt live along the arid coast of Peru and Chile, where they nest in burrows dug into guano deposits or small cliff caves. Punta San Juan was home to the largest colony in Peru.
By 2025, there were fewer than 500 penguins left. Avian flu had spread through the reserve in 2022 and 2023, crashing seabird populations and spreading to marine mammals such as sea lions and seals. El Niño struck next. The climate pattern is characterized by months of warmer than usual sea surface temperatures in the eastern equatorial Pacific. Those warm waters pushed anchovy — the penguins’ main food source — deeper and farther out to sea. Industrial fishing operations put even more pressure on the surviving animals.
Ecologist Susana Cárdenas-Alayza, who has run the Punta San Juan Program in partnership with Cayetano Heredia University, the Peruvian government and American zoos for more than 20 years, is increasingly alarmed. As a scientist, Cárdenas-Alayza says, she is used to dealing with numbers and controlled variables, “but diseases and climate events escape my control.”
Now, the reserve is facing a new threat: a potential “super” El Niño. Soaring sea surface temperatures are disrupting the cold, fish-rich waters of the Humboldt Current, which flows past the peninsula. When I returned in July, much had changed from my first trip, when streams of penguins lined the cliffs of the reserve. This time I saw only five penguins — and several abandoned nests with cold eggs. When food is scarce, penguins either stop reproducing or leave their nests altogether to search for a more favorable habitat, Cárdenas-Alayza says. They often starve along the way.
The destruction has also been hard on the reserve’s volunteers, who protect the penguins in what Cárdenas-Alayza calls a “living laboratory.” For decades, volunteers from around Peru and the rest of the world have counted birds, recorded their diets and built artificial nests to keep penguin chicks safe. In the summer of 2025, they even launched a “penguin patrol” to safeguard the Humboldts from workers harvesting guano, nitrogen-rich bird droppings essential for agriculture. Wanting to pitch in, the workers built a temporary, half-kilometer-long wall out of sacks of guano to shield the penguins on their daily walk to the sea.
Keeping research going — and morale high — in the emptying ecosystem has been one of the biggest challenges of Cárdenas-Alayza’s career. No one knows how long the current El Niño will last — or when the fish will return.
Nevertheless, Cárdenas-Alayza says she still has hope. Many species in Punta San Juan are philopatric, or loyal to their territory. That means that even when they leave in search of food or other resources, they eventually come back.
Biologist Patricia Majluf, who founded the Punta San Juan Program in 1979, shares one example of resilience: The El Niño event of 1997–98 decimated the reserve’s sea lions and seals. Penguin numbers dropped into the low hundreds. But the animals eventually mounted a remarkable recovery, helped by a major reduction in anchovy fishing quotas in 2006.
Scientists are busy preparing Punta San Juan for the animals’ return. Cárdenas-Alayza briefed incoming members of Peru’s Congress on the situation in July, and she and her fellow researchers are lobbying hard for stricter fishing quotas. They are also championing a new ecosystem restoration strategy, a collaborative framework that engages fishing communities, companies, students and even local chefs to help the reserve’s animals recover.
Back in Punta San Juan, Cárdenas-Alayza’s team is pressuring the government to reinforce a protective concrete wall around the reserve. In the meantime, they are trapping invasive species that prey on young birds, such as foxes and rats. They are also developing AI tools to speed data analysis from remote cameras monitoring breeding among the surviving Humboldt penguins.
As I prepared to leave, Cárdenas-Alayza, Majluf and I shared a meal of chifa, a Peruvian-Chinese cuisine that is a traditional Sunday dinner for Peruvian families. The three of us talked about our experiences teaching and people we had known at the reserve — and Cárdenas-Alayza teased Majluf, saying she was her “conservation mom.” It was at that moment that I realized what kept drawing me back to the reserve. I had come to document the region’s desert penguins, but I had learned so much more: Conservation isn’t just about science; it’s about relationships. At the end of the meal, we all opened our fortune cookies. Cárdenas-Alayza laughed when she saw hers: “Mountains are meant to be climbed.”
Anna Elisa Sotelo’s work on this story was supported by the Pulitzer Center.

Bose Launches New Wired Earbuds After More Than a Decade

22:00:00 KST

Bose used to make lots of wired headphones. But it’s been a minute. Specifically, it’s been 11 years. Since then, wired headphones entered 2026 having a serious moment, with sales up for the first time in five years—10 percent in the back half of 2025 and 20 percent at the start of 2026. Young people are driving the trend, including celebrities sporting wired earbuds and literally writing songs about them.
Bose president of consumer audio Raza Haider (among others at the company) noticed. He dropped off his teen at college last year and saw wired earbuds left and right. A return to wired earbuds seems to be a national trend—it’s certainly popular among the Gen Z and Gen A of New York City, and the teenage kids of WIRED staffers too.
The new $99 Bose Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds come to the market just in time to capitalize on this trend. Launching them, from idea to final product, took the company around eight or nine months, said Haider. This is much faster than most audio releases I’m familiar with. Haider explained that Bose has been working toward enabling faster, more efficient production to accelerate new product launches, revisions, and collaborations.
Testing the Bose Wired Earbuds: Are They Any Good?
I was one of a few reviewers to get these earbuds ahead of launch. I’ve had them for only four days, and they’re technically a late-stage prototype, not the final product, so this is more of an impression than a full review. But so far, so good.
As with any wired headphones, the simplicity is a big part of the appeal. There’s no battery to charge, no app to download, no Bluetooth to fiddle with, and no latency to ruin your TV show or video game.
Already, the Bose earbuds leapfrog cheaper wired pairs (like Apple EarPods) in sound quality and active noise canceling (ANC). They have clear detail across lows, mids, and highs, especially for something at this price point. More importantly, the noise canceling is a godsend. I can listen to music at more comfortable levels, even during a commute or café stop.
What I don’t love: The central control panel is a little heavy. It has a volume up and volume down, as well as a play/pause/noise-canceling mode switch button, but it weighs down the cable. It’s pretty flush against my torso, which is nice, but it also weighs down the earbuds in my ears. The cable tension it adds is annoying, especially compared to the tension-free experience of using wireless earbuds. The cable is thick and premium-feeling, but it inevitably ends up tangled inside of the included soft pouch.
The earbuds have (removable) silicone wing-tip stabilizers, and the box comes with extra ear tip and stabilizer sizes to find your best fit. The buds come in black, white, and a limited-edition mint color, and they start shipping October 15. You can preorder starting today at Bose and Best Buy.
While Bose's return to wired headphones feels significant, wired earbuds never truly went away. Here are some of WIRED's favorites that are currently available to buy.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent hires Wall Street economist David Zervos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:53:03 UTC
21:53:03 KST

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has hired veteran Wall Street economist David Zervos, the longtime chief market strategist at Jefferies, as a counselor in the Treasury Department. Zervos was a CNBC contributor.
Bessent announced the hire Monday in a statement obtained first by CNBC. Zervos will serve in a broad advisory capacity and is expected to begin immediately.
He has backed Bessent's recent decision to increase buybacks of some long-term Treasury debt and has called for lower interest rates from the Federal Reserve.
Zervos in a brief interview called himself a "Wall Street geek" and said he was excited for his third stint in government. Bessent "has done an incredible job in this administration at guiding the economy through a lot of tumultuous periods," Zervos said.
"Whether it's trade, whether it's war, he's stepped up," he said of Bessent.
Zervos will add intellectual firepower to the Treasury after a series of staff departures that have drawn some attention. Seven of the department's 16 Senate-confirmed appointees had left the department as of mid-August, the Washington Sun reported. Bessent is on his third chief of staff since becoming Treasury secretary in January 2025.
Fellow Wall Street economist Joseph Lavorgna of SMBC Nikko served in a similar role as counselor to Bessent before leaving in March. The position doesn't require Senate confirmation.
Bessent handles an especially broad portfolio for a Treasury secretary. He has been effectively President Donald Trump's top negotiator on China and has been closely involved in policy debates about artificial intelligence, although Trump on Friday said Bessent would not add a role as the administration's top AI advisor.
Zervos was considered by Trump to run the Federal Reserve, though the president ultimately chose Kevin Warsh for the job in January.
Zervos has worked at Jefferies, a New York-based investment bank, since 2010.
Zervos has a doctorate in economics and has worked twice for the Fed. The first time was at the start of his career, in the early 1990s, when he did technical economics and interest rate research. He left for the private sector and returned to the Fed in 2009 as a visiting advisor in the wake of the financial crisis. Warsh was a governor at the Fed then, though it isn't clear if he and Zervos worked together directly at the time.
Zervos will serve as a special government employee, he said in an email to his clients. That status allows him to avoid some often-onerous divestiture requirements that come with other federal appointments, but it restricts how long he can hold the position. Zervos said he expects his term to end in April 2027.
Zervos said last year he believed interest rates should be "much lower." Since Warsh took the job, Zervos has said he thinks Warsh can make room for lower interest rates by cutting the Fed's balance sheet. Those reductions are one of Warsh's top priorities.
The Fed raised interest rates earlier this month for the first time since 2023. That decision prompted frustration from some economists in the Trump administration, but Bessent has been more circumspect. He said Sunday in an appearance on Fox News that the Fed "should have an open mind" about how to manage the economy.
Bessent has intervened in Treasury markets as interest rates have continued to rise. The 10-year Treasury hit 5.2% on Friday, a level last seen in 2007, powered by a strong economy, competition for capital from the artificial intelligence build-out and concerns about inflation as the Iran war continues.
Zervos, in a CNBC appearance last month, backed Bessent's decision to increase buybacks of some long-term Treasury debt, a move that may have eased pressure on some Treasury yields. Some on Wall Street had criticized the buybacks, but Zervos said he supported them.
"I don't see how you could fight this when the firepower and the cards are all sitting in the Treasury Department," Zervos said.

U.S. Embassy Issues Security Alert to Citizens in U.K. Amid Suspected Terror Plot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:50:40 UTC
21:50:40 KST

The U.S. embassy in London has issued a security alert for American citizens in the U.K. following a suspected terror plot near an RAF airbase used by the U.S. military, which led to the arrests of five men who have since been released on bail.
“U.S. citizens are encouraged to exercise caution and be mindful of personal security,” read the notice responding to the Sunday incident near RAF Fairford. “U.S.-associated facilities, gatherings, and organizations may be at heightened risk. U.S. citizens are advised to follow instructions of local authorities for their personal safety and security.”
The alert reminded Americans that the U.K. in April raised its national terrorism threat level to “severe” from “substantial,” a decision made after an antisemitic attack in London was declared a terrorist incident by police. The “severe” level, according to the Metropolitan Police, means “an attack is highly likely.”
The warning came after British police arrested five men on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offenses after they were detained near RAF Fairford in southwest England, an airbase used by the U.S. to strike Iran, in the early hours of Sunday. Officers made the arrests after receiving a tip-off that three "suspicious vehicles" appeared to be heading toward the direction of the base, which Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) previously said could be a target on account of its use by the U.S. military.
The U.K.’s Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) confirmed in a statement to TIME that the five arrestees were British nationals in their 20s who live in London. They were all released on bail Monday afternoon, local time. "They are subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others. They absolutely remain under investigation as we explore multiple lines of enquiry," according to the CTP.
British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme early Monday that it is too soon to speculate over the motives during a live investigation. Questioned about a potential Iran link, he said: "We know that Iran and their proxies wish to do us harm. We know that they hate our democracy, and we know that we regularly have to thwart Iranian attempts to threaten either our interests or indeed our allies."
CTP’s deputy assistant commissioner Vicki Evans said she was “very aware of the levels of speculation about the motivation behind this incident, and the geopolitical questions that are being raised,” but stressed more time is needed to work through the case.
Additionally, the head of CTP Laurence Taylor emphasized his officers are considering this case from "every possible angle," including the potential that this "may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state."
The Iranian embassy in London has said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" any attempt to "link Iran to" the arrests made near RAF Fairford. "The circulation of such fabricated speculations... will serve no purpose other than to fuel Iranophobia propaganda in the U.K.," it said Monday.
What we know about the arrests at RAF Fairford
RAF Fairford is a NATO-designated standby deployment and a U.S. forward operating base for U.S. Global Strike Command, according to U.K. government records. It has been used extensively by U.S. military aircraft in previous conflicts, including "Operation Iraqi Freedom" in 2003.
Gloucestershire Police, the local authority responsible for the area, received a call from a concerned resident at 12:45 a.m. local time on Sunday, regarding three suspicious vehicles traveling toward the airbase.
The local resident, a farmer, told police she had found the road blocked by three white vans. “I saw a large group of hooded and masked men. When they saw me, they ran ahead of me… I then realised that something highly unusual was taking place,” she later told the BBC.
Armed officers responded to the call and five men were arrested on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act, as well as section 5 of the Terrorism Act.
Police evacuated residents from around 85 nearby households and put a cordon in place while the British Army’s specialist explosive ordnance disposal team examined the vehicles.
While the farmer who alerted police has been hailed for their actions, Streeting has indicated they only had a “partial picture” of the matter and appeared to suggest U.K. security forces had been aware of a suspected plot involving RAF Fairford.
U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday claimed the suspects had been “under view for a long time.”
"Working with Britain, it was an amazing job. We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big damage to our fort, and working with the British worked out great… and we got them,” Trump told reporters.
When asked if Trump had been correct, Streeting did not reject the assertion.
“Our security services and our police, they don’t ask for praise, but I think it was a proud moment yesterday to see the President of the United States recognize the extraordinary work that our police and our security and intelligence services do every day throughout the year and throughout the world to keep us safe,” he said. “That’s all I want to say this morning on that.”
TIME has asked the Ministry of Defense and Downing Street whether the British authorities were already investigating a potential plot.
Speaking at the Labour Party conference later Monday morning, Streeting celebrated the U.K. and U.S. alliance as “the closest of any two nations on Earth” and vowed the two countries “will always stand together against those who hate our freedom and those who wish us harm.”
British Foreign Minister Ed Miliband, meanwhile, referred to the incident near RAF Fairford as a “reminder of the threats our country faces.”
The U.K. must be prepared to “confront” all the security threats facing Europe and the world, he told conference attendees, adding that “we will act against the proxies of Iran.”
Prime Minister Andy Burnham referred to the seemingly foiled terror plot as "deeply concerning," ahead of holding a COBRA meeting (a session of the government’s emergencies committee) to discuss the incident with top advisers Monday afternoon.
Concerns over the risk Iran poses to the U.K.
The U.K. government gave authorization in March for the U.S. to use bombers based at RAF Fairford to carry out strikes on Iranian missile sites used to attack ships in the Strait of Hormuz. The base’s role in the U.S. military’s seven-month operation against Iran may have made the site a target.
While British police and lawmakers have said it's too early to determine who was behind the suspected terror plot, the U.K. government has repeatedly issued stern warnings regarding the threat the Iranian regime poses to the U.K.
On Feb. 28, former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer addressed the nation, explaining the U.K. had no involvement in the initial U.S.-Israeli strikes against Iran, but emphasizing the government’s belief that Iran cannot be allowed to possess a nuclear weapon.
“Even in the United Kingdom, the Iranian regime poses a direct threat to dissidents and the Jewish community,” he said. “Over the last year alone, they have backed more than 20 potentially lethal attacks on U.K. soil."
In March, four men were arrested on suspicion of conducting surveillance of locations and individuals linked to the Jewish community in London to assist Iran. One man was an Iranian national and the other three were British-Iranian nationals. The CTP said the arrests were “part of a long-running investigation and part of our ongoing work to disrupt malign activity where we suspect it.”
A separate investigation resulted in a man being charged in May with assisting a foreign intelligence service relating to Iran.
Earlier this month, a man and woman were arrested in London as part of National Security Act investigation. They were apprehended on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service. Again, the country to which the investigation was linked was Iran.
The IRGC was designated a threat to national security in the U.K. under new powers in July, after a series of antisemitic attacks across England., including arson offenses against Jewish ambulance services.
“These new powers will make it easier to prosecute and lock up anyone carrying out [Iran’s] dirty work here in Britain,” said Starmer at the time.

Blood tests reveal why astronauts get constipated in space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:49:59 UTC
21:49:59 KST

Blood tests reveal why astronauts get constipated in space
Astronauts’ gut bacteria shift within weeks of entering space, potentially revealing why constipation is so common in microgravity.
- Date:
- September 28, 2026
- Source:
- University of Copenhagen
- Summary:
- Spaceflight may dramatically change the gut within weeks, causing bacteria to break down more protein as food moves more slowly through the intestines. The shift could help explain astronaut constipation and may have wider effects on health, making it an important concern for future missions to Mars.
- Share:
Constipation is a familiar problem for astronauts, but scientists have not fully understood why spending time in space can disrupt normal digestion.
New research from the University of Copenhagen, conducted in collaboration with NASA, offers a possible explanation. Scientists analyzed blood samples from 52 astronauts who spent months aboard the International Space Station and found signs that the digestive system begins changing relatively soon after astronauts leave Earth.
"We see changes in astronauts' blood samples that indicate that the gut bacteria begin to ferment protein to a greater extent than usual within weeks after the astronauts arrive in space, and this change continues until they are back on Earth," says joint first author and associate professor at the Department of Nutrition, Exercise and Sports, Giorgia La Barbera.
Gut Bacteria Shift Toward Protein
Protein fermentation occurs when bacteria in the intestines begin breaking down protein rather than fiber because available dietary fiber has already been used. The process is not unique to astronauts and can also occur in people on Earth.
The researchers suspect that microgravity may slow the movement of food through the digestive tract. If food remains in the intestines longer, bacteria have more time to turn to protein fermentation.
"The lack of gravity in space probably causes food to move more slowly through the intestine, and this fits with the fact that we are seeing signs of increased protein fermentation. This may also help explain constipation in astronauts," says co-author of the article Henrik Roager, who is also an associate professor at the Department of Nutrition, Exercise and Sports.
Gut Changes Could Affect the Brain
The findings came from an investigation of metabolites in astronauts' blood. Metabolites are small molecules circulating through the bloodstream that can provide clues about how the body is functioning.
By analyzing these molecules, researchers can learn about processes ranging from diet and metabolism to what is happening inside the intestines.
The results could matter beyond digestion because changes in the gut can influence other parts of the body, including the brain.
"We know that products of protein fermentation [are] often associated with negative health consequences, such as kidney damage, potential effects on mood or reduced ability to focus, among others," says Lars Ove Dragsted, senior author of the study and professor at the Department of Nutrition, Exercise and Sports.
Why This Matters for Missions to Mars
The findings could become especially important as space agencies prepare for longer missions to the Moon and eventually Mars. Astronauts on those journeys may spend far more time away from Earth's gravity than crews currently stationed aboard the International Space Station.
"When we plan for longer journeys in space - for example to Mars countermeasures may be needed to mitigate negative effects of space travel on the intestines," says Giorgia La Barbera.
Researchers say several approaches might help reduce these digestive changes.
"Our findings can inform potential interventions - either directly through increasing dietary fiber, supplementation with prebiotics or other types of treatments that promote peristalsis and decrease gut transit time. This would help reduce protein fermentation and thus provide a healthy gut environment and avoid negative health consequences," adds Henrik Roager.
Peristalsis refers to the coordinated muscle contractions that move food and waste through the digestive system. Supporting that movement could shorten the amount of time material remains in the intestines and reduce the opportunity for excessive protein fermentation.
The Findings Could Also Help Patients on Earth
The work may also have implications far beyond spaceflight.
People who spend extended periods confined to bed often experience constipation as well. Researchers suggest that slowed intestinal movement in these patients could potentially produce similar changes in gut fermentation.
"You can use this knowledge to help bedridden patients. They also experience constipation and likely also have increased protein fermentation that may aggravate health conditions," concludes Lars Ove Dragsted, senior author of the paper.
What Is Protein Fermentation?
Protein fermentation happens when bacteria in the gut begin breaking down protein after they no longer have enough fiber available.
The process is more likely when food remains in the intestines for an extended period, even if a person does not feel noticeably constipated.
As bacteria digest protein, they produce various metabolites. These molecules can enter the bloodstream and travel throughout the body.
Some can also influence the brain through the gut-brain axis, the two-way communication system linking the digestive tract and the brain.
Previous research has associated metabolites produced during protein fermentation with effects on the brain, including anxiety and reduced ability to concentrate.
Why the Results Were Unusually Clear
Research on blood metabolites can be difficult to interpret because metabolism differs considerably from person to person.
The unusual nature of the astronaut data helped researchers overcome some of that variability and strengthened confidence in the pattern they observed.
"The samples we have analyzed come from a total of 52 different astronauts, on different missions and across many years. This is very different from how you normally do a study. So, it is quite impressive that our method has been able to show so clearly that there is consistently more protein fermentation," says joint first author and assistant professor Jan Stanstrup.
How the Study Was Conducted
The researchers examined how human metabolism changes during spaceflight by measuring metabolites in astronauts' blood.
Their analysis indicated that protein fermentation in the intestines increases when astronauts leave Earth and enter microgravity. The blood samples also revealed smaller changes associated with fish and caffeine consumption.
Rather than searching only for predetermined substances, the researchers used a so-called non-targeted approach. This allowed them to analyze the broad range of metabolites in the blood and identify which ones changed during spaceflight.
The samples came from three studies conducted aboard the International Space Station. Even though only small quantities of blood were available, researchers were able to perform additional analyses and extract more scientific information from the existing studies.
The collaboration between researchers at the University of Copenhagen and NASA also highlights the international scientific cooperation made possible by the ISS.
NASA researchers Sara R. Zwart and Scott M. Smith contributed to the study. University of Copenhagen researchers Giorgia La Barbera, Jan Stanstrup, Henrik M. Roager and Lars Ove Dragsted also contributed.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Copenhagen. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Giorgia La Barbera, Jan Stanstrup, Sara R. Zwart, Scott M. Smith, Henrik M. Roager, Lars Ove Dragsted. Longitudinal metabolomics profiles reveal increased gut microbial protein fermentation during Spaceflight. Nature Communications, 2026; 17 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-74979-w

The Trump-Xi Summit Is Over, But Taiwan Is Still Bracing for the Fallout
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:45:00 UTC
21:45:00 KST

The latest meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping led to much anxiety in Taiwan, with fears that Trump could potentially throw Taiwan under the bus in the course of negotiations with Xi. The two leaders agreed to dialogue on AI, as well as tariff reductions on $30 billion in “non-sensitive goods” going both ways. Even so, readouts between the two sides differed as to what was agreed to be purchased, and any discussion of semiconductors, chips, and export controls was not mentioned.
Besides trade deals, there have been few concrete outcomes from the meeting to date, and the two leaders initially remained silent when asked by reporters if Taiwan featured in their summit. Trump later denied that Taiwan was discussed at length, then stated that he and Xi “didn’t spend a lot of time talking about Taiwan.”
Other reports suggest that Xi tried press Trump to curtail support for Taiwan, and accept Beijing’s framing on Taiwan. Chinese state-run media quoted Xi as stating during the meeting: “I hope that the United States adheres to the correct position of opposing ‘Taiwan independence’ and handles the Taiwan issue prudently.”
In particular, ahead of the Trump-Xi meeting, international media reporting suggested that Xi would try to convince Trump to cut weapons sales to Taiwan. Although the Trump administration approved $11 billion in arms sales to Taiwan last December, the Trump administration has yet to approve a further $14 billion package.
It was generally understood that Trump would not approve the arms sale ahead of his meeting with Xi, in order to ensure that the talks went smoothly. For its part, the Taiwanese government has attempted to reassure the public that ties with the United States are stable, and reiterated that U.S. policy on Taiwan has not changed after the summit. Nevertheless, the real question will be whether Trump reveals any unexpected curveballs for Taiwan after the meeting itself.
If so, this would follow the precedent set by Trump after his meeting with Xi in May 2026 in Beijing. Little happened during the meeting itself, which was mostly a non-event. In May, as with this latest summit, Trump initially declined to answer questions on Taiwan from reporters. The readouts of the May 2026 meeting differed between the United States and China, with the U.S. denying that Taiwan had come up at all, while China claimed that it had been discussed. As if to forestall a potential shift in position by Trump, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio emphasized during the May trip that U.S. policy on Taiwan was unchanged in an interview with NBC.
During an interview with Fox News shortly after his return from China, however, Trump seemed to hit out at Taiwan, stating that he was “not looking to have somebody go independent,” and that Taiwan needed “cool down a bit.” Trump then moved on to attack Taiwan with accusations that it had stolen the U.S. semiconductor industry, while calling on semiconductor companies to move back to the United States.
Most alarming of all, Trump cast doubt on U.S. commitment to Taiwan as a whole, while suggesting that the Taiwan-U.S. relationship was mostly transactional. In particular, Trump suggested that arms sales to Taiwan were up for negotiation, and that this made for a “good bargaining chip” in talks with China.
Such comments provoked alarm in Taiwan, seeing as this contravenes U.S. commitments to provide weapons to Taiwan dating back to the Reagan-era Three Assurances. Trump also raised questions about whether the United States would intervene in the event of a conflict with China, stating that he did not think it was logical for American troops to “travel 9,500 miles to fight a war.”
Given that recent history, Taiwanese may have been more nervous after the latest Trump-Xi summit ended.
Indeed, indications have since emerged that Trump offered to sell arms to China during his September meeting with Xi. David Perdue, the U.S. ambassador to China, stated that Trump made such comments to Xi in an interview with Fox News on September 27. Although Perdue also stated that U.S. policy remained unchanged on Taiwan, this was an unusual comment by Trump. The offer came only a few days after controversy erupted about F-35 parts that were mistakenly diverted to Hong Kong, raising concerns about sensitive U.S. military technology ending up in Chinese hands.
As such, while Taiwan may have breathed a sigh of relief that the September summit has not resulted in any overt shift in U.S. policy on Taiwan, what remains is to see whether Trump shifts later on. As some analysts have noted, Trump has already echoed Chinese language on Taiwan on numerous occasions in the past. And while some elements of his administration, such as Rubio, may emphasize that policy remains unchanged, this is not reassuring when Trump himself contradicts those statements.
It is still uncertain when further U.S. arms sales to Taiwan will be approved. Trump and Xi are set to meet two more times this year, in November at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, as well as at the G20 summit in December at the Trump National Doral Miami Golf Club in Florida. It is possible that Trump will hold off on arms sales until after these meetings, or until 2027. Trump’s decision whether to approve arms sales or not could also be impacted by the U.S. midterm elections in November.
With the Trump administration holding off on approving arms sales to Taiwan, this may complicate the domestic debate on defense spending. In past years, the United States has sought to pressure Taiwan to increase defense spending to 5 percent or even 10 percent of GDP, with Trump himself suggesting that the U.S. should not defend Taiwan if Taiwan is not serious about its own defense.
But at a time of stark partisanship, the Kuomintang (KMT) delayed for over 200 days on reviewing the central government budget, while enacting widespread cuts to government ministries it views as antagonistic. The delays impacted defense spending, as well as spending on Taiwan’s domestic drone program. Even so, the KMT suddenly reversed course in August to finally approve the budget, though it limited drone spending by passing it as part of the central government budget rather than as a special expenditure.
Efforts by the United States to push Taiwan to increase defense spending are likely to ring hollow in Taiwan if Washington refuses to sell Taiwan arms. Likewise, comments by Trump will increase doubts about U.S. reliability as an ally in wartime – indeed, survey polling shows that skepticism about the U.S. is up across the board in Taiwan. (Such polling also shows an increase in the Taiwanese public’s willingness to fight – even without U.S. intervention.) Certainly, with the United States holding off on arms sales to Taiwan for so long, Trump suddenly offering to sell arms to China is not likely to reaffirm faith in the U.S. in Taiwan.
Increased skepticism about U.S. reliability is likely to lead to efforts to shore up Taiwan’s domestic defense programs, which are not reliant on the mercurial nature of arms sales. Taiwan is especially likely to seek cooperation from non-U.S. partners on drone development, while positioning itself as an alternative to drone supply chains highly reliant on China.
It can be expected that summits between Trump and Xi will fall into this familiar script going forward – even when the meetings themselves may result in little substance, the point is to see what occurs afterward, and how left-field comments or actions by Trump are perceived.

Defense Intelligence of Ukraine Strikes Russian L-39 Aircraft, Three Boats, and Multiple Radar Systems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:41:15 UTC
21:41:15 KST

Operators of the Prymary special unit of the Defense Intelligence of Ukraine struck a number of enemy military targets, including in Crimea.
The Defense Intelligence of Ukraine published footage of the operation on its social media pages.
During the operation, the intelligence officers struck a railway bridge over the North Crimean Canal, which Russian occupation forces use to provide logistical support to their units.
In addition, the unit destroyed nine communications and surveillance facilities, including communications towers, electronic warfare (EW) and electronic intelligence (ELINT) systems, airborne radar stations, and MESH repeaters that provide secure wireless communications between Russian units.
The Prymary unit struck a Nebo-U radar designed to detect and track airborne targets. The system can detect fighter aircraft at ranges up to 400 km at altitudes of 20 km, as well as ballistic missiles at distances up to 300 km and altitudes up to 50 km.
The special forces also struck the command post of a mobile two-coordinate P-18 Terek radar. The station operates in the meter-wave band and can detect airborne targets at ranges of up to 360 km and altitudes of up to 27 km, and can provide target designation to surface-to-air missile systems.
Two 39N6E Kasta-2E radars were also hit. This low-altitude, decimeter-band radar can detect aircraft, helicopters, and cruise missiles flying as low as 100 meters, at ranges up to 42 km. At higher altitudes, its detection range extends to up to 150 km.
Among the adversary’s aviation losses was an L-39 Albatros jet trainer/light attack aircraft. The aircraft has a maximum takeoff weight of 4.7 tonnes, a maximum speed of 750 km/h, a practical flight range of up to 1,100 km, and a weapons payload of up to 250 kg carried on external hardpoints.
At sea, the personnel of the Defense Intelligence of Ukraine engaged a BK-10 high-speed assault craft. The 10.4-meter vessel has a maximum speed of up to 40 knots, a range of up to 400 nautical miles, and a troop-carrying capacity of up to nine personnel.
Another maritime target was a BK-16 high-speed transport-and-assault craft. 16.4 meters long and displacing 19.5 tonnes, the vessel can reach speeds of up to 45 knots, has a range of up to 400 nautical miles, and can transport 19 troops in addition to a two-person crew.
In addition, the personnel of the Defense Intelligence of Ukraine destroyed a Project 12150 Mongoose high-speed patrol craft. With a displacement of 27.2 tonnes and a length of 19.45 meters, the vessel can reach speeds of up to 50 knots and has an endurance of up to two days, with a maximum range of up to 410 nautical miles.
On September 28, unmanned aerial vehicles attacked railway infrastructure in several areas of Russia’s Bryansk and Kaluga regions.

U.S. President Donald Trump has suggested the White House is still considering a diesel export ban as he faces mounting political pressure to tackle soaring fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections in November.
"We're thinking about it very seriously," Trump told a Fox News reporter on Sunday, while attending the Presidents Cup golf tournament in Illinois.
"That can oftentimes lead to a little bit of an increase on gasoline for cars, so we're looking at it very seriously. We may do it," he added.
Trump has previously indicated support for an export ban as retail diesel prices have climbed to fresh record highs, saying earlier this month that a decision would be made quickly "one way or another" on whether to implement a ban.
U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright has said the White House is considering restrictions rather than an outright ban, while Politico reported last week that the Trump administration was preparing a plan to ban diesel exports for 90 days.
The idea of the world's largest diesel exporter implementing an outright ban has prompted firm pushback from the U.S. energy industry, while analysts have warned that the move could backfire and exacerbate the global fuel crisis.
Diesel prices have soared amid hostilities between the U.S. and Iran, as well as Russia and Ukraine, with the conflicts disrupting vital oil and fuel trade routes. Average U.S. diesel prices hovered around $6.50 a gallon on Friday, according to AAA, up sharply from a year ago but just below their record high of $6.53 on Sept. 22.
Commodity strategists at Morgan Stanley have said an export restriction from the U.S., which has become an important source of marginal diesel supply amid reduced flow from Russia and the Middle East, would likely lower U.S. diesel prices initially — "but with potentially adverse reactions downstream."
"Not only would diesel prices be higher globally, but there could be a feedback loop to US gasoline prices as refinery runs adjust," strategists at Morgan Stanley said in a research note published Thursday.
'The biggest problem for the global oil system'
Benedict George, head of European product pricing at Argus Media, said some form of U.S. restriction on diesel exports would likely send European diesel prices and premiums against crude "to a new unprecedented level," noting that the U.S. has supplied about half of Europe's diesel imports over the last couple of months.
"It's really important to be clear that there is no measure yet and it's very unclear whether there will be a measure at all and what the measure will be even if there is a vision," George told CNBC by telephone.
When talking to oil traders in Europe, it's clear that they mostly doubt the U.S. is going to restrict diesel exports, given how challenging a move would be for U.S. oil companies, George said.
In the U.S., soaring diesel prices have put additional financial strain on farmers and agricultural workers as well as drivers and households ahead of the November midterm elections.
The American Petroleum Institute, an oil lobby group, was among those to have quickly contested the prospect of a U.S. diesel export ban when Trump initially appeared to back the idea last week.
In a statement, API CEO Mike Sommers said that "restricting U.S. energy exports would only compound the problem—exacerbating refining challenges and ultimately hurting consumers."
He added, "The answer is more supply and more flexibility—not new restrictions that risk making a difficult situation worse."
Trump has previously urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian oil refineries, saying the attacks are "hurting the world" as fuel supply disruptions continue to prop up U.S. diesel prices.
Ukraine, which fears an extremely difficult winter period amid expectations of another Russian assault on its energy infrastructure, has previously characterized Russian oil refineries as legitimate military targets.
Argus' George said Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries have added a whole new layer to the global supply crunch, making diesel "the biggest problem for the global oil system, whereas before it was one of several very big problems."
What next for the global diesel supply crunch?
Asked for his outlook on how long the global diesel supply crunch could last, George said the uncertainty is so extreme that some traders have simply given up trying to forecast the market.
"One trader was saying to me recently that he doesn't bother trying to forecast now because it feels like a waste of effort. You have literally no idea what is going to happen," George said.
"We don't know if the U.S. will introduce any restrictions, but I think all anybody has talked about is a short-term measure, so two or three months at an absolute most … so there is a kind of time horizon on the U.S. restriction of exports, if it were to happen," he said.
"But on the Russia-Ukraine conflict, who knows? I mean, literally nobody knows. Nothing has worked so far to resolve that situation and similarly for the semi-closure of the Strait of Hormuz."
— CNBC's Spencer Kimball and Michael Bloom contributed to this report.

Nvidia releases software platform to stop AI agents from misbehaving
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:32:15 UTC
21:32:15 KST

Nvidia is rolling out a new software platform to allow AI developers to set safeguards for agents and prevent them from breaking out of containment.
"You can't have agents roam around and drift around the company, and so you have to find a way to container it," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Monday.
Huang said the new platform is essentially "a browser for agents," providing a containment system that only allows access to things an agent needs to do its job.
The release on Monday of Nvidia's Open Agent Safety Platform comes after companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Google disclosed recent incidents in which their artificial intelligence models escaped their sandboxes and attempted to hack other companies and access their computer systems.
An Nvidia representative told reporters on a call on Sunday that its platform could have prevented OpenAI's Hugging Face incident in July. That's when OpenAI models escaped containment, accessed the open internet and breached Hugging Face, which operates an open-source developer platform.
"Each security incident is unique, and we have to look at all of them in detail," said Justin Boitano, vice president of enterprise AI at Nvidia, the world's most valuable company. "From what we know, Hugging Face reported over 17,000 agents attacking their infrastructure that went on for days and weeks."
Nvidia has been at the center of the generative AI boom since the launch of ChatGPT almost four years ago, as the chipmaker's graphics processing units are critical to the development of large language models and to the AI services offered by hyperscalers. But Huang has more recently emerged as a key voice in the AI safety debate, arguing that many security concerns are engineering issues that can be solved through computer science and product development.
"You have to think about what you could have done, what's the solution for it," Huang said in a podcast with The New York Times' Ezra Klein released last week, referring to recent incidents. "In the future, improve your process so that you could avoid this from happening again."
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei set off an industry firestorm two weeks ago, urging AI model developers to slow their pace of advancement due to fears of the models spinning out of control, an argument that was supported by OpenAI's Sam Altman and SpaceX's Elon Musk.
Nvidia's new offering is an engineering solution to the agent safety issue, Boitano said.
"Recent incidents have highlighted a fundamental hurdle for AI agents, and that is that model-level safeguards alone can't govern what agents can access or do," Boitano said.
One component of the platform is called Nvidia OpenShell, which runs on central processors and sets limits on agent capabilities. Nvidia also announced Sentry, which monitors agents and runs on network chips, not CPUs or GPUs.
Some of the software is open source, and Nvidia is calling its platform a reference design, which means partners are intended to build products on top of it to bring it to market.
Nvidia named Cisco, Microsoft, Oracle, CoreWeave, Dell, HPE, Lenovo, ARM and Intel as partners. Nvidia is also working with Anthropic to integrate cloud managed agents with OpenShell.
"We can't have a successful AI industry if the world doesn't think it's built or confident that it's built and deployed safely," Huang told CNBC on Monday.

The global electronics industry is entering a structural transition. That concentration is being diluted. But interpreting this as the decline of Chinese manufacturing would be a mistake.

BCG based its analysis on 942 publicly traded companies with annual revenues above US$500 million, including 314 headquartered in China. This transformation is remarkable.

Spanish government representative in Ceuta quits over border rush fallout
MADRID, Sept 28 - Spain's representative in its North African enclave of Ceuta resigned on Monday, citing personal reasons after weeks of intense scrutiny over the handling of a border rush involving the arrival of tens of thousands of migrants from Morocco.
The crisis erupted in late July, when more than 72,000 migrants reached Ceuta, overwhelming reception facilities and intensifying debate over migration policy at one of the European Union's two land borders in Africa.
Most of those migrants subsequently left, though thousands of others remain in the self-governing enclave, and the minority leftist government of Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez in Madrid has struggled to contain the political fallout.
Government Delegate Miguel Angel Perez Triano, who oversaw coordination between the Ceuta government and Spanish state agencies and security forces, defended his handling of the crisis but said the subsequent scrutiny, coupled with what he called a campaign of harassment against him and his family, had become unbearable.
"My family doesn't deserve that I should stay on any longer," he said, citing insults, threats and an instance when somebody left a funeral wreath outside his office.
He said the government delegation had no operational control over the border or security forces and that no information available beforehand indicated that so many migrants would enter the enclave.
The Madrid government has repeatedly said that although it received alerts of possible border crossings, nothing pointed to a rush on the scale ultimately seen in Ceuta.
Spain's High Court is conducting an investigation into the events and is due to hear testimony this week from Perez Triano's former chief of staff.
Speaking to Cope radio station on Monday, Spanish Territorial Policy Minister Angel Victor Torres estimated that up to 3,500 migrants remained in Ceuta outside the enclave's reception facilities. REUTERS

Scientists were wrong about this strange mammal for nearly 40 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
12:25:21 UTC
21:25:21 KST

Scientists were wrong about this strange mammal for nearly 40 years
A remarkably complete “Cretaceous rabbit” fossil from Mongolia has overturned a 40-year-old idea about early mammal evolution.
- Date:
- September 28, 2026
- Source:
- American Museum of Natural History
- Summary:
- A beautifully preserved fossil from Mongolia’s Gobi Desert has solved a mystery that puzzled paleontologists for nearly 40 years. Tamirkhan balcarceli shows that zhelestids were not early relatives of modern placental mammals, despite having teeth that seemed to suggest they were. Instead, the rabbit-like animal belonged to a separate lineage of small Cretaceous mammals.
- Share:
A remarkably complete fossil discovered in Mongolia's Gobi Desert is changing how scientists view mammal evolution during the age of dinosaurs. The newly identified species, described in the journal Nature by researchers from the American Museum of Natural History, Stony Brook University, University of Arizona, and Arcadia University, provides new evidence about an extinct group of mammals called zhelestids.
For decades, many scientists thought zhelestids were closely related to modern placental mammals. The new fossil suggests otherwise. Instead, zhelestids appear to have belonged to a very different branch of early mammals, overturning an interpretation that was based largely on fossil teeth.
"This discovery illustrates why fieldwork remains indispensable to understanding life's history," said the study's lead author Andres Giallombardo, who found the specimen as a graduate student on a Museum-sponsored expedition in 2004. "It was the thrill of a career to find a new species so completely preserved that also solves a longstanding scientific problem, and a reminder that the Gobi Desert, which is well known for fossils, continues to change science."
Fossil Teeth Pointed Scientists in the Wrong Direction
Zhelestids have been known to paleontologists for nearly 40 years, but most discoveries consisted of isolated teeth or incomplete remains. Their teeth were unusually specialized for eating plants compared with the sharper teeth used for eating insects that are common among many Cretaceous mammals.
Those features led some paleontologists to propose that zhelestids represented an unknown group of hoofed mammals. Scientists also debated whether they might have been placental mammals living during the Cretaceous, part of the broad group that today includes humans and most living mammal species, or whether they were part of a separate lineage that independently evolved similar characteristics.
Molecular clock studies have supported the possibility that placental mammals originated well before the end of the Cretaceous. The newly described fossil, however, provides physical evidence pointing in another direction.
"Molecular models based on living animals can predict the past, but fossils provide the evidence needed to test those predictions," said study coauthor Paul Velazco, a comparative biologist at Arcadia University.
A Nearly Complete Skeleton Reveals the Animal's True Identity
The new species, Tamirkhan balcarceli, was discovered in the eastern Gobi Desert and is the most complete zhelestid specimen found so far. Because so much of the animal is preserved, scientists can now see what members of this mysterious group actually looked like.
Tamirkhan has the low, rounded teeth associated with zhelestids. But it also possesses long, continuously growing incisors and several distinctive skull features seen in zalambdalestoids, a group of small, shrew-like insectivore mammals.
Its limbs provide another important clue.
"Tamirkhan's hind legs are long and slender with distinctive ankles, traits that are unmistakably zalambdalestoid," said study author Shawn Zack, a paleontologist at the University of Arizona.
Taken together, those features led the researchers to conclude that zhelestids were neither placental mammals nor especially similar to placentals. Instead, they were part of the zalambdalestoid group.
The finding also suggests that Cretaceous mammals may not have been as anatomically varied as scientists might have inferred from their teeth alone. The rounded teeth associated with zhelestids, which resemble those found in many plant-eating mammals, were probably an example of convergent evolution. This occurs when unrelated animals independently develop similar traits as they adapt to comparable ways of life.
Why Teeth Cannot Always Reveal the Whole Animal
The discovery highlights the risks of reconstructing an extinct animal from only a small part of its skeleton.
"More than 200 years ago, French naturalist Georges Cuvier famously argued that a single tooth could allow scientists to predict the anatomy of an entire animal," said study coauthor Maureen O'Leary, a paleontologist at Stony Brook University and research associate at the Museum. "While teeth remain among the most informative fossils available, this work demonstrates that teeth cannot always tell us how the whole animal looked."
Measuring between 6-7 inches from head to tail, Tamirkhan had unusually elongated hind limbs that gave it an appearance somewhat like a rabbit. Paleontologists have sometimes informally called zhelestids "Cretaceous rabbits" because they resembled rabbits despite being only distantly related to modern ones.
The Gobi Desert Continues To Reshape Mammal Evolution
The specimen also demonstrates the exceptional scientific value of the Gobi Desert. Along with fossil sites in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan, the region is one of the few places where zhelestids have been preserved.
"The Gobi is one of the only places where we routinely recover such remarkably complete Cretaceous mammals," said coauthor Michael Novacek, a curator in the Museum's Division of Paleontology who has co-led annual expeditions to the Gobi since 1990 in partnership with the Mongolian Academy of Sciences. "These extraordinary fossils continue to transform our understanding of mammalian evolution."
The researchers were also able to place the new species within the mammal family tree using MorphoBank, a comprehensive research platform for studying mammalian evolutionary relationships. First published in 2013, the database has grown for more than a decade as scientists have added an increasing number of important fossil species. It now provides the most comprehensive framework yet assembled for analyzing relationships among early mammals.
Other authors on this study include Eva Hoffman from Yale University.
Fieldwork and laboratory research in the Gobi Desert were supported in part by the Margaret and Will Hearst Paleontological Research Fund and the Frick Laboratory Endowment at the Museum. The research also received support from the U.S. National Science Foundation, grant numbers MRI-R2 0959384, EAR 2506729, and EAR 2506727.

Journal Reference:
- Andres Giallombardo, Eva A. Hoffman, Maureen A. O’Leary, Paúl M. Velazco, Shawn P. Zack, Michael J. Novacek. Cretaceous zhelestid mammals are zalambdalestoids. Nature, 2026; 657 (8133): 973 DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-10861-5

Turkish comedian convicted over Erdogan ‘insult’ but freed pending appeal
- Deniz Goktas, a Turkish comedian, was convicted of insulting President Erdogan and religious values, sentenced to 19 months, but released pending appeal after nearly three months in prison.
- Goktas defended his satire as political critique, arguing Erdogan should accept humour, highlighting a tougher stance on freedom of expression in Turkey today.
- His arrest sparked protests and inspired younger comedians like Fatih Yilmaz to continue stand-up, despite fears of government crackdown on critics.
AI generated
Istanbul – An Istanbul court convicted a popular Turkish comedian on Sept 28 of insulting President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and another offence but ordered his interim release pending appeal, an AFP reporter in the courtroom said.
Following a lively opening session in which Deniz Goktas, 32, offered a quick-witted defence that had much of the courtroom in stitches, the judge convicted him on two charges, sentencing him to just over 19 months prison.
But until the sentence is finalised – which happens only after it is reviewed by an appeals court – the judge ordered his release.
It was not immediately clear how long the process would take.
Known for his dry wit and political satire, Goktas has spent nearly three months in Karatepe high-security prison since his arrest on July 3, a week after a YouTube video of his Dead Sea show went viral, reaching nine million views.
He went on trial for insulting Erdogan, incitement to public hatred, and praising crime and criminals.
The judge convicted Goktas on the first charge.
The judge then amended the second charge to “insulting religious values” and convicted him of that too, while acquitting him on charge three, the correspondent said.
When the hearing opened, Goktas took to the stand to weave a defence rich in political satire, making witty observations that frequently had the courtroom in fits of laughter.
‘Can’t take a joke’
In the indictment, prosecutors singled out a line in which he called Erdogan “a shy dictator”, but Goktas insisted there was “no criminal element” there.
“Dictator is not an insult – it is a political characterisation,” he said.
“As the president and leader of the party that has ruled the country for 25 years, a political comedy show in which Erdogan’s name is never mentioned would be neither sincere nor have any connection to reality,” he reasoned.
“Erdogan should be open to the art of satire,” he added, denying the charges against him.
None of Turkey’s famous comedians or political satirists had been prosecuted in the past, when “these kinds of criticisms were received much more positively... by society and those in power than they are today”, Goktas continued.
“The laws protecting freedom of expression have not changed since that time. But today, a comedian is sitting in a cell,” he said.
“The joke hasn’t changed. What has changed is the increasingly fragile leadership that can no longer tolerate the joke.”
Among the audience were several comedians from Istanbul’s TuzBiber comedy club – where Goktas reportedly began his career in 2019 – alongside observers from the Dutch and American embassies.
Humour, Goktas told the court, was a centuries-old part of Turkish culture but there should be “no place for censorship, bans or detention when it comes to artistes on the stage”.
‘Makes me feel proud’
He asked to be acquitted and released.
“Three months have been taken away from my life. I quit smoking, so I’ll add three months to the end of my life anyway,” he said, drawing laughter and loud applause as he left the stand.
Goktas’ arrest was the latest in a widening crackdown on anyone seen as critical of Turkey’s Islamo-conservative government or its values.
The crackdown has netted hundreds of people, including politicians, artistes, musicians, journalists and LGBTQ activists.
Outside in the pouring rain, around 50 protesters gathered, chanting: “Denis Goktas is not alone!”
Among them was a student from Alanya, near the southern resort city of Antalya, whose appearance is strikingly similar to Goktas and who recently started doing stand-up.
“I am not afraid to do stand-up after his arrest. I will keep doing it,” said 22-year-old Fatih Yilmaz.
“His arrest made me feel proud. His strong stance and the way he keeps making jokes from his prison cell keep me going.”
Turkish media said the Ankara-born comedian began his career at TuzBiber in Istanbul and has gone on to perform at venues across Europe and the United States. AFP

Tourists watch an immersive drama at the former site of L'indo Bank of China in Tianjin, north China, Sept. 27, 2026. Built in 1912, the former site of L'indo Bank of China is one of the landmarks in Tianjin's Jiefang North Road historical and cultural block, witnessing the development of the city's financial industry in modern times.
This building had undergone many historical changes and had been used successively as an art museum, an international auction house, and a museum of Western art. However, due to the scarcity of exhibitions, it had been idle for a long time until the latest renovation.
In 2025, Beijing Performance & Arts Group, together with Tianjin North Performing Arts Group, initiated the revitalization of the building, creating an immersive performance scene while preserving its original appearance.
This April, the newly renovated building was officially opened to the public, and visitors can view a live-action exhibition here during the day and watch an immersive drama at night.
Up to now, the renovated building has received approximately 30,000 visitors. (Xinhua/Zhao Zishuo)

Iran has no plans for talks with U.S. during delegation's New York visit: media
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
20:14:09 CST
21:14:09 KST

TEHRAN, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Iran has no plans to hold negotiations with the United States during its delegation's current visit to New York, Iran's official news agency IRNA reported Sunday night.
IRNA cited a source close to the Iranian delegation, which is in New York to attend the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, as rejecting "contradictory" reports about talks between Tehran and Washington.
The source said Iran's considerations and positions were conveyed to the American side "explicitly and clearly" through the Qatari mediator on Sept. 22, and that Tehran is awaiting Washington's response.
According to the source, there is no plan for a new round of negotiations with the American side, and Iran's Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi will leave New York for Tehran on Tuesday.
On Sunday, Iran's Foreign Ministry quoted Araghchi as saying that the country had not yet received the U.S. "definitive" views through the mediators on its proposed seven-day plan to cease hostilities and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
He added that Iran had conveyed its plan and conditions to the American side through the mediating countries and had seen U.S. President Donald Trump's initial reaction to the plan, "but nothing has been conveyed to us yet by the mediators."
Araghchi noted, "Of course, the U.S. president has made many contradictory statements, something we unfortunately hear from him quite often. We are waiting for definitive views to be conveyed to us via the mediators, and we will make our decision based on that."
He had earlier said that under Iran's plan, the country would reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if the United States accepted its conditions.
On Feb. 28, Israel and the United States launched joint attacks on Tehran and other Iranian cities. Iran responded with waves of missile and drone attacks targeting Israel and U.S. bases and assets in the region, and tightened its grip on the Strait of Hormuz.
On June 18, the United States and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) on ending the war in the region on all fronts, including Lebanon. Under the MoU, they were scheduled to hold negotiations within a period of 60 days, which ended on Aug. 17, to reach a final agreement, but the talks' fate remains unclear following a series of recent escalations between the two countries. ■

Delhi gov't rolls out measures to tackle recurring winter air pollution
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
20:14:02 CST
21:14:02 KST

NEW DELHI, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- The local government in Delhi, India's capital territory, on Monday announced a slew of measures to curb air pollution, which typically worsens in the winter from November to February.
The measures include higher parking charges, a ban on construction and demolition work, staggered office timings, and a 50-percent cut in on-site staffing at government and private offices, with essential services exempted.
The steps will be introduced in phases from Nov. 1, with some curbs continuing until February 2027.
The measures to control air pollution well in advance are aimed at limiting pollution sources and reducing vehicular movement in the national capital during the months when air quality typically deteriorates sharply.
Delhi, home to over 30 million people, is among the most polluted cities in the world.
Industrial emissions and vehicular traffic are major sources of air pollution, alongside rampant construction activity. Poor wind speed and stubble burning, or farm fires, in neighbouring states also contribute to the decline in air quality.
For years, Delhi's air quality turns hazardous as winter approaches. ■

Ukraine defense spending to rise to 175 bln USD next year
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
20:14:01 CST
21:14:01 KST

KIEV, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- Ukraine's defense spending is expected to increase from 155 billion U.S. dollars this year to 175 billion dollars in 2027, the Interfax-Ukraine news agency reported Monday, citing First Deputy Minister of Finance Roman Yermolychev.
The draft budget currently allocates about 100 billion dollars for defense next year, Yermolychev said, adding that Ukraine needs to use various instruments, including cooperation with international partners, to cover the remaining amount.
Additional funding could be secured through the Ramstein format, the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List initiative and other mechanisms for the direct procurement of weapons, said Yermolychev.
On Sunday, Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said the country's defense budget deficit was estimated at 27 billion dollars this year. The government plans to cover 7 billion dollars of the shortfall through strict public finance austerity measures. ■
