Scientists found a surprising driver of Alzheimer’s outside the brain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
02:39:28 UTC
11:39:28 KST

Scientists found a surprising driver of Alzheimer’s outside the brain
A surprising immune pathway outside the brain may help drive Alzheimer’s-related damage, and blocking it dramatically protected mice from neurodegeneration.
- Date:
- September 27, 2026
- Source:
- WashU Medicine
- Summary:
- Scientists found that immune cells contributing to Alzheimer’s-related brain damage may be activated in lymph nodes outside the brain before traveling into the nervous system. Blocking this pathway in mice dramatically reduced neurodegeneration and preserved cognitive abilities, pointing to a potentially more accessible treatment target.
- Share:
Immune cells that usually defend the body by attacking infected or foreign cells appear in unusually high numbers in the brains of people with Alzheimer's disease and related conditions. Evidence suggests these cells contribute to neurodegeneration, but researchers have not known where they originate or what prompts them to gather in the brain.
A new study from Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis points to an unexpected source outside the brain. In experiments with mice, researchers found that T cells receive signals from lymph nodes that appear to prepare them to enter the brain and contribute to damage. When the scientists disrupted those signals, neurodegeneration was dramatically reduced.
The findings reveal a previously unrecognized immune pathway that may offer a way to slow or potentially halt damage associated with Alzheimer's disease and primary tauopathies. These disorders are marked by twisted accumulations of tau protein in the brain.
The study was published Sept. 3 in Nature Neuroscience.
An Alzheimer's Pathway Outside the Brain
David M. Holtzman, MD, the Barbara Burton and Reuben M. Morriss III Distinguished Professor in WashU Medicine's Department of Neurology and senior author of the study, said the discovery is especially intriguing because it identifies a disease related process that begins outside the brain. That could make it possible to target mechanisms that are easier to reach and better understood.
"One of the issues in developing treatments for neurological diseases is that you need to engineer your treatment so that it gets into the brain and past the blood-brain barrier, but we might not actually need to get the drugs into the central nervous system to mitigate neurodegeneration," Holtzman said. "There are lots of ways to manipulate T cells that have been studied extensively and that are approved treatments for other diseases, but many haven't yet been explored for neurodegenerative diseases."
Tracing T Cells Back to the Lymph Nodes
Holtzman's laboratory has played a leading role in investigating how the immune system contributes to neurodegenerative disease. In a previous study, the team showed that removing T cells from the brain prevented much of the neurodegeneration that normally develops in mice modeling the tau related damage seen in Alzheimer's disease and primary tauopathies.
The next question was where those immune cells came from and what caused them to move into the brain.
In the new study, Holtzman's team included Hao Hu, PhD, a postdoctoral fellow and the study's first author; co-senior author Jason Ulrich, PhD, a professor of neurology; and their collaborators.
Certain T cells rely on other immune cells, known as dendritic cells, to identify the molecular targets they should attack. Very few of the relevant dendritic cells, known as classical dendritic cells type 1 (cDC1), are found in the brain. Those that are present also do not appear to interact with the T cells that emerge after tau tangles develop.
That evidence suggested that both the dendritic cells and the T cell activation process were originating somewhere outside the brain.
Blocking Immune Signals Reduced Brain Damage
To test that possibility, the researchers eliminated dendritic cells from the lymph nodes and other locations in mice that would normally develop tau tangles and neurodegeneration.
The result was striking. Elevated numbers of T cells in the brain, particularly CD8 T cells, largely disappeared, along with the associated brain damage. Yet the amount of tau tangles in the brain did not change.
The mice also preserved their cognitive abilities. That finding suggests that suppressing T cell activity could potentially slow or reduce the cognitive decline associated with Alzheimer's disease, even when tau tangles remain present.
How Brain Damage May Trigger an Immune Attack
Researchers still do not know the exact signal that causes dendritic cells to activate the T cells.
Holtzman said one possibility is that damage caused by tau releases material from brain cells. That material may then travel to lymph nodes in the neck, where dendritic cells identify it and present it as a target for T cells.
The T cells could then be directed toward the brain, where their activity contributes to neurodegeneration.
A Potential New Route for Alzheimer's Treatment
Because this immune pathway operates outside the brain, it may provide several new therapeutic targets.
Holtzman's team is now testing whether interfering with dendritic cell activity in midlife, around the time tau tangles begin to emerge, can produce the same protection seen when the cells were blocked from birth in this study.
The researchers are also working to identify the specific signal that guides T cells toward the brain. If that signal can be determined, it could offer another way to prevent the immune cells from reaching brain tissue and contributing to damage.
"Until not that long ago, most people, including myself, did not think that the immune response was even involved in neurodegenerative diseases that are due to protein accumulation in the brain," Holtzman said. "That these dendritic cells are involved in neurodegenerative disease is exciting; we've shown they're important, and that they are a potential target for future therapy."
Story Source:
Materials provided by WashU Medicine. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Hao Hu, Peter Bor-Chian Lin, Carisa Zeng, Yongyi Li, Megan E. Bosch, Joshua T. Emmerson, Prabal Sharma, Ray A. Ohara, Wendy Dong, Tong Wu, Siling Du, Wenqing Gao, Hong Jiang, Liya Yuan, Xin Bao, Shasha Li, Anthony N. Vomund, Petra Erdmann-Gilmore, Yichen Gu, Miwei Hu, Jonathan Nulman, Timothy M. Miller, Wayne M. Yokoyama, Cheryl F. Lichti, Jeffrey Milbrandt, Richard J. Perrin, Jonathan Kipnis, Maxim N. Artyomov, Kenneth M. Murphy, Jason D. Ulrich, David M. Holtzman. Priming of CD8 T cells by peripheral dendritic cells exacerbates tau-mediated neurodegeneration. Nature Neuroscience, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41593-026-02427-5

Pakistan to host SCO coordinators’ meet from Sept 28-30
India will participate in a meeting of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) national coordinators that Pakistan will host on September 28-30, official sources said. The meeting is expected to approve the calendar of events under Pakistan’s presidency, leading up to the Council of Heads of State (CHS) summit for which Islamabad will soon send out invitations to the leaders of all member-states of the Eurasian bloc, including PM Narendra Modi.After joining the China-dominated grouping in 2017 as a full member, India has participated actively in various SCO mechanisms, with Modi representing India at the heads of state summits and external affairs minister S Jaishankar joining the heads of government meetings.Unlike with SAARC, India has ringfenced its involvement in SCO from outstanding bilateral differences with Pakistan, mainly the core issue of cross-border terrorism, while consistently reminding the Organisation that one of its original mandates was to fight terrorism, extremism and separatism. Government has backed SCO connectivity initiatives too but with the rider that these must respect sovereignty and territorial integrity of all States.India’s national coordinator Alok Dimri is expected to participate in the national coordinators’ meeting that will begin on Monday. Even without any substantive bilateral engagement for a decade, India and Pakistan have regularly seen their officials visiting each other’s country for SCO-related exercises and Jaishankar himself travelled to Pakistan in 2024 for the SCO heads of government meeting.
However, the key question remains – even if it’s too early to ask – whether Modi will attend the summit in Islamabad next year. The SAARC summit process remains blocked because of the PM’s reluctance to travel to Pakistan and, barring a dramatic change in the situation, the PM is unlikely to visit Islamabad.
According to Indian officials, any such change can only be effected by Islamabad through tangible and irreversible action against cross-border terrorism and UN-proscribed terror entities operating out of Pakistan. Government recently denied strongly that it is involved even in any track 2 dialogue with Islamabad.Pakistan had assumed presidency of the SCO at the Bishkek summit earlier this month. Modi said the same day in his address that countries that use terrorism as an instrument of state policy, providing shelter to terrorists, must be categorically told terrorism can never be a strategic asset for anyone.

Germany was warned in the 67th minute when Kimmich lost possession to Vangelis Pavlidis, who released Fotis Ioannidis, but the forward dragged his effort narrowly wide.
Greece made the host pay seven minutes later. Tzolis switched play across the German defense and Kourbelis found space on the edge of the area. His shot took a deflection off Kimmich and beat Alexander Nubel.
Klopp introduced Florian Wirtz and Jonathan Burkardt in search of an equalizer, but Germany struggled to break down the visitor in the closing stages.
"It wasn't an easy game. To be honest, we didn't do well enough," Germany defender Jonathan Tah said. "We had our chances but didn't take them. In the end, they made the most of their moments and scored the one they needed."
The result leaves Germany on one point from its opening two Group 2 matches, while Greece tops the group with six points.

Earlier on Friday, Marcos confirmed to reporters that he had signed a pardon the day before, without elaborating.
Veloso, a 41-year-old domestic worker and mother of two, was arrested in Yogyakarta in 2010 for trying to bring 2.6 kilograms of heroin into Indonesia. She was subsequently sentenced to death under Indonesia’s severe drug laws, but received a last-minute reprieve from execution in 2015 after Philippine officials asked then Indonesian President Joko “Jokowi” Widodo to let her testify against members of a prominent drug trafficking organization.
In December 2024, Indonesia agreed to repatriate Veloso after years of requests from the Philippines, where Veloso’s relatives and supporters had waged a persistent campaign for her release.
Veloso has always maintained her innocence, claiming that she was tricked into carrying the drugs by her godsister. She smiled as she left her prison cell in the Philippines on Friday, after more than 15 years behind bars. In a press conference with Catapang at the Bureau of Corrections, she held up the “absolute pardon” signed by Marcos, which removes the remaining legal consequences of her conviction, allowing her a fresh start, and offered a tearful thanks to the Philippine leader.
“I just want to tell our beloved President: Thank you so much for clearing my name and allowing me to return to my family,” she said, as per Inquirer.net. She added that she was looking forward to reuniting with her two sons, who have grown nearly to adulthood since her arrest.
“It was really hard being separated from them … I didn’t see my children grow, but I believe it’s not yet too late for me to be their guide,” Veloso said.
Veloso’s release was greeted with joy by family members and advocacy groups that have spent years campaigning for her release.
Veloso’s pardon marks a rare positive development in a story connected to Southeast Asia’s tough anti-drug regime. Indonesia is known particularly for its unforgiving approach to drug crimes, especially large-scale trafficking offenses.
Under the agreement Yusril Ihza Mahendra, then Indonesia’s senior minister for law and human rights affairs, said that the Philippines had agreed to respect the Indonesian court’s sentencing of Veloso and her status as prisoner in Indonesia.
However, Yusril also said that the Indonesian government would also respect any decision made by the Philippines once Veloso is back on Philippine soil, including the possible granting of clemency.
“This only proves that there are really second chances, and we are happy that Veloso can now enjoy her newfound freedom with her family,” Catapang said.

Love in Hinduism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Ask an English speaker what love is and they will struggle, partly because one word has to cover a parent’s tenderness, a lover’s passion, a friend’s loyalty and a saint’s devotion. Sanskrit never had this problem. It has separate words for all of these, and several more besides, and the Hindu traditions built distinct philosophies around each of them.
That is the first thing to know about love in Hinduism: there is no single doctrine, because there is no single Hinduism. The word covers three thousand years of texts, dozens of schools and many gods, and they do not agree about love any more than they agree about anything else. The second thing to know is that, out of this variety, one strand became dominant from roughly the seventh century onwards and has shaped Hindu religious life ever since. It is called bhakti – devotion – and its central claim is that the highest form of love, and the surest way to God, is to love God the way you would love a person: with longing, tenderness, jealousy, grief and joy.
This entry gives a map of the traditions and then focuses on bhakti, since that is where the Hindu philosophy of love is richest. Sanskrit terms are given in the standard scholarly spelling; well-known names (Krishna, Radha, Shiva, Vishnu) are left in their familiar English forms.
Daily Philosophy: Love in Islam
The Qur’an says that God loves and is loved, and Muslims have argued for fourteen centuries about what that means. This guide explains the key Arabic words, sets out the three main theories – the theologians’ love as obedience, the philosophers’ love as cosmic attraction, and the Sufis’ love as the secret of creation – and shows how the mystical tradition turned even Layla and Majnun into a parable of the soul. Part of our series on love in the world religions.
The words
Five terms recur throughout, and it helps to have them in view.
Kāma is desire, especially sensual and erotic desire, and also pleasure in general. It is personified as the god of love who shoots flower-arrows, but it is also, in the earliest texts, a cosmic force. Kāma is not sinful; it is one of the legitimate aims of human life. But it is self-directed – it seeks the satisfaction of the one who desires – and this becomes the crucial contrast.
Prema (or prīti) is love in the fuller sense: tender, selfless affection that seeks the good of the beloved. In devotional theology prema is the name for the highest love of God, the love that has burned away all desire for one’s own gratification.
Bhakti comes from a root meaning to share, to participate in, to belong to. It is usually translated “devotion,” and it means loving attachment to a personal God, expressed in worship, song, service and surrender. Bhakti is the relationship; prema is its perfected emotional content.

Love in Buddhism

One day in Sāvatthī, a wealthy woman named Visākhā came to see the Buddha at midday, her hair and clothes still wet from the funeral of her granddaughter. Visākhā was the greatest of the Buddha’s lay patrons, a mother of many children and grandmother of many more, and she had loved the dead girl dearly. The Buddha asked her whether she would like to have as many children and grandchildren as there were people in the city. She said she would. He asked how many people died in Sāvatthī each day. Some days ten, she said, some days one; the city was never free of the dying. “Then would you ever be without wet hair and wet clothes?” No, she admitted. And the Buddha said:
The story is in the Udāna (8.8), one of the oldest collections in the Pali canon, and it is the kind of passage that makes people say Buddhism is against love. Read on its own, it seems to be: love brings grief, grief is suffering, and the whole point of the path is the end of suffering. But the same canon contains the Mettā Sutta, in which the Buddha tells his monks to cherish every living thing as a mother cherishes her only child, and to let boundless love fill the whole world “above, below and across.” And the tradition that grew from that canon produced the bodhisattva, a figure who vows to remain in the world of birth and death, for as long as space endures, until every being is free – the most extravagant ideal of love in the history of religion.
How can both be true? The answer is that Buddhism drew a line through the middle of what other traditions call love, and put one half on the side of the problem and the other on the side of the cure. This entry is about that line: where it runs, why it was drawn there, and what the different Buddhist schools built on either side of it.
Pali terms are used for the early tradition and Sanskrit for the Mahāyāna; words that have entered English (Buddha, nirvana, karma, sutra, bodhisattva, Zen) are left in their usual forms.

Hinduism has no single word for love – it has a dozen. This guide explains the main ones, surveys how the Vedas, Upaniṣads, Advaita and the Gītā treat love, and then focuses on bhakti, the devotional tradition that made love of God the heart of religious life. Part of our series on love in the world religions.
The words
Buddhism has no single word for love, and the absence is deliberate. Its vocabulary separates the wishing-well from the wanting.

Love in Islam
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

In the year 878, in Baghdad, a Sufi named Abū ‘l-Ḥusayn al-Nūrī was put on trial for his life. Among the charges was that he had been heard to say “I passionately love God, and He passionately loves me.” The prosecutor’s objection was not that Nūrī loved God – every Muslim was supposed to do that – but that he had used the wrong word. The verb he chose, ʿashiqa, was the word for the love of a man for a woman: obsessive, bodily, unreasonable. To apply it to God was, in the prosecutor’s view, an indecency bordering on unbelief. Nūrī was acquitted, but the argument he started did not end. Over the next four centuries it produced one of the richest bodies of writing about love in any religious tradition.
That trial is a good way into the subject, because it shows two things at once. First, that love was never marginal in Islam: the disagreement was about how God is loved, not whether. Second, that the disagreement was real. Islam has a scripture that speaks of love in dozens of places, a law that regulates marriage and kinship, a rationalist theology that was nervous about attributing emotion to God, a philosophical tradition steeped in Plato and Aristotle, and a mystical movement that made love the answer to every question. They did not agree, and this entry maps their disagreements before following the mystical line, since that is where the Islamic philosophy of love went deepest.
Arabic and Persian terms are given in standard scholarly transliteration; familiar names and words (Muhammad, Qur’an, Sufi, Rumi, Mecca) are left in their usual English forms.
Daily Philosophy: Love in Hinduism
Hinduism has no single word for love – it has a dozen. This guide explains the main ones, surveys how the Vedas, Upaniṣads, Advaita and the Gītā treat love, and then focuses on bhakti, the devotional tradition that made love of God the heart of religious life. Part of our series on love in the world religions.
The words
Arabic distinguishes kinds of love as carefully as Sanskrit does, and the distinctions carry theological weight.
Ḥubb and its near-synonym maḥabba are the general words for love, from a root that also gives the word for a seed. This is the Qur’an’s word: God’s love for human beings and theirs for him are both ḥubb. It covers affection, attachment, preference and devotion, and it is morally neutral – one can have ḥubb for wealth or for God.
ʿIshq is passionate, excessive love: love that has become an affliction. Its root may be connected to a word for a creeping vine that strangles the tree it clings to. The Qur’an never uses it. It was the word of the love poets, and it became the word of the Sufis, precisely because it named a love that overwhelms the lover and cannot be controlled. Nūrī’s trial was about this word.

Virtue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

The word has a faintly musty smell. “Virtue” suggests Victorian sermons, chastity, and people who do not have much fun. It is not a word we reach for when we admire someone. We say they are kind, or brave, or have integrity – but we rarely say they are virtuous, and if we did, it would sound like a joke.
This is a historical accident, and a recent one. For most of the history of Western thought, from the fifth century BCE to the eighteenth century CE, virtue was not one moral idea among others. It was the moral idea – the central concept around which the whole of ethics was organised. The question philosophers asked was not “What should I do?” but “What kind of person should I be?”, and the answer was always given in terms of the virtues. Then, for roughly two centuries, the concept went into eclipse. Then, in the second half of the twentieth century, it came back. This entry tells that story and tries to say, at the end of it, what a virtue is.
The word
The Greek word is aretē, and its basic meaning is excellence – being outstandingly good at whatever it is you are for. The word is not specifically moral. A knife has aretē if it cuts well; a horse has aretē if it runs fast; an eye has aretē if it sees clearly. The aretē of a human being is whatever makes a human being excellent at being a human being.
The Latin translation, virtus, comes from vir, “man,” and originally meant something like manliness or valour – the qualities of a good soldier. It broadened, especially in Cicero, to cover the whole range of Greek aretē. Our word “virtue” inherits both, and older English still preserves the sense of excellence or power: a medicine has “virtues,” and something happens “by virtue of” a cause.
The point matters because the Greek concept is much wider, and much less prim, than the modern connotation. To ask about aretē is to ask what it is to be really, fully good at living. That is a question almost everyone finds interesting.
Before philosophy: Homer
In Homer, aretē belongs above all to the warrior. Achilles has it in abundance: strength, courage, skill in battle, a fierce sense of honour. It is competitive – to have aretē is to be better than others – and it is publicly displayed and publicly rewarded. But even in Homer the word is not confined to fighting. Penelope has aretē for her fidelity and cleverness, and Odysseus for his cunning and endurance as much as for his spear.
What Homer does not have is any thought that these excellences might conflict, or that the truly excellent person might have to give up glory for the sake of justice. That thought arrives with the philosophers.

Virtue Ethics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

A friend is in hospital. You visit. She is touched, and says so. “Don’t mention it,” you reply. “I worked out that visiting you would produce more overall happiness than anything else I could do this afternoon.” Or: “I recognised that I had a duty to visit, and I always do my duty.”
Something has gone badly wrong, and it is not that you did the wrong thing. You did the right thing. What is missing is you – the friend who visits because she cares about her friend, not because a theory told her to. The philosopher Michael Stocker used this example in 1976 to diagnose what he called the “schizophrenia” of modern ethical theories: they split what we ought to do from what a good person actually feels and wants. Virtue ethics is the attempt to put them back together.
This entry is about that attempt in its modern form. For the long history of the concept of virtue itself – from Homer through Aristotle and Aquinas to its eighteenth-century eclipse – see our separate entry on Virtue. Here we take up the story where that one leaves off: with the revival of virtue as the foundation of an ethical theory, the shape that theory has taken, and the arguments for and against it.
Daily Philosophy: Virtue
For two thousand years, ‘virtue’ was the central word in Western ethics – the name for whatever it is that makes a person good at being a person. Then it nearly disappeared, and then it came back. This entry traces the concept from Homer and Socrates through Plato, Aristotle, the Stoics and Aquinas to Hume, Kant and the twentieth-century revival, and asks what a virtue actually is.
What virtue ethics claims
Normative ethics – the part of philosophy that asks how we should live – is usually taught as a contest between three approaches. Consequentialism says that what matters is outcomes: the right act is the one that produces the best results. Deontology, in its Kantian form, says that what matters is duty: the right act is the one that conforms to the moral law, whatever the results. Virtue ethics says that what matters, first and foremost, is character: the fundamental moral question is not “What should I do?” but “What kind of person should I be?”, and the answer to the first question falls out of the answer to the second.
The point is one of priority. Every ethical theory talks about virtues; Kant wrote a whole Doctrine of Virtue, and Mill discusses it at length. What makes a theory a virtue ethics is that it treats virtue as basic and explains right action in terms of it, rather than the other way round. The Kantian defines a virtue as a disposition to do one’s duty; the utilitarian defines it as a trait that tends to produce happiness. The virtue ethicist reverses the direction of explanation: a right action is what a virtuous …

NEW DELHI: Overall acreage of kharif (summer-sown) crops in the country declined by just over 1% this year compared with last year and while the dip was expected due to deficient monsoon rainfall this year, the sowing season still ended up recording higher than 'normal' (average of last five years) acreage. Though only marginally above the 'normal', it reflects tweaks in farmers' strategy if warning comes in advance.Latest acreage data shows total sown area at 1,107 lakh hectares (ha) as of Friday was 3 lakh ha more than 'normal' acreage (1,104 lakh ha) despite a cumulative deficit of 12% (June 1-Sept 26) in monsoon rainfall. In the same period in 2025, which recorded 8% more than normal (surplus) rainfall, total acreage was 1,121 lakh ha.The most popular kharif crop and one of the most water-intensive, paddy, reported a 3.6% decline in acreage compared with last year, but this was still 4.6% higher than the 'normal' acreage. Another guzzler, sugarcane, too reported higher acreage than its normal sown area, reflecting farmers' preference for crops which assure them of better returns, even as they had to depend on excessive use of groundwater, at the risk of high input cost.
The real test of what rainfall deficit will entail, however, may be reflected in the yield of these crops, first estimates for which will soon be released by the Union agriculture ministry. The output of pulses (mainly pigeon peas), oilseeds (mainly soybean and groundnut), cotton and coarse cereals (mainly bajra and maize) may be a real concern due to deficient and skewed distribution of rainfall in the 'monsoon core zone' - the large part of central India and Bihar which depend on seasonal rains for farming in absence of adequate irrigation coverage.
Floods in certain parts of Bihar and Assam, and drought in parts of Maharashtra and Karnataka may also negatively impact the overall output.Apprehending the impact of deficient monsoon rainfall on the rabi (winter-sown) crops due to low moisture content in the soil and shortage of water for irrigation, the agriculture ministry will discuss contingency measures at a two-day meet starting Monday.

Ismat Ara on India’s Crackdown on Love
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
01:38:00 UTC
10:38:00 KST

Love and marriage across religious and caste lines have always been frowned upon and forbidden in India. However, Hindu right-wing organizations have taken this to a new extreme by conjuring up a conspiracy theory they term “love jihad.” India is witnessing a systematic strategy being implemented by Hindutva activists to not just prevent Hindu women from marrying Muslim men but to malign the latter by ascribing to them sinister motives of enticing Hindu women with false promises of love and marriage for the sole purpose of converting them to Islam. Bharatiya Janata Party politicians have used the “love jihad” bogey to deepen Hindu anxieties and polarize society. BJP governments in several states have enacted anti-religious conversion laws. Meanwhile, right-wing goons have wreaked enormous havoc in the lives of young couples who dare to love across religious lines.
In her recent book, “Under a Saffron Sky: Inside India’s Crackdown on Love,” author Ismat Ara recounts the enormous stress and suffering that Hindu-Muslim couples experience. She draws attention to how the “love jihad” “myth” has come to “define an entire community.” In an interview with The Diplomat’s South Asia editor, Sudha Ramachandran, Ara pointed out that while an interfaith relationship is a private matter between two people, “within the ‘love jihad’ narrative, the Muslim man is reimagined as part of a larger, organized project to convert Hindu women, increase the Muslim population, and eventually alter the country’s demographic and religious character.”
What is “love jihad”?
“Love jihad” is the idea that Muslim men are deliberately targeting Hindu women for relationships and marriage in order to convert them to Islam, and that this is part of a larger organized conspiracy. It is an elaborate example of political myth-making and what happens when paranoia about “Muslim danger” enters the mass psyche.
While doing fieldwork for my recent book, “Under a Saffron Sky,” what interested me was not only whether individual cases of deception or coercion exist — they can, as they do in any relationship — but how these individual cases are transformed into evidence of a larger, vast conspiracy, one that comes to define an entire community. The leap from “a Muslim man deceiving a woman” to “Muslim men are conducting an organized campaign against Hindu women to take over this country” is the crucial political leap. When it becomes part of a larger conspiracy, the myth then becomes powerful enough to shape families, communities, police action, and even public policy, acquiring a life of its own, with its own set of myths.
There have been cases such as the 2023 Purola episode in Uttarakhand, where an alleged attempt to abduct a 14-year-old girl was quickly branded as “love jihad,” triggering communal protests and the exodus of Muslim families. The case later collapsed in court, with the girl and her uncle contradicting the initial police version. The minor also told the court that police had tutored her to make allegations against the accused, who were subsequently acquitted.
Could you share with us an example of what an interfaith couple undergoes when they are accused of “love jihad”?
Once people believe the myth of “love jihad,” real couples have to live with its consequences. One of the stories I reported from Uttar Pradesh is of a Hindu woman and a Muslim man who got married. After their nikah (wedding), when the couple went to the district magistrate’s office for their marriage registration, the man was shot in the head by two unidentified assailants right outside the government office in broad daylight. The couple wanted to register their marriage, make it official so no harm could touch them. But the woman saw her husband die before her eyes, minutes before that.
What made the story particularly chilling is the context. The couple had received warnings for weeks and months from local right-wing outfits and people opposed to the relationship and believed that once they had an official stamp from the government, no harm could touch their marriage. So, what began as a deeply personal decision, two people deciding to marry, gradually becomes something that others felt entitled to intervene in, threaten, and violently police.
In another example, from Gujarat, a state still scarred by the communal violence of 2002, a stamp vendor who had sold the couple their marriage stamps went on to call the woman’s family to inform them of their daughter’s “misdoings,” escalating the tension further.
In your book, you argue that “love jihad” is all about controlling women. Could you explain how?
One of the book’s main premises is that this is ultimately about controlling women, and that control operates across communities, although in very different ways. When a Hindu woman is told that she cannot choose her own partner because he belongs to another faith, her agency is being taken away. She is often treated as someone who has been deceived or brainwashed rather than as an adult capable of making a decision. But I also looked at Muslim women in the book. There is a case of a Muslim woman whose parents oppose her marriage because the man she has chosen was not just Hindu, but also belonged to a lower caste. The woman was told by her family that they might have considered a Hindu man — but only if he was upper caste. So, the policing of women’s choices isn’t confined to one community.
It’s an old story of women’s choices being made to represent the honor of an entire community, but what is distinctive about the “love jihad” campaign specifically is the way the Hindu woman has increasingly been made into a symbol, used as a tool, almost as the keeper of her entire community’s honor, purity, and demographic future. Her personal choices are seen as a collective threat. She is considered incapable of making her own decision, but in reality, her decision is powerful enough to threaten the demographic future of an entire community.
Article 21 of the Indian Constitution guarantees the right to life and personal liberty, which includes an individual’s freedom to choose whom they wish to marry. In reality, less than 3 percent of marriages in India are actually interfaith, so this has never been an easy choice. It has always meant navigating disapproving parents, nosy neighbors and hostile looks. But increasingly, crossing that boundary can also mean the police coming to your home. These single-digit marriages are framed as “dangerous” or as something that could alter India’s demography.
“Love jihad” is fundamentally a threat-based concept: it brings together anxieties around women, community honor and national security. But what about the real wars being fought by women? The opposite can be opportunity-based concepts, focusing on potential gains, growth, and positive outcomes rather than on “avoiding dangers or risks.” We must look at the basics that affect the majority of our country’s women, from the girl child being killed to girls not getting education or healthcare access.
Could you share with us how right-wing organizations mobilize and prevent interfaith marriages?
The “foot soldiers,” as well as organizations that work around “love jihad” cases, have multiple sources of information and multiple ways of mobilizing. Some maintain strong local networks; others are highly visible on the street, actively watching for such cases. In some places, they don’t even need to go looking. They have become such recognized “authorities” that people from neighboring areas approach them directly to report what they see as suspicious behavior, or word that a Muslim man is trying to “lure” a Hindu woman.
There are also rehabilitation programs aimed specifically at women, meant to remind them of their religious identity and, in the language of these organizations, to “correct” or undo the ideological influence they are believed to have absorbed from Muslim men. It is not one form of mobilization but many: surveillance, family pressure, public intervention, ideological programming, and street action. Together, they create an environment in which an interfaith relationship becomes something the wider community feels entitled to police.
The Special Marriage Act of 1954 was supposed to help interfaith couples marry. Why hasn’t it worked?
A law can create a legal route, but societal adoption of that route is equally important. The Special Marriage Act was meant to allow people of different faiths to marry without requiring either person to convert. But over the years, interfaith marriage has become increasingly politicized, particularly when it involves a Hindu woman and a Muslim man. The problem is that couples aren’t operating in a social vacuum. They have to navigate families, communities, local officials, and, increasingly now, political scrutiny. A legal provision cannot by itself remove the social stigma or the fear surrounding the choice. The Special Marriage Act exists, but the real question is whether people feel genuinely safe to use it. What do couples do when the law gives you a right, but the process through which you exercise that right can expose you to physical, mental, emotional and legal risks?
Allegations of “love jihad” are usually hurled at Muslim men marrying Hindu women. Are such allegations levelled against Muslim women marrying Hindu men?
Yes, there have been cases where Muslim women have faced similar allegations, particularly allegations that they were attempting to convert Hindu men through marriage. In Uttar Pradesh, for instance, there have been cases where criminal complaints under anti-conversion laws were filed against Muslim women and their male relatives, with families alleging that conversions were being orchestrated through the promise of marriage. In some cases, Muslim women have even been sent to custody in connection with such allegations. So, the idea of a Muslim woman being an agent of conversion is certainly present in some cases.
If religious conversions did not happen, would anxieties that fuel “love jihad” allegations reduce?
Conversion sits at the center of the “love jihad” narrative, but I don’t think its absence would make the deeper anxiety disappear. One thing that became clear to me while reporting these stories is that suspicion often exists even where no conversion has taken place at all. A Hindu woman simply being in a relationship with a Muslim man can be enough to trigger the allegation of “love jihad.” There has been no substantial body of cases establishing an organized “love jihad” conspiracy behind forced conversions. Individual cases of coercion or deception can occur, of course, and deserve to be investigated on their own merits, but that is a very different thing from proving a larger, organized conspiracy.
What happens, then, is that the political idea becomes much larger than the evidence behind it. I sometimes think of it like Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein’s monster: something that is created and then acquires a life of its own. The narrative begins to generate its own evidence. An interfaith relationship becomes suspicious because people have already been told what such a relationship means; the absence of conversion does not necessarily dispel the suspicion. So, conversion is important to the mythology, but it is not really the whole story. The deeper anxiety is about the crossing of community boundaries through intimacy and marriage. Who is allowed to love whom? What happens when a woman chooses a partner from another community? What religion will the children follow? Will the family retain its religious identity? And that is why I see “love jihad” as part of a larger politics of controlling women’s choices.
The policing of interfaith marriage exists across communities. Muslim women too can face enormous family and social pressure when they marry outside the community. But “love jihad” has given that anxiety a particularly powerful political vocabulary when the relationship is between a Hindu woman and a Muslim man.
The Christian Church in Kerala has also accused Muslims of “love jihad.” How similar is their campaign against interfaith marriage?
While there are similarities, there are also important differences. The similarity is in the underlying anxiety: the fear that women from one’s own religious community are being targeted by men from another community, and that such relationships could lead to conversion, loss of community identity, or demographic change. But the Christian discourse in Kerala has been more localized and has emerged from a very different social and political context, rooted largely in concerns within the Christian community about young women, interfaith relationships, and conversion.
The “love jihad” narrative in the wider Hindu nationalist discourse, on the other hand, has acquired a much larger political vocabulary. It has been linked not just to conversion and interfaith marriage, but also to concerns about demography, population growth, religious identity and, at times, national security. It has therefore travelled far beyond individual relationships and become part of a broader political narrative. These campaigns may emerge from different contexts, but they draw upon an older anxiety around women, sexuality and community boundaries.
So I would say the resemblance is real, but the scale, impact, context, and political consequences are different.
The Sangh Parivar’s “love jihad” campaign, you write, brings together several strands of its agenda, including national security. Could you explain?
The idea of “love jihad” draws together things that might otherwise seem unrelated: women’s sexuality, interfaith marriage, religious conversion, demography, Muslim identity, and national security. That is precisely what makes “love jihad” such a potent political idea in the larger Hindu nationalist discourse. An interfaith relationship begins as a private matter between two people, but within the “love jihad” narrative, the Muslim man is reimagined as part of a larger, organized project to convert Hindu women, increase the Muslim population, and eventually alter the country’s demographic and religious character.
There is a kind of escalation at work: first, the relationship is framed as a question of conversion; then conversion is linked to demography and Muslim population growth; and from there, the narrative is stretched to a much larger claim, a threat to the nation’s social and national fabric. That is where national security enters. Once an intimate relationship is recast as part of an organized threat, intervention starts to look like protection. Surveillance, police action, restrictions on marriage, mobilization against individual couples, even mob violence, all justified in the name of the larger public interest.

Assam Government Encroaches Into a World Heritage Site in India’s Northeast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
01:31:00 UTC
10:31:00 KST

Manas National Park in the northeast Indian state of Assam is in danger. The Assam government, which should be protecting this 1,176-acre World Heritage Site, has encroached on the park for several years.
Originally part of the North Kamrup Reserve Forest, the land under contention, which is spread over 9.3 sq km, was given on a 30-year lease to the Indian government for setting up a seed farm. After the lease expired in 2001, the area became part of the Manas National Park and Tiger Reserve, the Assam forest department said in a letter to the Bodoland Territorial Council (BTC) that governs this region.
In the letter, the Assam forest department pointed out that the BTC had leased the encroached land for cultivation. Sources claimed that local farmers are engaged in farming in the area, which is officially not permitted inside a wildlife sanctuary, national park or World Heritage Site. The letter made a case for its handover to the forest department. The forest department also urged the Assam government to convince the BTC to return the encroached area to the Assam forest department
The area that has been allegedly encroached by local farmers with the BTC’s consent is part of the Manas National Park’s core tiger and Bengal florican habitats. This falls in the Bhuyanpara Range of the park, which is also where the erstwhile government-owned Kokilabari Seed Farm was located.
Concerned about the encroachment and its devastating impact on the park, the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) has also been reminding the Assam government to initiate action over the past few years.
In a communique dated July 30, 2026, which was also posted on social media, the NTCA asked the chief secretary of the Assam government to “intervene” and facilitate the “handing over” of the encroached area to the Manas Tiger Reserve authorities. It also reminded the government that a directive on the issue had been sent on June 11, but the authority was “not aware about the progress made in the matter so far.”
Manas National Park was designated as a reserve forest in 1907 and declared a wildlife sanctuary in 1928. In 1973, it became India’s first tiger reserve. Spread across an area of 2,837 sq km, the park was the largest in the country. In 2004, the park secured another feather in its cap when BirdLife International, a global partnership of bird conservation organizations, identified it as an Important Bird Area. UNESCO named it a World Heritage Site in 1985. “Manas has exceptional importance within the Indian sub-continent’s protected areas, as one of the most significant remaining natural areas in the region, where sizeable populations of a large number of threatened species continue to survive,” UNESCO observed.
Manas faced several challenges in the 1980s and 1990s. It was adversely impacted by the powerful insurgency that swept Assam in the late 1980s. With a large area of the park becoming a no-go zone for officials, environmental activists and tourists, conservation efforts suffered a big blow.
Poaching of the one-horned rhino also grew in this period. The number of rhinos reportedly dwindled from around 100 in the late 1980s to zero by the time peace returned to the region in the mid-2000s. Wildlife researcher Anwaruddin Choudhury estimated in 1996 that over 80 percent of the park’s large mammals had also been decimated. In 1992, UNESCO’s World Heritage Convention declared that Manas was “in danger.”
A former official of the forest department told The Diplomat that Assam’s Bharatiya Janata Party-led government was apprehensive of a “backlash” from the BTC if the encroachment is cleared from the park. The Bodoland People’s Front (BPF), which rules the council, is also an ally in the BJP-led coalition government in Assam.
Meanwhile, the Gauhati High Court has issued orders to the Assam government and the BTC to prevent further encroachment in the park after activist Rohit Choudhury filed a Public Interest Litigation (PIL).
The encroachment of national parks lays bare the lackadaisical approach of the Assam government towards the conservation of forests and wildlife in the country. The government evicted illegal settlers from the World Heritage Site of Kaziranga National Park, also in Assam, in 2016, only after the Gauhati High Court intervened and issued orders.

How Hong Kong is trying a new solution to its land value problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28

Advertisement
Opinion
How Hong Kong is trying a new solution to its land value problem
After decades of lucrative land sales, can the city finally build a system in which the land itself creates economic value?
3-MIN READ3-MIN
1
 Listen
Dr Ken Ip is an assistant professor specialising in business innovation and entrepreneurship at Saint Francis University, Hong Kong. 
When Hong Kong’s first chief executive, Tung Chee-hwa, announced his housing plan in 1997, the ambition was extraordinary. The government would produce at least 85,000 flats a year across the public and private sectors, and raise the home ownership rate to 70 per cent. The idea was simple. Build more homes, make housing more affordable and allow more families to own a piece of Hong Kong. Then history intervened.
The Asian financial crisis struck. Property prices collapsed. The economy weakened. The 85,000-flat target quickly became politically toxic, and the government retreated. Nearly three decades later, Hong Kong is still wrestling with the same dilemma: how much land can the government release without destabilising the value of the land already in the system? That is the uncomfortable question behind the Northern Metropolis today.
Rising land and property values can generate government revenue and household wealth, but they also make it harder for younger generations to enter the housing market. Hong Kong took this model to an extreme.

To live with joy, a person’s attention needs to be open and free. When it is open and free, it…
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
01:23:00 UTC
10:23:00 KST

To live with joy, a person’s attention needs to be open and free. When it is open and free, it becomes possible to see need and how it must be addressed, and it is by meeting need that joy is created. Conversely, attachment to particular intentions limits the range of attention, causing need to be ignored, which then produces suffering.
The experience of suffering is an indicator that attachment is present, and liberation from suffering is possible only by releasing attachment. Attachment is released through the awareness developed from open and free attention to experience, but it is attachment itself that causes attention to become limited and narrow.
The only feasible solution to this problem is to make a conscious effort to loosen attention until the awareness is developed to keep it loose. But loosening attention from the objects of attachment first requires the ability to loosen it in general. It is necessary to develop the skill of letting go of the many thoughts, feelings, memories, ideas, and so on that arise throughout ordinary life.

'Use lowest effective dose of Nsaids': Fresh advisory on kidney risks of painkiller abuse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-28
00:54:39 UTC
09:54:39 KST

Health Ministry warns against misuse of painkillers, antibiotics over kidney disease risk.
NEW DELHI: Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) has issued a fresh advisory on rational consumption of painkillers and antibiotics, in view of their repeated use, without proper medical advice, putting people at the risk of kidney complications and other adverse effects.The drug regulator's circular says non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (Nsaids) and antibiotics are prescription medicines under Drugs and Cosmetics Rules and should be used only when clinically indicated, at the appropriate dose and duration and under medical supervision. It has asked people not to take Nsaids, commonly used as painkillers, repeatedly or for a prolonged period without advice.
Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation has also cautioned against self-medication with antibiotics and advised people with existing kidney disease or other risk factors for renal impairment to inform their doctor before taking Nsaids.Prof Sandeep Mahajan, nephrologist at AIIMS, said unregulated and prolonged use of painkillers can accelerate the decline in kidney function. "All prescription medicines should be taken under the supervision of a qualified physician, with the prescribed dose and duration strictly followed."CDSCO has advised doctors to use the lowest effective dose of Nsaids for the shortest appropriate duration, with extra caution in patients at risk of kidney injury. This comes against the backdrop of a substantial chronic kidney disease burden in India. A 2025 review of community-based studies estimated pooled chronic kidney disease prevalence at 13.24%, although estimates varied widely across regions and studies.
